RIDGELINE MOTORS OF CALDER VALLEY
NEW ASSOCIATE ONBOARDING CHECKLIST AND REFERENCE MANUAL

Prepared by: Ines Lindqvist, Human Resources Coordinator
Reviewed and approved by: Zoltan Sorensen, General Manager
Issued to: Aiden Bergstrom, Sales Associate (full-time, new hire)
Effective date: Monday, 14 April
Document control: Onboarding Manual, Revision 12. All associates acknowledge receipt of the current revision on their first day; superseded revisions must be returned to Human Resources for shredding. If any statement in this manual appears to conflict with a directive from the General Manager, the directive governs, and the discrepancy should be reported to Ines Lindqvist the same week so the manual can be corrected.

SECTION 1. PURPOSE AND SCOPE

This manual exists to make your first ninety days at Ridgeline Motors orderly, consistent, and free of guesswork. It consolidates the onboarding checklist, the product knowledge syllabus, the desk procedures for keys and inventory, the working rules of the sales floor, the finance and insurance (F&I) basics every associate must understand before quoting money, the service lane orientation, and the compliance obligations that attach to every customer transaction at a licensed dealership in this state. It is deliberately long. Zoltan Sorensen has directed that no associate should have to rely on hallway folklore to learn how this store operates; folklore, he notes, is what stores rely on when their manuals are out of date, and our manuals are not out of date. Read the whole document once during your first week. During weeks two through thirteen, return to individual sections as your trainer assigns them. Bring your questions to Mateo Mensah, Sales Manager, who owns the training calendar, or to Ines Lindqvist for anything touching payroll, benefits, or personnel records.

The scope of this manual is the sales department. Technicians, detailers, and parts counter staff follow separate manuals maintained by their own supervisors, although Section 9 of this document provides a service lane orientation for sales associates, because customers will ask you service questions in the showroom whether or not you are qualified to answer them, and it is better for everyone that you know which questions to route to Esi Sorensen, our lead service advisor, rather than guessing.

SECTION 2. WHAT THIS STORE SELLS, AND TO WHOM

Ridgeline Motors is a full-line new and pre-owned dealership. Our new-vehicle franchise covers the Ridgeline brand: sedans, crossovers, sport utility vehicles, and a working line of half-ton and three-quarter-ton pickups, plus the electric model introduced two model years ago. Our pre-owned inventory runs from late-model lease returns to trade-ins of every age. Our customer base is the Calder Valley trade area: farms, contractors, two school districts, the hospital, and the professional households of the river towns. Roughly two-thirds of our volume is repeat or referral business. That statistic is repeated at every Monday meeting because it explains most of the rules in this manual: our business depends on people coming back, and people come back when the process is clean, honest, and boring in the best sense of the word. Nothing in this manual is designed to make a sale today at the cost of a customer tomorrow.

SECTION 3. DAY ONE CHECKLIST

Your first day is administrative and orientation only. You will not sell a car on your first day, and you should not try. Report to the HR office on the second floor at 8:30 a.m. Ines Lindqvist will walk you through the following items in order, initialing each line as it is completed. Keep your copy; several later items reference it.

3.1 Identity and eligibility verification. Present original documents establishing identity and work authorization. Photocopies cannot be accepted, and photographs on a phone cannot be accepted, no matter how clear.

3.2 Personnel file. Emergency contact, tax withholding forms, and direct deposit details. Direct deposit takes one to two pay cycles to activate; your first check, if paper, will be handed to you by Ines rather than mailed, so that nothing is lost to a wrong address.

3.3 Offer letter and pay plan. Your offer letter states your base draw, your commission schedule, and the spiff programs currently in effect. The commission schedule is summarized in Appendix C. Sign only the copy Ines provides; drafts circulated by anyone else have no standing.

3.4 Handbook acknowledgment. The general employee handbook covers conduct, attendance, and grievance procedures. This onboarding manual covers the sales floor. You sign for both, separately, because they are separate documents.

3.5 Systems access. Your user account for the dealership management system (DMS), the customer relationship manager (CRM), and the inventory pricing tool will be created on day one. Temporary passwords expire after the first login; if your account locks, call the help desk, do not ask a colleague to log in for you, and never work under another associate's login. Every deal you touch must be traceable to you.

3.6 Keys, badge, and locker. You will be issued an associate badge, which opens the staff entrance after hours, and a locker in the sales bullpen. The badge is property of the store; report a lost badge to Ines the same day. There is a replacement charge only if the badge is lost twice in one year.

3.7 Safety orientation. Fire exits, extinguisher locations, the spill kit in the detail bay, and the severe weather muster point at the interior wall of the service reception. This item takes twenty minutes and Ines will not rush it.

3.8 Lunch with Zoltan Sorensen. The General Manager takes every new associate to lunch on day one. It is not an interview and nothing you say over lunch goes in your file. Its purpose is simple: he wants every associate to be able to recognize him in the lot, and he wants to hear, in your words, why you took the job.

SECTION 4. WEEK ONE: THE FLOOR, THE DESK, AND THE KEYS

Week one is spent shadowing. You will be assigned to a senior associate each morning by Mateo Mensah and you will follow one customer interaction per day from greeting to close, or from greeting to a scheduled return, which is often the better outcome. In the afternoons you return to the classroom modules in Section 5. By Friday of week one you should be able to do the following without prompting: greet a walk-in within the standard described below, pull up a unit in the DMS, locate its key, walk the customer to the unit, and describe its equipment honestly — which sometimes means saying "I don't know; let me check," a sentence that costs nothing and is always available to you.

4.1 The greeting standard. Every customer entering the showroom or the lot is greeted within thirty seconds of arrival, by name if known, by eye contact and a hello if not. The greeting is a greeting. It is not an interrogation. Ask what brought them in; do not ask how they will be paying. Customers who want to browse alone should be told, truthfully, that you will be at the desk if anything comes up, and then you must actually be at the desk where you said you would be.

4.2 Key control. This is the rule the General Manager checks personally, so read this paragraph twice. All keys stay with the desk at all times. There are no exceptions for favorites, for units you are personally selling, for the EV demonstrator, or for the truck you think someone is about to come back for. Keys hang on the control board behind the sales desk, each on a numbered tag matching the stock number of the unit. To take a key, you sign it out on the clipboard with the stock number, your initials, and the time; you sign it back in the same way. Keys go back on the board the moment a customer leaves, not at the end of your shift, and never in a pocket, never in a drawer, and never taken home. If a customer is handed a key for a test drive, the associate conducting the drive holds the key for the entire drive; it does not go to the customer's pocket even for the leg of the drive the customer drives. Losing a key for a unit on the floor is a writeable incident because it strands a saleable vehicle behind the glass with no way to start it. Pre-owned units in the back lot keep their keys in the lockbox cabinet; the cabinet is emptied into the board each morning by the opening manager and returned at close.

4.3 The lot walk. Each morning at 8:50, the floor team walks the entire lot, front and back, before the doors open at 9:00. The walk checks four things: every unit is locked; every window sticker is present and legible; every unit is parked within its lined space with no overhang into the drive lanes; and any unit with body damage, flat tires, or missing equipment is flagged with a red card on the windshield and logged in the damage book at the desk. The lot walk takes fifteen minutes when done properly and forty minutes when done after the first customer arrives, which is why it is done before.

4.4 Showroom conduct. Coffee station restocked before open. Demo units inside polished, windows clean, trunks closed, and placards straight. Personal calls on the floor are taken outside or at the bullpen, not in the showroom, and never while a customer is within sight of you. The showroom telephone is answered by whoever is nearest when it rings, on the second ring at the latest, with "Ridgeline Motors, this is" and your first name.

SECTION 5. PRODUCT KNOWLEDGE SYLLABUS

You cannot sell what you cannot describe, and you will be tested. Module tests are administered by Mateo Mensah at the end of weeks one, three, and six. A score of eighty percent is passing; a lower score means you retake the module after a review session, and there is no penalty for a retake other than the time it takes.

Module 1 (week 1): The sedan line. Engines, trim ladder, standard versus optional equipment, and the three most common misconceptions customers arrive with, which are, in order of frequency: that the base trim has heated seats (it does not), that the hybrid sedan requires a plug (it does not; it self-charges), and that the top trim is required to get the safety package (it is not; the safety package is optional on every trim).

Module 2 (week 3): Crossovers and SUVs. Seating configurations, towing differences between the two- and three-row models, cargo measurements, and the family buyer's questions, which are almost always about the second row: does it fold flat, does it recline, does a rear-facing infant seat fit behind a six-foot driver. You will be expected to demonstrate the second-row fold in under thirty seconds and to install a display infant seat correctly. If you have never installed one, say so in training; this is exactly what training is for.

Module 3 (week 3): Pickups. Payload versus towing, the trailer brake controller, bed lengths, and the trade customer's calendar. Contractors buy on schedules, not on mood; the associate who understands that a crew cab with a short bed is a different tool than a regular cab with a long bed will earn the contractor's repeat business for a decade.

Module 4 (week 6): The electric model and the Level 2 charger program. Range figures and what they do and do not promise, home charging assessment, the federal and state incentive paperwork we assist with at the F&I desk, and the cold-weather range conversation, which must be honest. On the EV, honesty is a compliance matter as much as a sales matter: range claims in our advertising are manufacturer figures, and our obligation is to present them as manufacturer figures, not as promises made by this store.

Module 5 (week 6): Pre-owned certification. Which pre-owned units qualify for the certified program, the inspection the certification requires, the warranty terms, and, critically, what certification does not include. A certified unit is not a new unit. Its warranty is the certified program's warranty, and its coverage periods are printed in the buyer's guide on the window. Know where to point on the buyer's guide; never paraphrase warranty terms from memory during a sale.

SECTION 6. TRADE-INS AND APPRAISALS

The trade-in is where more customer trust is won or lost than anywhere else in the deal, because it is where the customer's emotions are highest and where the numbers are least understood. Ridgeline Motors appraises every trade honestly, in writing, whether or not the customer buys from us.

6.1 The intake. The customer's unit is walked with the customer present. You record mileage, equipment, tires, glass, body condition, interior condition, and service history the customer can recall. You do not appraise. Appraisal is performed by Mateo Mensah or by the pre-owned buyer using the store's subscription pricing tools, the auction terminal, and their own eyes on the unit. Your job on intake is to document accurately, because the written appraisal is only as good as the intake sheet behind it.

6.2 The written appraisal. Every appraisal is written, on the appraisal form, showing comparable market values and the adjustment for condition and reconditioning cost. The appraisal is presented to the customer by the associate with the manager available for questions. The customer keeps a copy whether they buy or not.

6.3 Negative equity. When a trade-in is worth less than the payoff owed on it, the difference between the appraised value and the payoff is negative equity. This is common, it is not a reflection on the customer, and it must never be described as though it were. Under our standard practice the difference is added to the amount financed at signing, so the customer finances the shortfall together with the new vehicle's balance rather than paying it out of pocket at the desk. The F&I manager, Wanjiru Kaur, will present the exact numbers. Associates do not improvise payment quotes on negative equity deals; the arithmetic belongs to the desk, because a wrong payment quote spoken in the showroom is a promise this store will be asked to keep.

6.4 Payoff quotes. A payoff quote is lender-specific and has an expiration date, usually ten days. A payoff quote older than its good-through date is not a payoff figure; it is a memory of one. Reconfirm payoffs older than their good-through date with the lender before drawing final paperwork, without exception, even when the customer insists the number has not changed, because the customer is sometimes wrong in a direction that costs them money.

SECTION 7. DEMONSTRATIONS AND ROAD TESTS

7.1 Licensing. No road test leaves the lot unless the customer presents a valid driver's license and the associate records the license number on the road test form. No license, no drive; a learner's permit without a licensed adult passenger is not a valid license for this purpose. This rule has no exception for the customer's spouse, for the customer who "always drives with an expired one and it's fine," or for anyone in a hurry.

7.2 Route. The standard road test route is posted at the desk: out the north exit, two laps of the park loop, and the merge onto Route 9 and back. The route takes twenty minutes and includes a hill, a rough patch of pavement for suspension feel, and a merge. Customers who ask to drive farther may, within reason and with the associate's judgment, but every road test returns to the lot before any paperwork is discussed. Driving a customer's trade as part of the appraisal follows the same route.

7.3 Insurance. The customer's own policy covers them on our plates under the standard garage endorsement for demonstration purposes; associates are additionally covered under the store's policy while riding along. If a customer states their license is suspended or revoked, do not proceed with any road test, and note the conversation in the CRM.

7.4 Accidents on road tests. Stop, check for injuries, call emergency services if anyone is hurt or if any other vehicle is involved, exchange information, and call the dealership immediately. Do not admit fault, do not discuss fault with anyone at the scene, and do not continue the demonstration after any collision, however minor. The sales manager comes to the scene. This is a rule about you as much as about the store: associates have been injured standing on the shoulder of Route 9 deciding to "just head back." Do not.

SECTION 8. WORKING THE F&I DESK

Wanjiru Kaur, Finance and Insurance Manager, owns every number that becomes a payment. Week five of your onboarding includes two full days sitting at the F&I desk as an observer. The purpose is not to train you to quote money — you will not — but so that you understand what happens to your deal after the customer says yes, and can therefore describe the process honestly and calmly to a nervous buyer.

8.1 What you may quote. You may discuss prices as marked, current advertised offers with their expiration dates, and the general structure of the process. You may not quote payments, APRs, term options, or monthly figures of any kind. The sentence to memorize is: "The exact numbers are prepared by our finance manager, and here is how that works." Every associate, however senior, defers payments to the desk. This is not a limitation on you; it is the store's promise to the customer that every payment figure they hear is prepared on the same calculator by the same accountable person.

8.2 Products presented at the desk. The F&I desk presents, where applicable and lawful: retail installment terms through our lending partners, the manufacturer's finance offers, service contracts, guaranteed asset protection (GAP) coverage on financed deals, and tire and wheel protection. Every product is presented with its price and its contract terms in writing; no product is described as "required" unless it is required by law or by the lender's condition, and the state regulator's wording on this point is in the compliance binder, which any customer may ask to see and which must be produced on request.

8.3 Spot delivery. When a customer signs the retail contract and takes the vehicle home the same day while the lender's final approval is still pending, the transaction is a spot delivery. Spot deliveries are lawful, common, and disclosed: the buyer's order states that the sale is contingent on assignment of the retail contract to a lender on the terms disclosed, and that if final terms cannot be assigned on the disclosed terms, the store will offer the customer terms as close as practicable or unwind the transaction and return the trade and down payment. Understand the definition before you observe the desk, because customers will ask you what "contingent" means while sitting in the F&I waiting area, and the honest one-sentence answer is that final approval can still take a day or two after the customer signs, which is why the paperwork says what it says. If a spot delivery cannot be assigned on the disclosed terms, Wanjiru calls the customer — the associate who sold the unit is welcome to join the call and often should, but the terms conversation belongs to the desk.

8.4 Money handling. Associates do not take cash deposits, do not hold checks, and do not accept payment cards on the floor. All money moves through the F&I office with a written receipt given at the moment of receipt. A customer who insists on handing you a deposit at the showroom table is walked to the F&I office, pleasantly, every time.

SECTION 9. THE SERVICE LANE ORIENTATION

Week four includes a half-day orientation with Esi Sorensen, lead service advisor. The purpose, again, is triage rather than expertise. You should come away able to do four things: book a service appointment at the advisor's counter; explain the difference between the express maintenance lane and a scheduled repair; hand a customer to Esi or her team by name; and recognize the three questions that must always go to the service department rather than being answered from the sales floor: anything about warranty coverage of a specific failure, anything about a repair charge estimate, and anything about a recall notice the customer received in the mail. You may confirm that a recall notice exists in the system; you may not characterize its scope or severity. Recall work is performed by the service department on the manufacturer's terms, and the associate who "helps" by paraphrasing a recall letter on the showroom floor is creating a commitment the service department did not make.

The service lane also matters to you commercially. Every oil change customer in the express lane is a future buyer of something. The associates who do best at this store long-term are the ones the service lane trusts, and the service lane trusts associates who tell customers the truth about what the service department does and does not do. Esi's standing offer to every new associate is a seat at her counter any morning it is slow, and her standing warning is that it is never slow on Saturdays.

SECTION 10. CUSTOMER FOLLOW-UP AND CRM

The CRM is the store's institutional memory. If it is not in the CRM, it did not happen, and if it is in the CRM, it belongs to the store, which is why the manual is explicit about what gets recorded.

10.1 Recording. Every customer contact is logged the day it occurs: walk-ins, calls, texts with the customer's consent noted, e-mails, road tests, appraisals, and no-shows for scheduled appointments. Log the substance in two sentences. Logs are read by your colleagues covering your days off, and the test of a good log entry is whether your colleague can serve the customer tomorrow from your entry alone.

10.2 Follow-up after a sale. The delivery of a vehicle is the beginning of the follow-up calendar, not the end of the deal. Within two business days of delivery, the selling associate must complete the following actions and log each one in the CRM under the delivery record: place and log the thank-you call to the customer, confirming that the vehicle is performing as expected and that the customer knows who to call if anything is not; confirm that the customer has registered on the owner's portal and, if not, walk them through registration while you have them on the phone; schedule the first service reminder in the CRM so that the system generates the maintenance reminder for the customer's first service interval; and send the post-delivery satisfaction survey link. The survey link goes out in the same two-business-day window, not later, because response rates fall sharply once the newness of the vehicle wears off. Later actions sit on their own schedule: the thirty-day check-in call, the sixty-day courtesy contact, and the annual needs review, each generated by the CRM and each requiring the associate to record an outcome, including the outcome "customer asked not to be contacted," which must be honored immediately and logged verbatim.

10.3 Unsold customers. A customer who leaves without purchasing is logged with the reason, the units of interest, and the agreed next contact date. The next contact is made on the date agreed, not earlier, because "I said Friday and he called Wednesday" is the single most common complaint in any follow-up file, and it is entirely preventable.

10.4 Do-not-contact. Any customer request to stop contact is honored across all channels within one business day of the request, and the flag is never removed without written direction from Zoltan Sorensen. This rule has no exception for a customer who "only meant the texts."

SECTION 11. COMPLIANCE BASICS FOR THE SALES FLOOR

Compliance at a dealership is not a department; it is a set of habits on the floor. The habits you must build in your first ninety days are these.

11.1 Truth in advertising. Advertised prices include all dealer-added equipment already on the unit and disclose rebates that require specific qualifications. When a customer asks about an advertised price, produce the advertisement and read it together rather than paraphrasing it. If the customer does not qualify for a qualification-based rebate, say which qualification they do not meet, and let Wanjiru's desk do the rest.

11.2 Buyer's guide on used units. Every pre-owned unit displays the federal buyer's guide stating whether it is sold as-is or with a warranty, and what the warranty covers. The buyer's guide that is on the window at the time of sale is the buyer's guide that goes into the deal jacket. If the window card is missing or defaced at the time of sale, stop the deal and get a replacement printed; do not proceed and fix it later, because there is no later for a disclosure that was never made.

11.3 Licensing and titling. Title applications, lien recording, and temporary plates are handled by the title clerk. Associates never tell a customer that a title will "take about a week" unless the title clerk has said so for that transaction; the honest answer is "our title clerk handles this and will call you with the exact date," followed by making sure the title clerk actually calls.

11.4 Equal treatment. Every customer receives the same process, the same product presentations, the same pricing transparency, and the same follow-up, without regard to any protected characteristic, and without regard to any assumption about who is the decision-maker in a couple or a group. Ask who will be the registered owner; never assume it from who spoke first.

11.5 Prompt reporting. Suspected odometer discrepancies, flood-damaged trade-ins presented as clean, or any customer statement suggesting title fraud go to Zoltan Sorensen the same day, in writing, even if you are not sure. Uncertainty is a reason to report; it is not a reason to wait.

SECTION 12. HOURS, PAY, AND ATTENDANCE

Showroom hours are 9:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Monday through Saturday, closed Sunday. Sales floor schedules are published two weeks ahead by Mateo Mensah. Weekend coverage is a condition of the sales role; the standard floor week includes every other Saturday. Your pay plan is summarized in Appendix C and consists of a weekly draw against commissions, with commission computed on delivered units per the schedule, and manufacturer spiffs paid when the manufacturer pays them, which can lag a cycle. Attendance: call Mateo by 7:30 a.m. for a same-day absence. Three unlogged absences in ninety days triggers a review under the handbook, not this manual. PTO is requested in the HR system; PTO during the last three days of a month, which is our delivery peak, requires the General Manager's approval, and he grants it more often than people assume, but he cannot grant what he is not asked for.

SECTION 13. FIRST-NINETY-DAY MILESTONES

Day 30: modules 1 and 2 passed; ten logged customer interactions; lot walk certified by the opening manager. Day 60: modules 3 and 4 passed; one supervised deal delivered start to finish; service lane orientation completed. Day 90: all modules passed; two deals delivered with the trainer observing rather than assisting; F&I observation days completed; ninety-day review with Zoltan Sorensen and Mateo Mensah, which is a conversation, not an examination, and which begins with the question the General Manager asks everyone at ninety days: "What in this manual turned out to be wrong?" He asks because it is how the manual gets its next revision, and Revision 13 will be written, in part, from your answer.

APPENDIX A. DOCUMENTARY FEES AND STANDARD CHARGES (CURRENT)
Documentation fee: $225 per retail transaction, itemized on the buyer's order. Title and registration: passed through at cost, itemized. Temporary plate: $12. Dealer-installed accessories: at the marked price on the buyer's order, never bundled silently into the vehicle price. Miscellaneous shop supplies, where incurred on a serviced unit: itemized per the service menu. There is no charge for the first owner's portal registration, the first remote battery replacement, or coffee, ever, and any customer told otherwise should be introduced to Ines Lindqvist personally.

APPENDIX B. NEW MODEL LINEUP SNAPSHOT (TRAINING COPY)
Base sedan, 4 cyl, 8-speed automatic; Hybrid sedan, self-charging, no plug; Premium sedan, turbo 4, optional safety package; Crossover S, 2-row, 5-passenger; Crossover L, 3-row, 7-passenger, optional tow package; Sport utility, body-on-frame, standard tow rating per brochure in deal jacket; Half-ton pickup, three cab styles, two bed lengths; Three-quarter-ton pickup, crew cab only this model year, diesel optional; Electric crossover, single motor standard, dual motor optional, home charger assessment through the F&I desk. Fuel economy figures on this snapshot are the manufacturer's and are quoted from the window sticker, never from this appendix, which is a training copy and expires when the model year does.

APPENDIX C. PAY PLAN SUMMARY (SUMMARY ONLY; THE OFFER LETTER GOVERNS)
Weekly draw against commission, drawn amount recovered from earned commission per the offer letter schedule. Commission schedule per delivered unit: new vehicles per the published grid by model line; pre-owned per the front-end gross grid; certified units carry the certified increment. Manufacturer spiffs are additional and paid on manufacturer timing. No commission is earned on a deal that unwinds, and no associate is penalized for a deal that is walked away from honestly — the store's position, stated by the General Manager at hire, is that a clean lost sale is a future customer and a dirty won one is a former one.

APPENDIX D. FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS FROM NEW ASSOCIATES
"Can I park in the customer lot?" No; the staff lot is behind the pre-owned row.
"What if I know the answer to a payment question?" You still defer to the desk. The rule is about accountability, not ability.
"Can I take a demo home overnight?" Demonstration assignments are made by Zoltan Sorensen in writing only, after ninety days, and never to associates still in draw recovery.
"Who do I call if the alarm goes off when I'm closing?" The list is at the desk; you call the manager on duty first, non-emergency line second, and you stay on the property only if it is safe to do so.
"Do I have to log the rude customer?" You log the facts of the interaction, not your assessment of the person's character, and you take the incident to Mateo if it involved threats, discrimination, or anyone feeling unsafe.
"What does 'contingent' mean on the buyer's order?" It means what Section 8.3 says it means, and Section 8.3 is the answer you give.

APPENDIX E. GLOSSARY (SELECTION)
Buyer's order: the purchase agreement itemizing vehicle, price, trade, and fees. Buyer's guide: the federal window disclosure on pre-owned units. DMS: dealership management system. CRM: customer relationship manager. Draw: advance against earned commission. F&I: finance and insurance. GAP: guaranteed asset protection coverage on financed deals. Payoff: amount owed on an existing loan, valid through its good-through date. Spot delivery: see Section 8.3. Unwind: reversal of a delivered transaction, returning all parties to their prior positions.

End of manual. Acknowledge receipt to Ines Lindqvist. Questions on content to Mateo Mensah; questions on personnel matters to Ines Lindqvist; anything the manual does not cover, to Zoltan Sorensen, whose door is genuinely open, which you may verify on day one at lunch.

question.instruction: According to Section 8.3, a "spot delivery" means the customer takes the vehicle home before the lender's final approval is complete: is that an accurate reading?

notes: Section 8.3 defines spot delivery as signing and taking the vehicle while final lender approval is still pending, disclosed on the buyer's order.

Your first day is administrative and orientation only. You will not sell a car on your first day, and you should not try. 3.1 Identity and eligibility verification. Present original documents establishing identity and work authorization. Photocopies cannot be accepted, and photographs on a phone cannot be accepted, no matter how clear.

3.3 Offer letter and pay plan. Your offer letter states your base draw, your commission schedule, and the spiff programs currently in effect. The commission schedule is summarized in Appendix C. Sign only the copy Ines provides; drafts circulated by anyone else have no standing.

3.4 Handbook acknowledgment. The general employee handbook covers conduct, attendance, and grievance procedures. This onboarding manual covers the sales floor. You sign for both, separately, because they are separate documents.

Week one is spent shadowing. You will be assigned to a senior associate each morning by Mateo Mensah and you will follow one customer interaction per day from greeting to close, or from greeting to a scheduled return, which is often the better outcome. In the afternoons you return to the classroom modules in Section 5. By Friday of week one you should be able to do the following without prompting: greet a walk-in within the standard described below, pull up a unit in the DMS, locate its key, walk the customer to the unit, and describe its equipment honestly — which sometimes means saying "I don't know; let me check," a sentence that costs nothing and is always available to you.

4.1 The greeting standard. Every customer entering the showroom or the lot is greeted within thirty seconds of arrival, by name if known, by eye contact and a hello if not. Customers who want to browse alone should be told, truthfully, that you will be at the desk if anything comes up, and then you must actually be at the desk where you said you would be.

Pre-owned units in the back lot keep their keys in the lockbox cabinet; the cabinet is emptied into the board each morning by the opening manager and returned at close.

The lot walk takes fifteen minutes when done properly and forty minutes when done after the first customer arrives, which is why it is done before.

Personal calls on the floor are taken outside or at the bullpen, not in the showroom, and never while a customer is within sight of you. The showroom telephone is answered by whoever is nearest when it rings, on the second ring at the latest, with "Ridgeline Motors, this is" and your first name.

Range figures and what they do and do not promise, home charging assessment, the federal and state incentive paperwork we assist with at the F&I desk, and the cold-weather range conversation, which must be honest. On the EV, honesty is a compliance matter as much as a sales matter: range claims in our advertising are manufacturer figures, and our obligation is to present them as manufacturer figures, not as promises made by this store.

Module 5 (week 6): Pre-owned certification. Which pre-owned units qualify for the certified program, the inspection the certification requires, the warranty terms, and, critically, what certification does not include. A certified unit is not a new unit. Its warranty is the certified program's warranty, and its coverage periods are printed in the buyer's guide on the window. Know where to point on the buyer's guide; never paraphrase warranty terms from memory during a sale.

SECTION 6. TRADE-INS AND APPRAISALS

The trade-in is where more customer trust is won or lost than anywhere else in the deal, because it is where the customer's emotions are highest and where the numbers are least understood. Ridgeline Motors appraises every trade honestly, in writing, whether or not the customer buys from us.

6.1 The intake. The customer's unit is walked with the customer present. You record mileage, equipment, tires, glass, body condition, interior condition, and service history the customer can recall. You do not appraise. Appraisal is performed by Mateo Mensah or by the pre-owned buyer using the store's subscription pricing tools, the auction terminal, and their own eyes on the unit. Your job on intake is to document accurately, because the written appraisal is only as good as the intake sheet behind it.

6.2 The written appraisal. Every appraisal is written, on the appraisal form, showing comparable market values and the adjustment for condition and reconditioning cost. The appraisal is presented to the customer by the associate with the manager available for questions. The customer keeps a copy whether they buy or not.

6.3 Negative equity. When a trade-in is worth less than the payoff owed on it, the difference between the appraised value and the payoff is negative equity. This is common, it is not a reflection on the customer, and it must never be described as though it were. Under our standard practice the difference is added to the amount financed at signing, so the customer finances the shortfall together with the new vehicle's balance rather than paying it out of pocket at the desk. The F&I manager, Wanjiru Kaur, will present the exact numbers. Associates do not improvise payment quotes on negative equity deals; the arithmetic belongs to the desk, because a wrong payment quote spoken in the showroom is a promise this store will be asked to keep.

6.4 Payoff quotes. A payoff quote is lender-specific and has an expiration date, usually ten days. A payoff quote older than its good-through date is not a payoff figure; it is a memory of one. Reconfirm payoffs older than their good-through date with the lender before drawing final paperwork, without exception, even when the customer insists the number has not changed, because the customer is sometimes wrong in a direction that costs them money.

SECTION 7. DEMONSTRATIONS AND ROAD TESTS

7.1 Licensing. No road test leaves the lot unless the customer presents a valid driver's license and the associate records the license number on the road test form. No license, no drive; a learner's permit without a licensed adult passenger is not a valid license for this purpose. This rule has no exception for the customer's spouse, for the customer who "always drives with an expired one and it's fine," or for anyone in a hurry.

7.2 Route. The standard road test route is posted at the desk: out the north exit, two laps of the park loop, and the merge onto Route 9 and back. The route takes twenty minutes and includes a hill, a rough patch of pavement for suspension feel, and a merge. Customers who ask to drive farther may, within reason and with the associate's judgment, but every road test returns to the lot before any paperwork is discussed. Driving a customer's trade as part of the appraisal follows the same route.

7.3 Insurance. The customer's own policy covers them on our plates under the standard garage endorsement for demonstration purposes; associates are additionally covered under the store's policy while riding along. If a customer states their license is suspended or revoked, do not proceed with any road test, and note the conversation in the CRM.

7.4 Accidents on road tests. Stop, check for injuries, call emergency services if anyone is hurt or if any other vehicle is involved, exchange information, and call the dealership immediately. Do not admit fault, do not discuss fault with anyone at the scene, and do not continue the demonstration after any collision, however minor. The sales manager comes to the scene. This is a rule about you as much as about the store: associates have been injured standing on the shoulder of Route 9 deciding to "just head back." Do not.

SECTION 8. WORKING THE F&I DESK

Wanjiru Kaur, Finance and Insurance Manager, owns every number that becomes a payment. Week five of your onboarding includes two full days sitting at the F&I desk as an observer. The purpose is not to train you to quote money — you will not — but so that you understand what happens to your deal after the customer says yes, and can therefore describe the process honestly and calmly to a nervous buyer.

8.1 What you may quote. You may discuss prices as marked, current advertised offers with their expiration dates, and the general structure of the process. You may not quote payments, APRs, term options, or monthly figures of any kind. The sentence to memorize is: "The exact numbers are prepared by our finance manager, and here is how that works." Every associate, however senior, defers payments to the desk. This is not a limitation on you; it is the store's promise to the customer that every payment figure they hear is prepared on the same calculator by the same accountable person.

8.2 Products presented at the desk. The F&I desk presents, where applicable and lawful: retail installment terms through our lending partners, the manufacturer's finance offers, service contracts, guaranteed asset protection (GAP) coverage on financed deals, and tire and wheel protection. Every product is presented with its price and its contract terms in writing; no product is described as "required" unless it is required by law or by the lender's condition, and the state regulator's wording on this point is in the compliance binder, which any customer may ask to see and which must be produced on request.

8.3 Spot delivery. When a customer signs the retail contract and takes the vehicle home the same day while the lender's final approval is still pending, the transaction is a spot delivery. Spot deliveries are lawful, common, and disclosed: the buyer's order states that the sale is contingent on assignment of the retail contract to a lender on the terms disclosed, and that if final terms cannot be assigned on the disclosed terms, the store will offer the customer terms as close as practicable or unwind the transaction and return the trade and down payment. Understand the definition before you observe the desk, because customers will ask you what "contingent" means while sitting in the F&I waiting area, and the honest one-sentence answer is that final approval can still take a day or two after the customer signs, which is why the paperwork says what it says. If a spot delivery cannot be assigned on the disclosed terms, Wanjiru calls the customer — the associate who sold the unit is welcome to join the call and often should, but the terms conversation belongs to the desk.

8.4 Money handling. Associates do not take cash deposits, do not hold checks, and do not accept payment cards on the floor. All money moves through the F&I office with a written receipt given at the moment of receipt. A customer who insists on handing you a deposit at the showroom table is walked to the F&I office, pleasantly, every time.

SECTION 9. THE SERVICE LANE ORIENTATION

Week four includes a half-day orientation with Esi Sorensen, lead service advisor. The purpose, again, is triage rather than expertise. You should come away able to do four things: book a service appointment at the advisor's counter; explain the difference between the express maintenance lane and a scheduled repair; hand a customer to Esi or her team by name; and recognize the three questions that must always go to the service department rather than being answered from the sales floor: anything about warranty coverage of a specific failure, anything about a repair charge estimate, and anything about a recall notice the customer received in the mail. You may confirm that a recall notice exists in the system; you may not characterize its scope or severity. Recall work is performed by the service department on the manufacturer's terms, and the associate who "helps" by paraphrasing a recall letter on the showroom floor is creating a commitment the service department did not make.

The service lane also matters to you commercially. Every oil change customer in the express lane is a future buyer of something. The associates who do best at this store long-term are the ones the service lane trusts, and the service lane trusts associates who tell customers the truth about what the service department does and does not do. Esi's standing offer to every new associate is a seat at her counter any morning it is slow, and her standing warning is that it is never slow on Saturdays.

SECTION 10. CUSTOMER FOLLOW-UP AND CRM

The CRM is the store's institutional memory. If it is not in the CRM, it did not happen, and if it is in the CRM, it belongs to the store, which is why the manual is explicit about what gets recorded.

10.1 Recording. Every customer contact is logged the day it occurs: walk-ins, calls, texts with the customer's consent noted, e-mails, road tests, appraisals, and no-shows for scheduled appointments. Log the substance in two sentences. Logs are read by your colleagues covering your days off, and the test of a good log entry is whether your colleague can serve the customer tomorrow from your entry alone.

10.2 Follow-up after a sale. The delivery of a vehicle is the beginning of the follow-up calendar, not the end of the deal. Within two business days of delivery, the selling associate must complete the following actions and log each one in the CRM under the delivery record: place and log the thank-you call to the customer, confirming that the vehicle is performing as expected and that the customer knows who to call if anything is not; confirm that the customer has registered on the owner's portal and, if not, walk them through registration while you have them on the phone; schedule the first service reminder in the CRM so that the system generates the maintenance reminder for the customer's first service interval; and send the post-delivery satisfaction survey link. The survey link goes out in the same two-business-day window, not later, because response rates fall sharply once the newness of the vehicle wears off. Later actions sit on their own schedule: the thirty-day check-in call, the sixty-day courtesy contact, and the annual needs review, each generated by the CRM and each requiring the associate to record an outcome, including the outcome "customer asked not to be contacted," which must be honored immediately and logged verbatim.

10.3 Unsold customers. A customer who leaves without purchasing is logged with the reason, the units of interest, and the agreed next contact date. The next contact is made on the date agreed, not earlier, because "I said Friday and he called Wednesday" is the single most common complaint in any follow-up file, and it is entirely preventable.

10.4 Do-not-contact. Any customer request to stop contact is honored across all channels within one business day of the request, and the flag is never removed without written direction from Zoltan Sorensen. This rule has no exception for a customer who "only meant the texts."

SECTION 11. COMPLIANCE BASICS FOR THE SALES FLOOR

Compliance at a dealership is not a department; it is a set of habits on the floor. The habits you must build in your first ninety days are these.

11.1 Truth in advertising. Advertised prices include all dealer-added equipment already on the unit and disclose rebates that require specific qualifications. When a customer asks about an advertised price, produce the advertisement and read it together rather than paraphrasing it. If the customer does not qualify for a qualification-based rebate, say which qualification they do not meet, and let Wanjiru's desk do the rest.

11.2 Buyer's guide on used units. Every pre-owned unit displays the federal buyer's guide stating whether it is sold as-is or with a warranty, and what the warranty covers. The buyer's guide that is on the window at the time of sale is the buyer's guide that goes into the deal jacket. If the window card is missing or defaced at the time of sale, stop the deal and get a replacement printed; do not proceed and fix it later, because there is no later for a disclosure that was never made.

11.3 Licensing and titling. Title applications, lien recording, and temporary plates are handled by the title clerk. Associates never tell a customer that a title will "take about a week" unless the title clerk has said so for that transaction; the honest answer is "our title clerk handles this and will call you with the exact date," followed by making sure the title clerk actually calls.

11.4 Equal treatment. Every customer receives the same process, the same product presentations, the same pricing transparency, and the same follow-up, without regard to any protected characteristic, and without regard to any assumption about who is the decision-maker in a couple or a group. Ask who will be the registered owner; never assume it from who spoke first.

11.5 Prompt reporting. Suspected odometer discrepancies, flood-damaged trade-ins presented as clean, or any customer statement suggesting title fraud go to Zoltan Sorensen the same day, in writing, even if you are not sure. Uncertainty is a reason to report; it is not a reason to wait.

SECTION 12. HOURS, PAY, AND ATTENDANCE

Showroom hours are 9:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Monday through Saturday, closed Sunday. Sales floor schedules are published two weeks ahead by Mateo Mensah. Weekend coverage is a condition of the sales role; the standard floor week includes every other Saturday. Your pay plan is summarized in Appendix C and consists of a weekly draw against commissions, with commission computed on delivered units per the schedule, and manufacturer spiffs paid when the manufacturer pays them, which can lag a cycle. Attendance: call Mateo by 7:30 a.m. for a same-day absence. Three unlogged absences in ninety days triggers a review under the handbook, not this manual. PTO is requested in the HR system; PTO during the last three days of a month, which is our delivery peak, requires the General Manager's approval, and he grants it more often than people assume, but he cannot grant what he is not asked for.

SECTION 13. FIRST-NINETY-DAY MILESTONES

Day 30: modules 1 and 2 passed; ten logged customer interactions; lot walk certified by the opening manager. Day 60: modules 3 and 4 passed; one supervised deal delivered start to finish; service lane orientation completed. Day 90: all modules passed; two deals delivered with the trainer observing rather than assisting; F&I observation days completed; ninety-day review with Zoltan Sorensen and Mateo Mensah, which is a conversation, not an examination, and which begins with the question the General Manager asks everyone at ninety days: "What in this manual turned out to be wrong?" He asks because it is how the manual gets its next revision, and Revision 13 will be written, in part, from your answer.

APPENDIX A. DOCUMENTARY FEES AND STANDARD CHARGES (CURRENT)
Documentation fee: $225 per retail transaction, itemized on the buyer's order. Title and registration: passed through at cost, itemized. Temporary plate: $12. Dealer-installed accessories: at the marked price on the buyer's order, never bundled silently into the vehicle price. Miscellaneous shop supplies, where incurred on a serviced unit: itemized per the service menu. There is no charge for the first owner's portal registration, the first remote battery replacement, or coffee, ever, and any customer told otherwise should be introduced to Ines Lindqvist personally.

APPENDIX B. NEW MODEL LINEUP SNAPSHOT (TRAINING COPY)
Base sedan, 4 cyl, 8-speed automatic; Hybrid sedan, self-charging, no plug; Premium sedan, turbo 4, optional safety package; Crossover S, 2-row, 5-passenger; Crossover L, 3-row, 7-passenger, optional tow package; Sport utility, body-on-frame, standard tow rating per brochure in deal jacket; Half-ton pickup, three cab styles, two bed lengths; Three-quarter-ton pickup, crew cab only this model year, diesel optional; Electric crossover, single motor standard, dual motor optional, home charger assessment through the F&I desk. Fuel economy figures on this snapshot are the manufacturer's and are quoted from the window sticker, never from this appendix, which is a training copy and expires when the model year does.

APPENDIX C. PAY PLAN SUMMARY (SUMMARY ONLY; THE OFFER LETTER GOVERNS)
Weekly draw against commission, drawn amount recovered from earned commission per the offer letter schedule. Commission schedule per delivered unit: new vehicles per the published grid by model line; pre-owned per the front-end gross grid; certified units carry the certified increment. Manufacturer spiffs are additional and paid on manufacturer timing. No commission is earned on a deal that unwinds, and no associate is penalized for a deal that is walked away from honestly — the store's position, stated by the General Manager at hire, is that a clean lost sale is a future customer and a dirty won one is a former one.

APPENDIX D. FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS FROM NEW ASSOCIATES
"Can I park in the customer lot?" No; the staff lot is behind the pre-owned row.
"What if I know the answer to a payment question?" You still defer to the desk. The rule is about accountability, not ability.
"Can I take a demo home overnight?" Demonstration assignments are made by Zoltan Sorensen in writing only, after ninety days, and never to associates still in draw recovery.
"Who do I call if the alarm goes off when I'm closing?" The list is at the desk; you call the manager on duty first, non-emergency line second, and you stay on the property only if it is safe to do so.
"Do I have to log the rude customer?" You log the facts of the interaction, not your assessment of the person's character, and you take the incident to Mateo if it involved threats, discrimination, or anyone feeling unsafe.
"What does 'contingent' mean on the buyer's order?" It means what Section 8.3 says it means, and Section 8.3 is the answer you give.

APPENDIX E. GLOSSARY (SELECTION)
Buyer's order: the purchase agreement itemizing vehicle, price, trade, and fees. Buyer's guide: the federal window disclosure on pre-owned units. DMS: dealership management system. CRM: customer relationship manager. Draw: advance against earned commission. F&I: finance and insurance. GAP: guaranteed asset protection coverage on financed deals. Payoff: amount owed on an existing loan, valid through its good-through date. Spot delivery: see Section 8.3. Unwind: reversal of a delivered transaction, returning all parties to their prior positions.

End of manual. Acknowledge receipt to Ines Lindqvist. Questions on content to Mateo Mensah; questions on personnel matters to Ines Lindqvist; anything the manual does not cover, to Zoltan Sorensen, whose door is genuinely open, which you may verify on day one at lunch.

SECTION 1. PURPOSE AND SCOPE

This manual exists to make your first ninety days at Ridgeline Motors orderly, consistent, and free of guesswork. It consolidates the onboarding checklist, the product knowledge syllabus, the desk procedures for keys and inventory, the working rules of the sales floor, the finance and insurance (F&I) basics every associate must understand before quoting money, the service lane orientation, and the compliance obligations that attach to every customer transaction at a licensed dealership in this state. It is deliberately long. Zoltan Sorensen has directed that no associate should have to rely on hallway folklore to learn how this store operates; folklore, he notes, is what stores rely on when their manuals are out of date, and our manuals are not out of date. Read the whole document once during your first week. During weeks two through thirteen, return to individual sections as your trainer assigns them. Bring your questions to Mateo Mensah, Sales Manager, who owns the training calendar, or to Ines Lindqvist for anything touching payroll, benefits, or personnel records.

The scope of this manual is the sales department. Technicians, detailers, and parts counter staff follow separate manuals maintained by their own supervisors, although Section 9 of this document provides a service lane orientation for sales associates, because customers will ask you service questions in the showroom whether or not you are qualified to answer them, and it is better for everyone that you know which questions to route to Esi Sorensen, our lead service advisor, rather than guessing.

SECTION 2. WHAT THIS STORE SELLS, AND TO WHOM

Ridgeline Motors is a full-line new and pre-owned dealership. Our new-vehicle franchise covers the Ridgeline brand: sedans, crossovers, sport utility vehicles, and a working line of half-ton and three-quarter-ton pickups, plus the electric model introduced two model years ago. Our pre-owned inventory runs from late-model lease returns to trade-ins of every age. Our customer base is the Calder Valley trade area: farms, contractors, two school districts, the hospital, and the professional households of the river towns. Roughly two-thirds of our volume is repeat or referral business. That statistic is repeated at every Monday meeting because it explains most of the rules in this manual: our business depends on people coming back, and people come back when the process is clean, honest, and boring in the best sense of the word. Nothing in this manual is designed to make a sale today at the cost of a customer tomorrow.

SECTION 3. DAY ONE CHECKLIST

Your first day is administrative and orientation only. You will not sell a car on your first day, and you should not try. Report to the HR office on the second floor at 8:30 a.m. Ines Lindqvist will walk you through the following items in order, initialing each line as it is completed. Keep your copy; several later items reference it.

3.1 Identity and eligibility verification. Present original documents establishing identity and work authorization. Photocopies cannot be accepted, and photographs on a phone cannot be accepted, no matter how clear.

3.2 Personnel file. Emergency contact, tax withholding forms, and direct deposit details. Direct deposit takes one to two pay cycles to activate; your first check, if paper, will be handed to you by Ines rather than mailed, so that nothing is lost to a wrong address.

3.3 Offer letter and pay plan. Your offer letter states your base draw, your commission schedule, and the spiff programs currently in effect. The commission schedule is summarized in Appendix C. Sign only the copy Ines provides; drafts circulated by anyone else have no standing.

3.4 Handbook acknowledgment. The general employee handbook covers conduct, attendance, and grievance procedures. This onboarding manual covers the sales floor. You sign for both, separately, because they are separate documents.

3.5 Systems access. Your user account for the dealership management system (DMS), the customer relationship manager (CRM), and the inventory pricing tool will be created on day one. Temporary passwords expire after the first login; if your account locks, call the help desk, do not ask a colleague to log in for you, and never work under another associate's login. 3.7 Safety orientation. Fire exits, extinguisher locations, the spill kit in the detail bay, and the severe weather muster point at the interior wall of the service reception. This item takes twenty minutes and Ines will not rush it.
