SECTION 4. WEEK ONE: THE FLOOR, THE DESK, AND THE KEYS

Week one is spent shadowing. You will be assigned to a senior associate each morning by Mateo Mensah and you will follow one customer interaction per day from greeting to close, or from greeting to a scheduled return, which is often the better outcome. In the afternoons you return to the classroom modules in Section 5. By Friday of week one you should be able to do the following without prompting: greet a walk-in within the standard described below, pull up a unit in the DMS, locate its key, walk the customer to the unit, and describe its equipment honestly — which sometimes means saying "I don't know; let me check," a sentence that costs nothing and is always available to you.

4.1 The greeting standard. Every customer entering the showroom or the lot is greeted within thirty seconds of arrival, by name if known, by eye contact and a hello if not. The greeting is a greeting. It is not an interrogation. Ask what brought them in; do not ask how they will be paying. Customers who want to browse alone should be told, truthfully, that you will be at the desk if anything comes up, and then you must actually be at the desk where you said you would be.

4.2 Key control. This is the rule the General Manager checks personally, so read this paragraph twice. All keys stay with the desk at all times. There are no exceptions for favorites, for units you are personally selling, for the EV demonstrator, or for the truck you think someone is about to come back for. Keys hang on the control board behind the sales desk, each on a numbered tag matching the stock number of the unit. To take a key, you sign it out on the clipboard with the stock number, your initials, and the time; you sign it back in the same way. Keys go back on the board the moment a customer leaves, not at the end of your shift, and never in a pocket, never in a drawer, and never taken home. If a customer is handed a key for a test drive, the associate conducting the drive holds the key for the entire drive; it does not go to the customer's pocket even for the leg of the drive the customer drives. Losing a key for a unit on the floor is a writeable incident because it strands a saleable vehicle behind the glass with no way to start it. Pre-owned units in the back lot keep their keys in the lockbox cabinet; the cabinet is emptied into the board each morning by the opening manager and returned at close.

4.3 The lot walk. Each morning at 8:50, the floor team walks the entire lot, front and back, before the doors open at 9:00. The walk checks four things: every unit is locked; every window sticker is present and legible; every unit is parked within its lined space with no overhang into the drive lanes; and any unit with body damage, flat tires, or missing equipment is flagged with a red card on the windshield and logged in the damage book at the desk. The lot walk takes fifteen minutes when done properly and forty minutes when done after the first customer arrives, which is why it is done before.

4.4 Showroom conduct. Coffee station restocked before open. Demo units inside polished, windows clean, trunks closed, and placards straight. Personal calls on the floor are taken outside or at the bullpen, not in the showroom, and never while a customer is within sight of you. The showroom telephone is answered by whoever is nearest when it rings, on the second ring at the latest, with "Ridgeline Motors, this is" and your first name.

SECTION 5. PRODUCT KNOWLEDGE SYLLABUS

You cannot sell what you cannot describe, and you will be tested. Module tests are administered by Mateo Mensah at the end of weeks one, three, and six. A score of eighty percent is passing; a lower score means you retake the module after a review session, and there is no penalty for a retake other than the time it takes.

Module 1 (week 1): The sedan line. Engines, trim ladder, standard versus optional equipment, and the three most common misconceptions customers arrive with, which are, in order of frequency: that the base trim has heated seats (it does not), that the hybrid sedan requires a plug (it does not; it self-charges), and that the top trim is required to get the safety package (it is not; the safety package is optional on every trim).

Module 2 (week 3): Crossovers and SUVs. Seating configurations, towing differences between the two- and three-row models, cargo measurements, and the family buyer's questions, which are almost always about the second row: does it fold flat, does it recline, does a rear-facing infant seat fit behind a six-foot driver. You will be expected to demonstrate the second-row fold in under thirty seconds and to install a display infant seat correctly. If you have never installed one, say so in training; this is exactly what training is for.

Module 3 (week 3): Pickups. Payload versus towing, the trailer brake controller, bed lengths, and the trade customer's calendar. Contractors buy on schedules, not on mood; the associate who understands that a crew cab with a short bed is a different tool than a regular cab with a long bed will earn the contractor's repeat business for a decade.

Module 4 (week 6): The electric model and the Level 2 charger program. Range figures and what they do and do not promise, home charging assessment, the federal and state incentive paperwork we assist with at the F&I desk, and the cold-weather range conversation, which must be honest. On the EV, honesty is a compliance matter as much as a sales matter: range claims in our advertising are manufacturer figures, and our obligation is to present them as manufacturer figures, not as promises made by this store.

Module 5 (week 6): Pre-owned certification. Which pre-owned units qualify for the certified program, the inspection the certification requires, the warranty terms, and, critically, what certification does not include. A certified unit is not a new unit. Its warranty is the certified program's warranty, and its coverage periods are printed in the buyer's guide on the window. Know where to point on the buyer's guide; never paraphrase warranty terms from memory during a sale.

SECTION 6. TRADE-INS AND APPRAISALS

The trade-in is where more customer trust is won or lost than anywhere else in the deal, because it is where the customer's emotions are highest and where the numbers are least understood. Ridgeline Motors appraises every trade honestly, in writing, whether or not the customer buys from us.

6.1 The intake. The customer's unit is walked with the customer present. You record mileage, equipment, tires, glass, body condition, interior condition, and service history the customer can recall. You do not appraise. Appraisal is performed by Mateo Mensah or by the pre-owned buyer using the store's subscription pricing tools, the auction terminal, and their own eyes on the unit. Your job on intake is to document accurately, because the written appraisal is only as good as the intake sheet behind it.

6.2 The written appraisal. Every appraisal is written, on the appraisal form, showing comparable market values and the adjustment for condition and reconditioning cost. The appraisal is presented to the customer by the associate with the manager available for questions. The customer keeps a copy whether they buy or not.

6.3 Negative equity. When a trade-in is worth less than the payoff owed on it, the difference between the appraised value and the payoff is negative equity. This is common, it is not a reflection on the customer, and it must never be described as though it were. Under our standard practice the difference is added to the amount financed at signing, so the customer finances the shortfall together with the new vehicle's balance rather than paying it out of pocket at the desk. The F&I manager, Wanjiru Kaur, will present the exact numbers. Associates do not improvise payment quotes on negative equity deals; the arithmetic belongs to the desk, because a wrong payment quote spoken in the showroom is a promise this store will be asked to keep.

6.4 Payoff quotes. A payoff quote is lender-specific and has an expiration date, usually ten days. A payoff quote older than its good-through date is not a payoff figure; it is a memory of one. Reconfirm payoffs older than their good-through date with the lender before drawing final paperwork, without exception, even when the customer insists the number has not changed, because the customer is sometimes wrong in a direction that costs them money.

SECTION 7. DEMONSTRATIONS AND ROAD TESTS

7.1 Licensing. No road test leaves the lot unless the customer presents a valid driver's license and the associate records the license number on the road test form. No license, no drive; a learner's permit without a licensed adult passenger is not a valid license for this purpose. This rule has no exception for the customer's spouse, for the customer who "always drives with an expired one and it's fine," or for anyone in a hurry.

7.2 Route. The standard road test route is posted at the desk: out the north exit, two laps of the park loop, and the merge onto Route 9 and back. The route takes twenty minutes and includes a hill, a rough patch of pavement for suspension feel, and a merge. Customers who ask to drive farther may, within reason and with the associate's judgment, but every road test returns to the lot before any paperwork is discussed. Driving a customer's trade as part of the appraisal follows the same route.

7.3 Insurance. The customer's own policy covers them on our plates under the standard garage endorsement for demonstration purposes; associates are additionally covered under the store's policy while riding along. If a customer states their license is suspended or revoked, do not proceed with any road test, and note the conversation in the CRM.

7.4 Accidents on road tests. Stop, check for injuries, call emergency services if anyone is hurt or if any other vehicle is involved, exchange information, and call the dealership immediately. Do not admit fault, do not discuss fault with anyone at the scene, and do not continue the demonstration after any collision, however minor. The sales manager comes to the scene. This is a rule about you as much as about the store: associates have been injured standing on the shoulder of Route 9 deciding to "just head back." Do not.

SECTION 8. WORKING THE F&I DESK

Wanjiru Kaur, Finance and Insurance Manager, owns every number that becomes a payment. Week five of your onboarding includes two full days sitting at the F&I desk as an observer. The purpose is not to train you to quote money — you will not — but so that you understand what happens to your deal after the customer says yes, and can therefore describe the process honestly and calmly to a nervous buyer.

8.1 What you may quote. You may discuss prices as marked, current advertised offers with their expiration dates, and the general structure of the process. You may not quote payments, APRs, term options, or monthly figures of any kind. The sentence to memorize is: "The exact numbers are prepared by our finance manager, and here is how that works." Every associate, however senior, defers payments to the desk. This is not a limitation on you; it is the store's promise to the customer that every payment figure they hear is prepared on the same calculator by the same accountable person.

8.2 Products presented at the desk. The F&I desk presents, where applicable and lawful: retail installment terms through our lending partners, the manufacturer's finance offers, service contracts, guaranteed asset protection (GAP) coverage on financed deals, and tire and wheel protection. Every product is presented with its price and its contract terms in writing; no product is described as "required" unless it is required by law or by the lender's condition, and the state regulator's wording on this point is in the compliance binder, which any customer may ask to see and which must be produced on request.

8.3 Spot delivery. When a customer signs the retail contract and takes the vehicle home the same day while the lender's final approval is still pending, the transaction is a spot delivery. Spot deliveries are lawful, common, and disclosed: the buyer's order states that the sale is contingent on assignment of the retail contract to a lender on the terms disclosed, and that if final terms cannot be assigned on the disclosed terms, the store will offer the customer terms as close as practicable or unwind the transaction and return the trade and down payment. Understand the definition before you observe the desk, because customers will ask you what "contingent" means while sitting in the F&I waiting area, and the honest one-sentence answer is that final approval can still take a day or two after the customer signs, which is why the paperwork says what it says. If a spot delivery cannot be assigned on the disclosed terms, Wanjiru calls the customer — the associate who sold the unit is welcome to join the call and often should, but the terms conversation belongs to the desk.

8.4 Money handling. Associates do not take cash deposits, do not hold checks, and do not accept payment cards on the floor. All money moves through the F&I office with a written receipt given at the moment of receipt. A customer who insists on handing you a deposit at the showroom table is walked to the F&I office, pleasantly, every time.

SECTION 9. THE SERVICE LANE ORIENTATION

Week four includes a half-day orientation with Esi Sorensen, lead service advisor. The purpose, again, is triage rather than expertise. You should come away able to do four things: book a service appointment at the advisor's counter; explain the difference between the express maintenance lane and a scheduled repair; hand a customer to Esi or her team by name; and recognize the three questions that must always go to the service department rather than being answered from the sales floor: anything about warranty coverage of a specific failure, anything about a repair charge estimate, and anything about a recall notice the customer received in the mail. You may confirm that a recall notice exists in the system; you may not characterize its scope or severity. Recall work is performed by the service department on the manufacturer's terms, and the associate who "helps" by paraphrasing a recall letter on the showroom floor is creating a commitment the service department did not make.

The service lane also matters to you commercially. Every oil change customer in the express lane is a future buyer of something. The associates who do best at this store long-term are the ones the service lane trusts, and the service lane trusts associates who tell customers the truth about what the service department does and does not do. Esi's standing offer to every new associate is a seat at her counter any morning it is slow, and her standing warning is that it is never slow on Saturdays.

SECTION 10. CUSTOMER FOLLOW-UP AND CRM

The CRM is the store's institutional memory. If it is not in the CRM, it did not happen, and if it is in the CRM, it belongs to the store, which is why the manual is explicit about what gets recorded.

10.1 Recording. Every customer contact is logged the day it occurs: walk-ins, calls, texts with the customer's consent noted, e-mails, road tests, appraisals, and no-shows for scheduled appointments. Log the substance in two sentences. Logs are read by your colleagues covering your days off, and the test of a good log entry is whether your colleague can serve the customer tomorrow from your entry alone.

10.2 Follow-up after a sale. The delivery of a vehicle is the beginning of the follow-up calendar, not the end of the deal. Within two business days of delivery, the selling associate must complete the following actions and log each one in the CRM under the delivery record: place and log the thank-you call to the customer, confirming that the vehicle is performing as expected and that the customer knows who to call if anything is not; confirm that the customer has registered on the owner's portal and, if not, walk them through registration while you have them on the phone; schedule the first service reminder in the CRM so that the system generates the maintenance reminder for the customer's first service interval; and send the post-delivery satisfaction survey link. The survey link goes out in the same two-business-day window, not later, because response rates fall sharply once the newness of the vehicle wears off. Later actions sit on their own schedule: the thirty-day check-in call, the sixty-day courtesy contact, and the annual needs review, each generated by the CRM and each requiring the associate to record an outcome, including the outcome "customer asked not to be contacted," which must be honored immediately and logged verbatim.

10.3 Unsold customers. A customer who leaves without purchasing is logged with the reason, the units of interest, and the agreed next contact date. The next contact is made on the date agreed, not earlier, because "I said Friday and he called Wednesday" is the single most common complaint in any follow-up file, and it is entirely preventable.

10.4 Do-not-contact. Any customer request to stop contact is honored across all channels within one business day of the request, and the flag is never removed without written direction from Zoltan Sorensen. This rule has no exception for a customer who "only meant the texts."

SECTION 11. COMPLIANCE BASICS FOR THE SALES FLOOR

Compliance at a dealership is not a department; it is a set of habits on the floor. The habits you must build in your first ninety days are these.

11.1 Truth in advertising. Advertised prices include all dealer-added equipment already on the unit and disclose rebates that require specific qualifications. When a customer asks about an advertised price, produce the advertisement and read it together rather than paraphrasing it. If the customer does not qualify for a qualification-based rebate, say which qualification they do not meet, and let Wanjiru's desk do the rest.

11.2 Buyer's guide on used units. Every pre-owned unit displays the federal buyer's guide stating whether it is sold as-is or with a warranty, and what the warranty covers. The buyer's guide that is on the window at the time of sale is the buyer's guide that goes into the deal jacket. If the window card is missing or defaced at the time of sale, stop the deal and get a replacement printed; do not proceed and fix it later, because there is no later for a disclosure that was never made.

11.3 Licensing and titling. Title applications, lien recording, and temporary plates are handled by the title clerk. Associates never tell a customer that a title will "take about a week" unless the title clerk has said so for that transaction; the honest answer is "our title clerk handles this and will call you with the exact date," followed by making sure the title clerk actually calls.

11.4 Equal treatment. Every customer receives the same process, the same product presentations, the same pricing transparency, and the same follow-up, without regard to any protected characteristic, and without regard to any assumption about who is the decision-maker in a couple or a group. Ask who will be the registered owner; never assume it from who spoke first.

11.5 Prompt reporting. Suspected odometer discrepancies, flood-damaged trade-ins presented as clean, or any customer statement suggesting title fraud go to Zoltan Sorensen the same day, in writing, even if you are not sure. Uncertainty is a reason to report; it is not a reason to wait.

SECTION 12. HOURS, PAY, AND ATTENDANCE

Showroom hours are 9:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Monday through Saturday, closed Sunday. Sales floor schedules are published two weeks ahead by Mateo Mensah. Weekend coverage is a condition of the sales role; the standard floor week includes every other Saturday. Your pay plan is summarized in Appendix C and consists of a weekly draw against commissions, with commission computed on delivered units per the schedule, and manufacturer spiffs paid when the manufacturer pays them, which can lag a cycle. Attendance: call Mateo by 7:30 a.m. for a same-day absence. Three unlogged absences in ninety days triggers a review under the handbook, not this manual. PTO is requested in the HR system; PTO during the last three days of a month, which is our delivery peak, requires the General Manager's approval, and he grants it more often than people assume, but he cannot grant what he is not asked for.

SECTION 13. FIRST-NINETY-DAY MILESTONES

Day 30: modules 1 and 2 passed; ten logged customer interactions; lot walk certified by the opening manager. Day 60: modules 3 and 4 passed; one supervised deal delivered start to finish; service lane orientation completed. Day 90: all modules passed; two deals delivered with the trainer observing rather than assisting; F&I observation days completed; ninety-day review with Zoltan Sorensen and Mateo Mensah, which is a conversation, not an examination, and which begins with the question the General Manager asks everyone at ninety days: "What in this manual turned out to be wrong?" He asks because it is how the manual gets its next revision, and Revision 13 will be written, in part, from your answer.

APPENDIX A. DOCUMENTARY FEES AND STANDARD CHARGES (CURRENT)
Documentation fee: $225 per retail transaction, itemized on the buyer's order. Title and registration: passed through at cost, itemized. Temporary plate: $12. Dealer-installed accessories: at the marked price on the buyer's order, never bundled silently into the vehicle price. Miscellaneous shop supplies, where incurred on a serviced unit: itemized per the service menu. There is no charge for the first owner's portal registration, the first remote battery replacement, or coffee, ever, and any customer told otherwise should be introduced to Ines Lindqvist personally.

APPENDIX B. NEW MODEL LINEUP SNAPSHOT (TRAINING COPY)
Base sedan, 4 cyl, 8-speed automatic; Hybrid sedan, self-charging, no plug; Premium sedan, turbo 4, optional safety package; Crossover S, 2-row, 5-passenger; Crossover L, 3-row, 7-passenger, optional tow package; Sport utility, body-on-frame, standard tow rating per brochure in deal jacket; Half-ton pickup, three cab styles, two bed lengths; Three-quarter-ton pickup, crew cab only this model year, diesel optional; Electric crossover, single motor standard, dual motor optional, home charger assessment through the F&I desk. Fuel economy figures on this snapshot are the manufacturer's and are quoted from the window sticker, never from this appendix, which is a training copy and expires when the model year does.

APPENDIX C. PAY PLAN SUMMARY (SUMMARY ONLY; THE OFFER LETTER GOVERNS)
Weekly draw against commission, drawn amount recovered from earned commission per the offer letter schedule. Commission schedule per delivered unit: new vehicles per the published grid by model line; pre-owned per the front-end gross grid; certified units carry the certified increment. Manufacturer spiffs are additional and paid on manufacturer timing. No commission is earned on a deal that unwinds, and no associate is penalized for a deal that is walked away from honestly — the store's position, stated by the General Manager at hire, is that a clean lost sale is a future customer and a dirty won one is a former one.

APPENDIX D. FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS FROM NEW ASSOCIATES
"Can I park in the customer lot?" No; the staff lot is behind the pre-owned row.
"What if I know the answer to a payment question?" You still defer to the desk. The rule is about accountability, not ability.
"Can I take a demo home overnight?" Demonstration assignments are made by Zoltan Sorensen in writing only, after ninety days, and never to associates still in draw recovery.
"Who do I call if the alarm goes off when I'm closing?" The list is at the desk; you call the manager on duty first, non-emergency line second, and you stay on the property only if it is safe to do so.
"Do I have to log the rude customer?" You log the facts of the interaction, not your assessment of the person's character, and you take the incident to Mateo if it involved threats, discrimination, or anyone feeling unsafe.
"What does 'contingent' mean on the buyer's order?" It means what Section 8.3 says it means, and Section 8.3 is the answer you give.

APPENDIX E. GLOSSARY (SELECTION)
Buyer's order: the purchase agreement itemizing vehicle, price, trade, and fees. Buyer's guide: the federal window disclosure on pre-owned units. DMS: dealership management system. CRM: customer relationship manager. Draw: advance against earned commission. F&I: finance and insurance. GAP: guaranteed asset protection coverage on financed deals. Payoff: amount owed on an existing loan, valid through its good-through date. Spot delivery: see Section 8.3. Unwind: reversal of a delivered transaction, returning all parties to their prior positions.

End of manual. Acknowledge receipt to Ines Lindqvist. Questions on content to Mateo Mensah; questions on personnel matters to Ines Lindqvist; anything the manual does not cover, to Zoltan Sorensen, whose door is genuinely open, which you may verify on day one at lunch.

question.instruction: Which actions does the manual require the selling associate to complete "within two business days of delivery"?

candidates.description: (a) Place and log the thank-you call to the customer.
(b) Confirm the customer has registered on the owner's portal.
(c) Schedule the first service reminder in the CRM.
(d) Send the post-delivery satisfaction survey link.
(e) Wash and detail the trade-in for resale on the front line.
(f) Notify the lender of the completed sale in writing.

notes: Section 10.2 lists exactly four required actions in the two-business-day window; detailing the trade and lender notification are not among them.

Replaced high-pressure switch, part GBP 96.00, labour 1.5 hrs. Pump restored and running at 16:00. Downtime for the tenant from first report of loss of heating: approx. 22 hours, which is within the landlord's 24-hour emergency restoration standard for heating and hot water, so no standard compensation is due to the tenant under the tenancy agreement clause 7(b) (compensation applies only where restoration exceeds 24 hours).

SUBJECT: RE: RE: Notice of Alleged Breach — Maintenance Agreement MA-2021-118 (Larkspur Labs / Granite Health)

Dear Ms. Petrov,

We acknowledge receipt of Granite Health's formal notice dated 14 March 2024. We respond point by point below, quoting your notice where necessary. For the record, we also attach the ticket history for the September incident.

----- ORIGINAL MESSAGE (Granite Health, 14 March 2024) -----

Dear Mr. Haddad,

Pursuant to Section 9 (Remedies) of the Maintenance Agreement MA-2021-118 dated 1 April 2021 ("Agreement"), Granite Health hereby gives notice of the following breaches:

1. SERVICE LEVEL BREACH. Ticket #4471 (radiology interface outage) was logged with your service desk on Thursday 5 September 2024 at 09:12. Your records show the remedy was not completed until Monday 16 September 2024. Section 4.2 requires a first response within four (4) business hours and a full remedy within five (5) business days of logging. While we accept the first response (12:47 on 5 September) was within the four-hour window, the remedy exceeded the permitted period.

2. INEFFECTIVE AMENDMENT. Amendment No. 3 (increased user ceiling from 250 to 400 seats, effective 1 October 2023) was never countersigned by Granite Health. Section 11.4 provides that amendments take effect only upon countersignature by both parties. Larkspur has nonetheless invoiced at the amended seat count.

3. OVERCHARGE. Purchase Order PO-GH-2024-031 authorised a quarterly maintenance fee of USD 12,400. Invoice 2024-118 dated 3 April 2024 demands USD 14,900, reflecting a rate-card increase of 20% implemented by Larkspur unilaterally and without a change order as required by Section 7.2.

4. UNAUTHORISED SUBCONTRACTING. Our site log records that on 11 September 2024, personnel from Meridian Field Services (a third party) attended our Riverton clinic to complete the remedy, and no consent was sought from Granite Health as required by Section 5.6.

We reserve our rights under Sections 8, 9 and 12.

Nadia Petrov
Contracts Manager, Granite Health

----- END ORIGINAL MESSAGE -----

Mr. Haddad's response of 18 March 2024:

Dear Ms. Petrov,

1. Regarding Ticket #4471: our engineers diagnose a corrupted certificate chain. The ticket was parked for three days awaiting client security clearance (documented in the ticket trail: status "Awaiting Customer" 6–9 September). We consider the remedy completed within a reasonable period, and in any case the outage originated with a third-party certificate authority.

2. Regarding Amendment No. 3: our records show the amendment was executed by your then-Operations Director at a renewal call on 22 September 2023, and your team has been using 380+ seats since October. Ms. Petrov will recall she wrote to me on 2 October 2023 confirming "the additional seats are live and in use."

3. Regarding Invoice 2024-118: the 20% uplift reflects our published 2024 rate card, circulated 15 December 2023.

4. Regarding Meridian Field Services: Schedule C to the Agreement expressly permits us to engage certified subcontractors for on-site remediation, provided they are bound by equivalent confidentiality terms. Meridian's engagement letter of 10 September 2024 confirms such terms were in place.

Separately, we remind Granite Health that under Section 8.3 the Agreement renews automatically for successive twelve-month periods unless either party delivers written notice of non-renewal at least thirty (30) days before the renewal date of 1 April. We have no record of any non-renewal notice. Your message of 14 March, whatever its characterisation, was received fourteen (14) days before the renewal date and therefore does not satisfy Section 8.3. The Agreement accordingly stands renewed for the period 1 April 2024 – 31 March 2025 at the rates in force.

With regard to the annual training session referenced in our Statements of Work: the training session scheduled for 15 February 2024 was delivered as planned; the signed attendance sheet (14 attendees, Granite Health Riverton clinic) is enclosed.

Finally, and without prejudice, we ask that your service desk classify Ticket #4471 as "remedied — client-attributable delay" in the shared tracking system, as this will assist both parties' reporting.

Kind regards,
Sven Haddad
Account Director, Larkspur Labs

----- INTERNAL NOTE (Rosa Lindqvist to Nadia Petrov, 19 March 2024) -----

Nadia,

Points for the escalation file: (a) the subcontractor consent clause in Schedule C is genuine and appears to cover the Meridian visit, so point 4 of our notice may be weaker than we thought; (b) the countersignature point is strong — nothing in Section 11.4 permits effect by email confirmation alone; (c) the invoice exceeds the PO by USD 2,500 with no change order, which is a straightforward breach of Section 7.2; (d) on the ticket, the delay was 7 business days from logging (6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 16) against a 5-business-day remedy window, assuming no valid suspension; the "Awaiting Customer" parking was never formally notified to us as a clock-stop under Section 4.6, which requires written notification within 24 hours. Please confirm before we respond to Larkspur.

Rosa

#4471 | Outage — radiology interface | Logged Thu 05 Sep 2024 09:12 | First response Thu 05 Sep 2024 12:47 | Status: Awaiting Customer 06–09 Sep | Engineer dispatched Tue 10 Sep | Third-party attendance (Meridian Field Services) Wed 11 Sep | Certificate replacement Fri 13 Sep | Validation and closure Mon 16 Sep 2024 17:40.

question.instruction: We need to check one thing only: did Larkspur take too long to fully fix Ticket #4471, meaning more than the 5 business days that Section 4.2 allow from the day ticket was logged (Thursday 5 September 2024, fixed/closed Monday 16 September 2024)? EXHIBIT F — DISTRICT COURT FILING, EXCERPT (as transcribed; typos and irregular punctuation from the original are preserved)

IN RE: COPPERLEAF HEALTH SYSTEMS, INC. v. GRANITE SOFTWARE CORP. and UNKNOWN THREAT ACTORS
Case No. 22-cv-01984
DECLARATION OF JONAS MOREAU, CHIEF INFORMATION SECURITY OFFICER, COPPERLEAF HEALTH

1. I, Jonas Moreau, am the Chief Information Security Officer ("CISO") of Copperleaf Health, a regional operator of eleven clinics and two surgical centers. I make this declaration from personal knowledge and from business records kept in the ordinary course. I have worked in incident response for nineteen years. My sister, Ines Moreau, is employed by Granite Software as the lead support engineer assigned to the Copperleaf account; her role is described below and is not a role I supervise.

2. This declaration is filed in support of Copperleaf's motion for a preliminary injunction. Paragraphs 3 through 41 describe the chronology of the intrusion of March 2025 (the "Incident"). Exhibits A through G are incorporated by reference and quoted in part below. Where I quote emails or chat messages, I preserve the original wording, including typographical errors, exactly as produced by the parties during discovery.

3. Copperleaf uses Granite Software's "MedLane" integration suite to move pharmacy orders, insurance eligibility checks, and surgical scheduling records between Copperleaf's electronic health record and the systems of its business partners, which include Saltmarsh Logistics (warehousing and medical courier work) and Bluefin Freight (interfacility transport). Granite operates the MedLane cloud; Copperleaf operates its own data center in Duluth. Saltmarsh and Bluefin do not have direct network connections to each other; all partner-to-partner traffic is relayed through the MedLane cloud, which is administered by Granite, not by Copperleaf.

4. On March 4, 2025, at approximately 07:52 Central, an email arrived in the inboxes of four Copperleaf clinicians. The email purported to come from "MedLane Support <support@medlane-updates.net>" and displayed the subject line "URGENT: MedLane security patch required before 10am — your integration will be disable." The reply-to domain, medlane-updates.net, was registered on February 27, 2025, five days before the Incident. It was not a Granite domain. Granite's actual support domain is support.granitesoftware.com.

5. The email read, in full:

"Dear MedLane customer,

A critical vulnerability was discover in the MedLane connector. You must apply the security patch before 10:00 AM today or your integration will be disable and orders will not flow. Please log in with your MedLane admin credential at the portal below:

https://portal.medlane-updates.net/patch

Do not contact your IT department, as they are already aware and the portal will show them you have complyed. Apply the patch now.

— MedLane Support Team"

6. The instruction not to contact IT is significant. It is my professional opinion that this line was included to delay internal reporting. Two of the four recipients forwarded the email to our SOC. Two did not. Of the two who did not, one, Dr. P. Whitfield, navigated to the linked portal from a workstation in the Duluth surgical center and entered his MedLane administrative username and password at approximately 08:31 Central. The portal then displayed the message "Patch applied. Thank you for your cooperation." No patch existed. The page harvested credentials.

7. The fake portal was hosted at 198.51.100.77 on port 443 and served a visually convincing copy of the Granite login page, including Granite's logo, which had been scraped from Granite's public marketing site. The portal was live from 07:41 Central until 08:58 Central, when its hosting provider, acting on a report that had been submitted — as set out in paragraph 9 — took the site offline. In total the fake portal was live for 77 minutes. Approximately 40 minutes into that window, at 08:21, Granite's own abuse-monitoring system flagged inbound customer reports of the phishing domain, and Granite's security team began calling affected accounts, including ours.

8. I was in a budget meeting when my phone rang at 08:22. I reproduce my recollection of the call from my call log and from the notes of Beatriz Fischer, the SOC duty analyst who listened in on the recorded line, as follows.

9. THE 08:22 CALL. Ines Moreau of Granite Software called Copperleaf's main SOC line. She identified herself as the assigned support lead for our account. She said words to the effect of: "Jonas, we are getting customer reports of a phishing domain impersonating the MedLane portal. Do not log in to any portal today except from your bookmark. If any of your staff already did, tell me now and we will kill the session server-side." Note that it was Granite who called us. I want to be explicit, because a great deal of confusion later arose: we did not call Granite first. The vendor notified us within the hour of the phishing campaign starting — in fact within about forty minutes — and I want that plainly understood because defense counsel has suggested the reverse.

10. Beatriz Fischer checked our identity-provider logs during the call. She found a successful interactive login by the credential MedLaneAdmin-PW (Dr. Whitfield's) at 08:31:04 — wait, I correct myself: the login occurred at 08:31:04 per the IdP log, and the call from Granite began at 08:22, meaning the credential theft had not yet occurred when Granite first called. Granite called because other customers had reported the email, not because they had seen our credential used. The credential was harvested after Granite's call. I state this precisely because the sequence matters to the motion now before the court.

11. On the call, Ms. Moreau stated that she could see, from Granite's side, a suspicious session initiating from an IP address 198.51.100.77 under Dr. Whitfield's account. She asked whether that IP belonged to Copperleaf. It did not. She stated: "I'm terminating that session now and locking the account. Your staff should not use the MedLane admin login until we say so." She then terminated the session at 08:34:12 from Granite's side. This is a point I also want plainly understood: the account lockout of Dr. Whitfield's MedLane admin account was performed by Granite, on Granite's systems, at Granite's initiative. Copperleaf did not lock that account, because the account lived on Granite's platform.

12. At 08:40 I convened our incident bridge. Attendees by initials: JM (me), BF (Beatriz Fischer, SOC), DO (Dalia Okonkwo, network engineering — no relation to any party), plus Yara Okafor of Ashgrove Forensics, our retained external IR consultant, dialed in at 08:47. Dalia Alvarez of Saltmarsh Logistics and Rosa Nakamura of Bluefin Freight were not on the initial bridge; their involvement is described in paragraphs 22 through 34.

13. Between 08:41 and 09:14 Copperleaf took the following containment actions, which I enumerate exactly and no further, because in depositions there has been a tendency to attribute to Copperleaf actions we did not take:
  (a) At 08:41, we revoked the MedLane API service account credential used by our pharmacy integration (svc-pharm-bridge) and issued a replacement. The old credential was dead by 08:42.
  (b) At 08:47, we rotated the shared password on the Saltmarsh warehouse gateway device, because that gateway authenticated with a static password that had been included in the MedLane configuration bundle. I confirmed the rotation with Dalia Alvarez of Saltmarsh by phone at 08:49.
  (c) At 09:14, we killed the integration creds. By this I refer to the remaining set of MedLane-issued client credentials: the surgical scheduling service account and the insurance eligibility service account. We killed those integration creds at 09:14 per our change log, exhibit B, line 331. We did NOT kill Granite's own administrative accounts — we had no ability to, and still do not, since those live on Granite's platform.
  (d) Also at 09:14, on request from Ms. Moreau and with her on the line, I confirmed verbally that Ines Moreau's Granite console admin login — meaning her named administrator login into the MedLane administrative console — had been suspended by Granite's security team as a precaution while they investigated whether attacker activity had touched accounts she administered. To be clear as day: we did not suspend it. Granite suspended her own console admin login. I was asked to confirm on the line and I did, and that confirmation was later misread by the defendant's expert as Copperleaf having performed the suspension. We performed none.
  (e) We did not force a password reset for all clinicians at that time. A clinic-wide reset was discussed on the bridge and deliberately deferred until after business hours to avoid disrupting the surgical schedule. It is not accurate to say Copperleaf forced a client-wide password reset on March 4. We deferred it. It happened on March 7 in a controlled window, after the intrusion was contained.

14. What we did NOT do on March 4, and could not have done: block Granite's IP ranges at our perimeter. Granite's HQ egress ranges appear in exhibit D page 4; the only IPs we blocked that day were 198.51.100.77 (the phishing host), 203.0.113.0/28 (the relay used by the harvested-credential session), and one lone VPN exit in Amsterdam that showed up in our VPN logs at 09:02. Blocking Granite's own ranges would have severed MedLane for our entire pharmacy chain; no one proposed it seriously and it was not done.

15. At 09:03, the intruder — using the harvested MedLane admin credential before the 08:34 termination? No. I must correct the record here, and I ask the court's patience: the timeline was reconstructed twice, once on March 5 and again on March 12, and the second reconstruction moved two events. The harvested credential was used successfully at 08:31:04. Granite terminated the active session at 08:34:12. However, before termination the intruder had used the session to mint an API token, and it was the token, not the credential, that carried the intruder forward. This is the key fact that the initial reconstruction missed. The token was not detected until March 6.

16. Between 08:35 on March 4 and 11:22 on March 6, the token enumerated patient folders in the MedLane relay cache and pulled approximately 2.3 GB of data: mostly scheduling metadata and insurance eligibility responses, containing in aggregate the identifiers of roughly 4,187 patients. No clinical records were in the relay cache. I say this with confidence and note that opposing counsel's brief claims clinical records were taken; they were not, and we will file a correcting declaration if that claim is repeated.

17. On March 5 at 14:00, I sent the following email to Granite's security team, with a copy to my opposite number at Granite and to outside counsel:

"From: jonas.moreau@copperleafhealth.example
To: security@granitesoftware.example
Subject: RE: incident bridge notes — actions and owners

Team,

Writing down who did what so we don't argue about it later.

- You (Granite) called us at 08:22 on the 4th. First contact came from your side. The vendor notified us within the hour of the phish going out and I've told our board the same.
- You killed Dr. Whitfield's MedLane admin session at 08:34 and locked the account. We did not and could not.
- We killed the integration creds at 09:14 (svc-pharm-bridge was earlier, 08:41). Both actions ours, on our side of the fence.
- We rotated the Saltmarsh gateway password. Dalia has the new one under her seal.
- Ines's console admin login: your team suspended it. I confirmed on the call. Please don't let the court filings drift on this point.
- We blocked three attacker IPs. We did not touch your ranges.

Jonas"

18. Granite's counsel has since characterized the account in paragraph 17 as "self-serving." It is not; it was written contemporaneously, on March 5, before any litigation was contemplated, and it matches the logs. I resent the same email to their counsel on April 2 and received no correction until April 18, after which their expert produced the report discussed in paragraph 38.

19. On March 6 at 11:22, Beatriz Fischer identified the minted token during a manual review of the MedLane relay cache audit trail. The token had been created under the name "svc-billing-sync" — a name calculated to look like one of ours, but there is no Copperleaf service by that name, and Granite's directory shows the token was created at the tenant level, which only Granite-side admins or an admin credential acting on the tenant could do. Dr. Whitfield's harvested credential was a tenant admin credential. The token was revoked by Granite at 11:31 on March 6, ninety-one seconds after Ms. Fischer escalated to Granite — I note this because Granite's response here was fast and competent and I have said so in every declaration I have filed, including this one.

20. The following chat log, from Copperleaf's internal incident channel (#ir-bridge, Mattermost, retained per legal hold), is quoted as exhibit E, lines 110-214. Typos preserved.

[08:44] bfischer: jonas you there

21. I adopt that chat log as accurate. I direct the court's attention to line [08:56], written by our own analyst, contemporaneously, warning that "people WILL confuse this later." That confusion arrived, in the form of the defendant's expert report, in April.

22. I turn now to the Saltmarsh and Bluefin relationships, where further confusion has been sown.

23. Saltmarsh Logistics stores Copperleaf's non-refrigerated supplies and runs the courier loop between our Duluth campus and the depot. Saltmarsh connects to Copperleaf's inventory system through a MedLane relay, and connects to Bluefin Freight's dispatch system through a second MedLane relay. Bluefin transports surgical instruments and specimens for us. Bluefin and Saltmarsh are, in a sense, both our vendors and, on one corridor, each other's counterparties. They are not affiliated companies.

24. On March 5 at 16:40, Rosa Nakamura, Bluefin's operations director, sent me an email that I quote in full because its wording has been the subject of a discovery dispute:

"From: r.nakamura@bluefinfreight.example
To: jonas.moreau@copperleafhealth.example
Subject: FYI — precautionary actions on our side

Jonas,

Heads up on what we did this morning, since you'll hear about it from the rumor mill otherwise. You called me yesterday about the phish, and we checked our inbound MedLane feeds. Two of the scheduled courier manifests in yesterday's relay showed a source IP outside the expected range. We don't think it was us who was compromised — our broker logs are clean — but the manifests passed through the MedLane cloud, which is Granite's house, not ours and not yours.

So this morning: we pulled their plug pending the review. Meaning: the Saltmarsh-to-Bluefin dispatch feed, which enters OUR dispatch system from Saltmarsh, is dark. Saltmarsh can't push manifests to us until the review is done. To be plain about who did what to whom: Bluefin cut the inbound feed FROM Saltmarsh. We did not cut anything from you, and nothing of yours was cut by us. Your own feeds to Bluefin are still running and I'd rather they stayed that way.

Also for the record, we did NOT block Copperleaf and we did NOT ask anyone to block Saltmarsh on our behalf. We did it ourselves, in our own firewall, at 09:05 this morning.

Your feed into us is dark until futher notice — no wait, scratch that, I keep mixing myself up. Let me restate: THEIR feed into us is dark. YOUR feed into us is fine. I've had three people call me today asking whether we lost access to Saltmarsh and the answer is no, we have all the access, we're the ones who closed the door on OUR side and it's Saltmarsh who can't get in. Sorry for the sloppy drafting, it's been a long day.

Rosa"

25. I quote Ms. Nakamura's email not because Copperleaf takes a position on the Bluefin-Saltmarsh corridor but because defendants' exhibit 12 mischaracterizes it as evidence that "Bluefin lost its connection to Saltmarsh." It did not. Read in full, the email says the opposite, three times, including in the correction paragraph.

26. On March 6 at 10:15, Dalia Alvarez of Saltmarsh emailed Ms. Nakamura and me:

"From: d.alvarez@saltmarshlogistics.example
To: r.nakamura@bluefinfreight.example; jonas.moreau@copperleafhealth.example
Subject: RE: dispatch feed

Rosa, Jonas,

Confirming we can see the door is closed on Bluefin's side. We are not able to push manifests to Bluefin as of 09:05 yesterday. On our side nothing is closed. Our outbound feed to Bluefin is configured and permitted; Bluefin's firewall rejects it. Our feed to Copperleaf is untouched and flowing, so Jonas, your replenishment loop is fine.

One thing I want to correct from the conference call: I said 'we suspended the feed' on the call. I misspoke. We did not suspend anything. Bluefin suspended our feed into them. My English is not always precise on calls, and I apologize.

Dalia"

27. Ms. Alvarez's correction in paragraph 26 matches Bluefin's own change record, produced as defendants' exhibit 13, which shows a firewall rule named "INBOUND-SALT-DISPATCH" set to REJECT at 09:05:00 Central on March 5 by user r.nakamura.

28. Between March 6 and March 10, Yara Okafor of Ashgrove Forensics performed the forensic reconstruction. Her preliminary report is exhibit G. Relevant findings:

  (a) The phishing email was sent from a bulk-mail infrastructure in Kyiv that had not previously touched Copperleaf.
  (b) The credential harvesting page posted the stolen credential to a collector at 203.0.113.44 within two seconds of Dr. Whitfield's submission.
  (c) The minted token "svc-billing-sync" was used from 203.0.113.51, an address in the same /28 as the collector — the two near-miss numbers have caused confusion in the press coverage, which reported them as "the same address." They are different addresses in the same block.
  (d) Exfiltration occurred in 14 sessions between 08:41 on March 4 and 11:18 on March 6, totaling 2.31 GB, of which 2.14 GB was scheduling metadata. 0.17 GB was insurance eligibility responses. 0 GB was clinical records.
  (e) No evidence of persistence inside Copperleaf's data center. The intruder never entered our network; they lived entirely inside the MedLane cloud using the tenant token. Our own perimeter held.
  (f) No evidence that Granite personnel were complicit. Ms. Moreau's actions on March 4 were, in Ms. Okafor's words, "textbook and fast."

29. Copperleaf notified affected patients starting March 12, within the 10-day window required by the state breach statute counted from March 6, the date we confirmed the token's use. The statute counts from confirmation of a reasonable likelihood of breach, not from the first phishing email; the Attorney General's office has accepted our dating and closed its inquiry on April 30.

30. On March 7 at 21:00, in the deferred window, we performed the clinic-wide password reset described in paragraph 13(e). All clinician accounts, 1,842 of them, were required to reset at next login. Three help-desk tickets were opened that night; two were resolved by 22:00 and one the next morning.

31. On March 10, Granite's chief security officer, by email, offered to pay Copperleaf's forensic costs up to $75,000 and to credit three months of MedLane fees, "without admission of fault." Copperleaf accepted the forensic-cost cap and declined the fee credit as insufficient. Litigation followed. Those settlement communications are privileged and I do not describe them further.

32. On March 14, a reporter for a trade publication called our communications office and asked whether it was true that "Bluefin Freight pulled the plug on Copperleaf Health's orders." Our communications lead, answering only from the first line of Ms. Nakamura's email, initially answered "not exactly, but there was a plug pulled, ask Bluefin." The resulting article was headlined "Bluefin severs customer's feeds amid health-data breach." Bluefin's general counsel called me the same afternoon, understandably upset. We issued a joint correction on March 15 stating that Bluefin cut one inbound feed from Saltmarsh, and cut nothing belonging to Copperleaf.

33. I mention paragraph 32 because it is my sworn belief that the defendant's expert report, discussed next, drew its theory of the case not from the logs but from that erroneous article, which our own correction had already fixed.

34. On April 18, the defendants served the report of their retained expert, Dr. H. Voss. Dr. Voss's opinion 4 states: "Copperleaf's CISO declared that his team 'killed the integration creds at 09:14,' a statement which, together with Ines Moreau's phone call, demonstrates that Copperleaf locked accounts on the MedLane platform, including the Granite console administrator account belonging to Ms. Moreau, and severed the Saltmarsh dispatch connection." I have read this sentence many times and I can report that every clause of it is wrong in a different way. We killed our own client-side integration credentials, which is what the words plainly say and what our change log shows. We did not, could not, and did not attempt to lock anything on the MedLane platform. Ms. Moreau's own employer suspended her console login, as recorded by our analyst at 08:56 on March 4 and by Granite's directory at 08:57 on March 4. EXHIBIT F — DISTRICT COURT FILING, EXCERPT (as transcribed; typos and irregular punctuation from the original are preserved)

IN RE: COPPERLEAF HEALTH SYSTEMS, INC. v. GRANITE SOFTWARE CORP. and UNKNOWN THREAT ACTORS
Case No. 22-cv-01984
DECLARATION OF JONAS MOREAU, CHIEF INFORMATION SECURITY OFFICER, COPPERLEAF HEALTH

1. I, Jonas Moreau, am the Chief Information Security Officer ("CISO") of Copperleaf Health, a regional operator of eleven clinics and two surgical centers. I make this declaration from personal knowledge and from business records kept in the ordinary course. I have worked in incident response for nineteen years. My sister, Ines Moreau, is employed by Granite Software as the lead support engineer assigned to the Copperleaf account; her role is described below and is not a role I supervise.

2. This declaration is filed in support of Copperleaf's motion for a preliminary injunction. Paragraphs 3 through 41 describe the chronology of the intrusion of March 2025 (the "Incident"). Exhibits A through G are incorporated by reference and quoted in part below. Where I quote emails or chat messages, I preserve the original wording, including typographical errors, exactly as produced by the parties during discovery.

3. Copperleaf uses Granite Software's "MedLane" integration suite to move pharmacy orders, insurance eligibility checks, and surgical scheduling records between Copperleaf's electronic health record and the systems of its business partners, which include Saltmarsh Logistics (warehousing and medical courier work) and Bluefin Freight (interfacility transport). Granite operates the MedLane cloud; Copperleaf operates its own data center in Duluth. Saltmarsh and Bluefin do not have direct network connections to each other; all partner-to-partner traffic is relayed through the MedLane cloud, which is administered by Granite, not by Copperleaf.

4. On March 4, 2025, at approximately 07:52 Central, an email arrived in the inboxes of four Copperleaf clinicians. The email purported to come from "MedLane Support <support@medlane-updates.net>" and displayed the subject line "URGENT: MedLane security patch required before 10am — your integration will be disable." The reply-to domain, medlane-updates.net, was registered on February 27, 2025, five days before the Incident. It was not a Granite domain. Granite's actual support domain is support.granitesoftware.com.

5. The email read, in full:

"Dear MedLane customer,

A critical vulnerability was discover in the MedLane connector. You must apply the security patch before 10:00 AM today or your integration will be disable and orders will not flow. Please log in with your MedLane admin credential at the portal below:

https://portal.medlane-updates.net/patch

Do not contact your IT department, as they are already aware and the portal will show them you have complyed. Apply the patch now.

— MedLane Support Team"

6. The instruction not to contact IT is significant. It is my professional opinion that this line was included to delay internal reporting. Two of the four recipients forwarded the email to our SOC. Two did not. Of the two who did not, one, Dr. P. Whitfield, navigated to the linked portal from a workstation in the Duluth surgical center and entered his MedLane administrative username and password at approximately 08:31 Central. The portal then displayed the message "Patch applied. Thank you for your cooperation." No patch existed. The page harvested credentials.

7. The fake portal was hosted at 198.51.100.77 on port 443 and served a visually convincing copy of the Granite login page, including Granite's logo, which had been scraped from Granite's public marketing site. The portal was live from 07:41 Central until 08:58 Central, when its hosting provider, acting on a report that had been submitted — as set out in paragraph 9 — took the site offline. In total the fake portal was live for 77 minutes. Approximately 40 minutes into that window, at 08:21, Granite's own abuse-monitoring system flagged inbound customer reports of the phishing domain, and Granite's security team began calling affected accounts, including ours.

8. I was in a budget meeting when my phone rang at 08:22. I reproduce my recollection of the call from my call log and from the notes of Beatriz Fischer, the SOC duty analyst who listened in on the recorded line, as follows.

9. THE 08:22 CALL. Ines Moreau of Granite Software called Copperleaf's main SOC line. She identified herself as the assigned support lead for our account. She said words to the effect of: "Jonas, we are getting customer reports of a phishing domain impersonating the MedLane portal. Do not log in to any portal today except from your bookmark. If any of your staff already did, tell me now and we will kill the session server-side." Note that it was Granite who called us. I want to be explicit, because a great deal of confusion later arose: we did not call Granite first. The vendor notified us within the hour of the phishing campaign starting — in fact within about forty minutes — and I want that plainly understood because defense counsel has suggested the reverse.

10. Beatriz Fischer checked our identity-provider logs during the call. She found a successful interactive login by the credential MedLaneAdmin-PW (Dr. Whitfield's) at 08:31:04 — wait, I correct myself: the login occurred at 08:31:04 per the IdP log, and the call from Granite began at 08:22, meaning the credential theft had not yet occurred when Granite first called. Granite called because other customers had reported the email, not because they had seen our credential used. The credential was harvested after Granite's call. I state this precisely because the sequence matters to the motion now before the court.

11. On the call, Ms. Moreau stated that she could see, from Granite's side, a suspicious session initiating from an IP address 198.51.100.77 under Dr. Whitfield's account. She asked whether that IP belonged to Copperleaf. It did not. She stated: "I'm terminating that session now and locking the account. Your staff should not use the MedLane admin login until we say so." She then terminated the session at 08:34:12 from Granite's side. This is a point I also want plainly understood: the account lockout of Dr. Whitfield's MedLane admin account was performed by Granite, on Granite's systems, at Granite's initiative. Copperleaf did not lock that account, because the account lived on Granite's platform.

12. At 08:40 I convened our incident bridge. Attendees by initials: JM (me), BF (Beatriz Fischer, SOC), DO (Dalia Okonkwo, network engineering — no relation to any party), plus Yara Okafor of Ashgrove Forensics, our retained external IR consultant, dialed in at 08:47. Dalia Alvarez of Saltmarsh Logistics and Rosa Nakamura of Bluefin Freight were not on the initial bridge; their involvement is described in paragraphs 22 through 34.

13. Between 08:41 and 09:14 Copperleaf took the following containment actions, which I enumerate exactly and no further, because in depositions there has been a tendency to attribute to Copperleaf actions we did not take:
  (a) At 08:41, we revoked the MedLane API service account credential used by our pharmacy integration (svc-pharm-bridge) and issued a replacement. The old credential was dead by 08:42.
  (b) At 08:47, we rotated the shared password on the Saltmarsh warehouse gateway device, because that gateway authenticated with a static password that had been included in the MedLane configuration bundle. I confirmed the rotation with Dalia Alvarez of Saltmarsh by phone at 08:49.
  (c) At 09:14, we killed the integration creds. By this I refer to the remaining set of MedLane-issued client credentials: the surgical scheduling service account and the insurance eligibility service account. We killed those integration creds at 09:14 per our change log, exhibit B, line 331. We did NOT kill Granite's own administrative accounts — we had no ability to, and still do not, since those live on Granite's platform.
  (d) Also at 09:14, on request from Ms. Moreau and with her on the line, I confirmed verbally that Ines Moreau's Granite console admin login — meaning her named administrator login into the MedLane administrative console — had been suspended by Granite's security team as a precaution while they investigated whether attacker activity had touched accounts she administered. To be clear as day: we did not suspend it. Granite suspended her own console admin login. I was asked to confirm on the line and I did, and that confirmation was later misread by the defendant's expert as Copperleaf having performed the suspension. We performed none.
  (e) We did not force a password reset for all clinicians at that time. A clinic-wide reset was discussed on the bridge and deliberately deferred until after business hours to avoid disrupting the surgical schedule. It is not accurate to say Copperleaf forced a client-wide password reset on March 4. We deferred it. It happened on March 7 in a controlled window, after the intrusion was contained.

14. What we did NOT do on March 4, and could not have done: block Granite's IP ranges at our perimeter. Granite's HQ egress ranges appear in exhibit D page 4; the only IPs we blocked that day were 198.51.100.77 (the phishing host), 203.0.113.0/28 (the relay used by the harvested-credential session), and one lone VPN exit in Amsterdam that showed up in our VPN logs at 09:02. Blocking Granite's own ranges would have severed MedLane for our entire pharmacy chain; no one proposed it seriously and it was not done.

15. At 09:03, the intruder — using the harvested MedLane admin credential before the 08:34 termination? No. I must correct the record here, and I ask the court's patience: the timeline was reconstructed twice, once on March 5 and again on March 12, and the second reconstruction moved two events. The harvested credential was used successfully at 08:31:04. Granite terminated the active session at 08:34:12. However, before termination the intruder had used the session to mint an API token, and it was the token, not the credential, that carried the intruder forward. This is the key fact that the initial reconstruction missed. The token was not detected until March 6.

16. Between 08:35 on March 4 and 11:22 on March 6, the token enumerated patient folders in the MedLane relay cache and pulled approximately 2.3 GB of data: mostly scheduling metadata and insurance eligibility responses, containing in aggregate the identifiers of roughly 4,187 patients. No clinical records were in the relay cache. I say this with confidence and note that opposing counsel's brief claims clinical records were taken; they were not, and we will file a correcting declaration if that claim is repeated.

17. On March 5 at 14:00, I sent the following email to Granite's security team, with a copy to my opposite number at Granite and to outside counsel:

"From: jonas.moreau@copperleafhealth.example
To: security@granitesoftware.example
Subject: RE: incident bridge notes — actions and owners

Team,

Writing down who did what so we don't argue about it later.

- You (Granite) called us at 08:22 on the 4th. First contact came from your side. The vendor notified us within the hour of the phish going out and I've told our board the same.
- You killed Dr. Whitfield's MedLane admin session at 08:34 and locked the account. We did not and could not.
- We killed the integration creds at 09:14 (svc-pharm-bridge was earlier, 08:41). Both actions ours, on our side of the fence.
- We rotated the Saltmarsh gateway password. Dalia has the new one under her seal.
- Ines's console admin login: your team suspended it. I confirmed on the call. Please don't let the court filings drift on this point.
- We blocked three attacker IPs. We did not touch your ranges.

Jonas"

18. Granite's counsel has since characterized the account in paragraph 17 as "self-serving." It is not; it was written contemporaneously, on March 5, before any litigation was contemplated, and it matches the logs. I resent the same email to their counsel on April 2 and received no correction until April 18, after which their expert produced the report discussed in paragraph 38.

19. On March 6 at 11:22, Beatriz Fischer identified the minted token during a manual review of the MedLane relay cache audit trail. The token had been created under the name "svc-billing-sync" — a name calculated to look like one of ours, but there is no Copperleaf service by that name, and Granite's directory shows the token was created at the tenant level, which only Granite-side admins or an admin credential acting on the tenant could do. Dr. Whitfield's harvested credential was a tenant admin credential. The token was revoked by Granite at 11:31 on March 6, ninety-one seconds after Ms. Fischer escalated to Granite — I note this because Granite's response here was fast and competent and I have said so in every declaration I have filed, including this one.

20. The following chat log, from Copperleaf's internal incident channel (#ir-bridge, Mattermost, retained per legal hold), is quoted as exhibit E, lines 110-214. Typos preserved.

[08:44] bfischer: bridge is up. who's on
[08:44] bfischer: jonas you there

[08:46] jmoreau: yara is NOT on granite payroll, to be clear, she's ours

[08:48] bfischer: thats whitfield

21. I adopt that chat log as accurate. I direct the court's attention to line [08:56], written by our own analyst, contemporaneously, warning that "people WILL confuse this later." That confusion arrived, in the form of the defendant's expert report, in April.

22. I turn now to the Saltmarsh and Bluefin relationships, where further confusion has been sown.

23. Saltmarsh Logistics stores Copperleaf's non-refrigerated supplies and runs the courier loop between our Duluth campus and the depot. Saltmarsh connects to Copperleaf's inventory system through a MedLane relay, and connects to Bluefin Freight's dispatch system through a second MedLane relay. Bluefin transports surgical instruments and specimens for us. Bluefin and Saltmarsh are, in a sense, both our vendors and, on one corridor, each other's counterparties. They are not affiliated companies.

24. On March 5 at 16:40, Rosa Nakamura, Bluefin's operations director, sent me an email that I quote in full because its wording has been the subject of a discovery dispute:

"From: r.nakamura@bluefinfreight.example
To: jonas.moreau@copperleafhealth.example
Subject: FYI — precautionary actions on our side

Jonas,

Heads up on what we did this morning, since you'll hear about it from the rumor mill otherwise. You called me yesterday about the phish, and we checked our inbound MedLane feeds. Two of the scheduled courier manifests in yesterday's relay showed a source IP outside the expected range. We don't think it was us who was compromised — our broker logs are clean — but the manifests passed through the MedLane cloud, which is Granite's house, not ours and not yours.

So this morning: we pulled their plug pending the review. Meaning: the Saltmarsh-to-Bluefin dispatch feed, which enters OUR dispatch system from Saltmarsh, is dark. Saltmarsh can't push manifests to us until the review is done. To be plain about who did what to whom: Bluefin cut the inbound feed FROM Saltmarsh. We did not cut anything from you, and nothing of yours was cut by us. Your own feeds to Bluefin are still running and I'd rather they stayed that way.

Also for the record, we did NOT block Copperleaf and we did NOT ask anyone to block Saltmarsh on our behalf. We did it ourselves, in our own firewall, at 09:05 this morning.

Your feed into us is dark until futher notice — no wait, scratch that, I keep mixing myself up. Let me restate: THEIR feed into us is dark. YOUR feed into us is fine. I've had three people call me today asking whether we lost access to Saltmarsh and the answer is no, we have all the access, we're the ones who closed the door on OUR side and it's Saltmarsh who can't get in. Sorry for the sloppy drafting, it's been a long day.

Rosa"

25. I quote Ms. Nakamura's email not because Copperleaf takes a position on the Bluefin-Saltmarsh corridor but because defendants' exhibit 12 mischaracterizes it as evidence that "Bluefin lost its connection to Saltmarsh." It did not. Read in full, the email says the opposite, three times, including in the correction paragraph.

26. On March 6 at 10:15, Dalia Alvarez of Saltmarsh emailed Ms. Nakamura and me:

"From: d.alvarez@saltmarshlogistics.example
To: r.nakamura@bluefinfreight.example; jonas.moreau@copperleafhealth.example
Subject: RE: dispatch feed

Rosa, Jonas,

Confirming we can see the door is closed on Bluefin's side. We are not able to push manifests to Bluefin as of 09:05 yesterday. On our side nothing is closed. Our outbound feed to Bluefin is configured and permitted; Bluefin's firewall rejects it. Our feed to Copperleaf is untouched and flowing, so Jonas, your replenishment loop is fine.

One thing I want to correct from the conference call: I said 'we suspended the feed' on the call. I misspoke. We did not suspend anything. Bluefin suspended our feed into them. My English is not always precise on calls, and I apologize.

Dalia"

27. Ms. Alvarez's correction in paragraph 26 matches Bluefin's own change record, produced as defendants' exhibit 13, which shows a firewall rule named "INBOUND-SALT-DISPATCH" set to REJECT at 09:05:00 Central on March 5 by user r.nakamura.

28. Between March 6 and March 10, Yara Okafor of Ashgrove Forensics performed the forensic reconstruction. Her preliminary report is exhibit G. Relevant findings:

  (a) The phishing email was sent from a bulk-mail infrastructure in Kyiv that had not previously touched Copperleaf.
  (b) The credential harvesting page posted the stolen credential to a collector at 203.0.113.44 within two seconds of Dr. Whitfield's submission.
  (c) The minted token "svc-billing-sync" was used from 203.0.113.51, an address in the same /28 as the collector — the two near-miss numbers have caused confusion in the press coverage, which reported them as "the same address." They are different addresses in the same block.
  (d) Exfiltration occurred in 14 sessions between 08:41 on March 4 and 11:18 on March 6, totaling 2.31 GB, of which 2.14 GB was scheduling metadata. 0.17 GB was insurance eligibility responses. 0 GB was clinical records.
  (e) No evidence of persistence inside Copperleaf's data center. The intruder never entered our network; they lived entirely inside the MedLane cloud using the tenant token. Our own perimeter held.
  (f) No evidence that Granite personnel were complicit. Ms. Moreau's actions on March 4 were, in Ms. Okafor's words, "textbook and fast."

29. Copperleaf notified affected patients starting March 12, within the 10-day window required by the state breach statute counted from March 6, the date we confirmed the token's use. The statute counts from confirmation of a reasonable likelihood of breach, not from the first phishing email; the Attorney General's office has accepted our dating and closed its inquiry on April 30.

30. On March 7 at 21:00, in the deferred window, we performed the clinic-wide password reset described in paragraph 13(e). All clinician accounts, 1,842 of them, were required to reset at next login. Three help-desk tickets were opened that night; two were resolved by 22:00 and one the next morning.

31. On March 10, Granite's chief security officer, by email, offered to pay Copperleaf's forensic costs up to $75,000 and to credit three months of MedLane fees, "without admission of fault." Copperleaf accepted the forensic-cost cap and declined the fee credit as insufficient. Litigation followed. Those settlement communications are privileged and I do not describe them further.

32. On March 14, a reporter for a trade publication called our communications office and asked whether it was true that "Bluefin Freight pulled the plug on Copperleaf Health's orders." Our communications lead, answering only from the first line of Ms. Nakamura's email, initially answered "not exactly, but there was a plug pulled, ask Bluefin." The resulting article was headlined "Bluefin severs customer's feeds amid health-data breach." Bluefin's general counsel called me the same afternoon, understandably upset. We issued a joint correction on March 15 stating that Bluefin cut one inbound feed from Saltmarsh, and cut nothing belonging to Copperleaf.

33. I mention paragraph 32 because it is my sworn belief that the defendant's expert report, discussed next, drew its theory of the case not from the logs but from that erroneous article, which our own correction had already fixed.

34. On April 18, the defendants served the report of their retained expert, Dr. H. Voss. Dr. Voss's opinion 4 states: "Copperleaf's CISO declared that his team 'killed the integration creds at 09:14,' a statement which, together with Ines Moreau's phone call, demonstrates that Copperleaf locked accounts on the MedLane platform, including the Granite console administrator account belonging to Ms. Moreau, and severed the Saltmarsh dispatch connection." I have read this sentence many times and I can report that every clause of it is wrong in a different way. We killed our own client-side integration credentials, which is what the words plainly say and what our change log shows. We did not, could not, and did not attempt to lock anything on the MedLane platform. Ms. Moreau's own employer suspended her console login, as recorded by our analyst at 08:56 on March 4 and by Granite's directory at 08:57 on March 4. And the Saltmarsh dispatch connection was severed by Bluefin, on Bluefin's firewall, per Bluefin's own change record, which Dr. Voss cites elsewhere in his report without reconciling it to this opinion.

35. Copperleaf's claim is not that Granite is liable for the phishing email. Our claim is that Granite's tenant token design allowed a single harvested admin credential to mint a long-lived token that outlived Granite's otherwise excellent session revocation, and that this design decision, documented in Granite's own 2023 internal review (exhibit H, quoted in our brief), was negligent. That 2023 review, written by a Granite engineer whose name is not among the individuals listed in this declaration, stated: "session kill should cascade to descendant tokens. Currently does not. Risk: high. Fix scheduled Q2." The fix was not made.

36. I am often asked, including in this litigation, whether I blame Dr. Whitfield. I do not. The phishing email told him not to contact IT, and it arrived at 07:52 during a morning clinic with a surgical list that started at 08:00. Sixty seconds of a busy clinician's attention, taken by a page built to look exactly like the page he uses every week. Granite's own engineers fell for a nearly identical test in their 2023 phishing exercise, at a 31 percent click rate, per exhibit H. This is not a Dr. Whitfield problem. It is a design problem and it sits on the platform.

37. On March 6 at 11:40, after the token was revoked, I sent the following note to our board, quoted for completeness because a copy was produced by the defendants:

"Board —

Status. Phishing on the 4th, one credential taken, session killed by Granite in 12 minutes from the phish landing. Token minted in the gap, found by Beatriz today, dead by 11:31 with Granite's help. 2.3 GB out, no clinical records, ~4,200 patient identifiers affected. Notification letter going out March 12.

Who did what: Granite called us first. They suspended the stolen session and, separately, their own admin's console login. We killed our client-side integration creds and rotated the Saltmarsh gateway password. Bluefin, on its own initiative, cut Saltmarsh's dispatch feed into Bluefin — nothing of ours.

Jonas"

38. Dr. Voss's supplemental report, served May 6, concedes the session-revocation point but repeats that Copperleaf "performed account lockouts on the vendor's platform." It cites paragraph 11 of this declaration. Paragraph 11 says the opposite. I am at a loss.

39. On May 9, Granite moved to exclude Ms. Okafor's testimony on the ground that Ashgrove Forensics was "retained by the attacker's ultimate victim and thus aligned." I do not understand this motion and do not address it further here.

40. Copperleaf's damages calculation, which I oversee as CISO for the forensic component: $198,000 forensic and IR labor (of which $63,400 was ours and $134,600 Ashgrove's), $41,500 patient notification, $12,900 legal hold and e-discovery, $8,750 overtime, and $28,000 for the credential-reset help desk and clinic downtime on the evening of March 7. Total $289,150, which does not include the fee-credit dispute. Defendants' brief asserts $412,000; we have asked their expert to show the additional $122,850 and have received no reconciliation.

41. I declare under penalty of perjury that the foregoing is true and correct. Executed May 14, 2025, Duluth.

/s/ Jonas Moreau
