This has been open since July, when our insurance broker pointed out that our E&O policy does not cover us for claims arising from a vendor's infringing code, a sentence that made everyone in Legal feel a specific kind of cold. The issue is closed for substance. I will report the executed signature when it exists, so that I may experience a positive emotion twice in one quarter.

2. WORK ORDERS

WO-114 — Warehouse label printer integration (Rocky Ridge DC, Callum's site). Scope: 40 printers, label templates, firmware baseline. Delivered Feb 2024, accepted, closed, paid in full March 2024 ($58,400). Zero open items. Occasionally a project simply ends. We should study it.

WO-118 — Data migration, on-prem WMS to Larkspur Cloud WMS. This is the disputed one. The SOW caps the effort at ninety (90) professional-services hours at $185/hour, which is $16,650, plus fixed infrastructure fees of $9,800, total $26,450. Larkspur's invoice of Nov 8 bills 140 hours — $25,900 in labor, plus the $9,800 infrastructure, total $35,700 — and includes in the delivered scope a "reverse synchronization module" that is not in the SOW, was never delivered in working order (it runs, in Callum's words, "with the reliability of a mood"), and which we never asked for. We issued a formal dispute notice under §15.2 on Nov 14, disputing the 50 hours above cap and the undelivered module. Larkspur's position, per their project director's Nov 22 email, is that the reverse sync was "implied by the phrase 'migration and associated integration services.'" It was not implied. If it were implied, it would not need implying. The dispute is live; the next step is the executive escalation meeting Dec 9. I have prepared a deck. The deck has eleven slides, which is nine more than the situation needs and three fewer than I originally wrote.

WO-121 — Returns portal phase two (customer-facing returns self-service). Drafted, priced at a not-to-exceed $74,000, sent to Larkspur for countersignature Nov 26. Not signed yet. It is not in dispute — nothing about it is disputed, it simply is not yet executed — and I mention it here so that nobody reads "dispute" into every work order that isn't closed. There is exactly one disputed work order, and it is WO-118, and I will keep saying that until the meeting invites stop multiplying.

3. DPA AMENDMENT — UNRESOLVED

The data processing addendum requires an updated subprocessor schedule whenever the processing chain changes. Larkspur added a new infrastructure subprocessor (hosting) in August. The DPA amendment reflecting it was drafted in September, negotiated in October, and as of today, Dec 1, it remains UNEXECUTED. Both sides agree on the text. Neither side has signed. I have sent three signature requests, each more politely worded than the last, an achievement in restraint that has gone entirely unremarked. This stays on the open-items list until a signed PDF lands in the contract file. It is a risk item because our subprocessor disclosures to the retail partners are now stale by one entry, and stale disclosures have a way of becoming interesting questions during partner audits, which brings me, conveniently, to —

4. SSAE-16 AUDIT FINDINGS — RESOLVED, DO NOT CARRY THESE FORWARD

The mid-year SSAE-16 (SOC 1) review of Larkspur's controls produced four findings in June: two around access reviews, one around change-management evidence, one around backup restoration testing. All four findings were remediated by Larkspur and independently verified in October. The verification letter is in the file, dated Oct 24. I am stating this with the bluntness of a man who has watched "audit findings" appear on three separate risk lists this quarter because someone copied an old spreadsheet. The audit findings are closed. If this item appears on a Q1 risk register I will simply lie down on the floor of the conference room.

5. INSURANCE CERTIFICATE — UNRESOLVED

The master agreement §7.3 requires Larkspur to maintain cyber liability coverage of at least $5M per occurrence and provide an annual certificate of insurance. The current certificate expired Sept 30, 2024. Larkspur's broker sent a renewal quote confirmation on Oct 3 saying the policy renewed and the certificate would follow "within the week." It is Dec 1. The week, as a unit of time, has been exceeded. We do not have the certificate. We have a promise of a certificate, which is worth less than a certificate. Open item, chased weekly, escalating to a formal §7.3 notice if not received by Dec 13.

6. LICENSE TRUE-UP — UNRESOLVED

The enterprise license covers 350 named seats for the WMS operator console. Larkspur's automated seat audit on Nov 10 counted 412 seats in active use. Sixty-two seats over. That is not a rounding error; that is a small revolt. Under §4.6, over-deployment triggers a true-up at the then-current list rate for the overage period. Larkspur issued a preliminary true-up quote of $18,600 on Nov 17. I have challenged the count — we believe roughly 40 of the overage seats are temporary accounts created during the WO-118 migration cutover and never deprovisioned, which is Larkspur's migration tooling leaving its own lights on — and Larkspur has agreed to re-run the count, but the re-run has not happened and the quote remains open. Until the corrected count and final true-up amount are issued, this is unresolved, and it sits on the risk list. I have built a seat-reconciliation worksheet. Its name is "seats." Growth.

7. NOVEMBER OUTAGE AND THE FORCE MAJEURE QUESTION

On Nov 6–7, Larkspur Cloud WMS was unavailable for 31 hours across the Rocky Ridge and two satellite DCs. Root cause, per Larkspur's incident report of Nov 12: a failed patch on their side, applied outside their own change window, which cascaded into the sync layer. During the outage, Callum — who was on site and watching 200 people suddenly rediscover paper — drafted a force majeure notice, the theory being that if Larkspur's cloud was down, their contractual service commitments were excused and, symmetrically, our own obligations downstream might need excusing. Dana and I reviewed the draft. We concluded that a patch applied by Larkspur, inside Larkspur's systems, in violation of Larkspur's own change-management procedures, is not an "act of God" in any sense recognized by §16.4 or by theology. It is an act of Larkspur. The draft force majeure letter was never sent. No force majeure was invoked by anyone, on either side, at any point. What was invoked instead was the SLA regime: see next section. I am flagging this explicitly because Callum's original draft letter is in the file, and someone reading the file without context might think we invoked something. We invoked nothing. The draft is marked DRAFT — NOT SENT in red, by Callum, who now appreciates that contracts are a genre where a filing cabinet can lie to you.

8. SLA CREDITS AND RECONCILIATION — PARTIALLY OPEN

The November outage breached the 99.5% availability commitment for the month of November. Larkspur computed and issued service credits of $4,180 for the month, per the SLA table, without us having to ask, which I acknowledge with the same suspicious gratitude one extends to a cat that finally uses the litter box. However: the credits were issued as a standalone credit memo, and they have not yet been reconciled against the open WO-118 invoice of $35,700 — which is itself in dispute. So the arithmetic reality is: disputed invoice $35,700, disputed hours portion $9,250, undelivered module $0 (we didn't order it), credit memo $4,180 floating unattached, true-up quote $18,600 also floating. Nobody's ledger matches anybody's ledger. The credit reconciliation is an unresolved open item at month end; the credit issuance itself is done and correct. If we could simply not conflate those two facts, my December would improve by a measurable amount.

9. EMAIL MIGRATION — RESOLVED, ON TIME, STOP ASKING

The migration of Foxglove's corporate mail to "Larkspur Mail" completed Oct 20, on schedule, under budget, with a cutover window that was planned, communicated, and respected. It went so smoothly that I have nothing sarcastic to say about it, which unsettles me more than the outage did. It is on the "done" list. It appears on no risk list. If it appears on a risk list I will know we have collectively given up.

10. OPEN ITEMS AT MONTH END (DEC 1)

a. WO-118 dispute — active, escalation meeting Dec 9.
b. DPA amendment — agreed, unexecuted, signature chased.
c. Cyber insurance certificate — expired Sept 30, renewal certificate not received, §7.3 notice threatened for Dec 13.
d. License true-up — count challenged, re-run pending, $18,600 preliminary quote open.
e. SLA credit reconciliation — $4,180 credit memo not yet applied against the disputed WO-118 invoice.

Closed this quarter, do not reopen: IP indemnity agreement (in writing, Nov 19), SSAE-16 audit findings (verified remediated, Oct 24), WO-114 (paid), email migration (on time).

APPENDIX A — TYPED-UP SITE NOTE, CALLUM OKAFOR, ROCKY RIDGE DC (ORIGINALLY HANDWRITTEN, NOV 21)

"Typed this up myself because last time I sent the scan Legal said my handwriting 'presented an evidentiary challenge,' which I have chosen to be flattered by. Site note for the file, Nov 21, Rocky Ridge:

Migration cutover under WO-118 went live Nov 3. Weekend of Nov 2–3, 90 hours of planned work became 140 actual hours because their migration tool doesn't handle our item master variants and someone had to build field mapping by hand. By 'someone' I mean their consultant and me, at 2 a.m., on a whiteboard we photographed like a crime scene. The 50 hours over the cap happened on their side of the board. I have the photos. The reverse sync module: runs sometimes. It synced a return twice on Nov 19 and we caught it in the daily exception report, which is a sentence I'd like carved somewhere. We never asked for this module. Their PM showed it to us in a demo in September like a magic trick we hadn't requested. We did not sign for a magic trick.

The Nov 6–7 outage: 31 hours, 200 staff on paper processes, the loudest quiet I have ever heard in a DC. I drafted a force majeure letter that Tuesday because 'force majeure' was the only French phrase in my notes app. Dana and Oren talked me out of it by Wednesday with the reasoning that their failed patch is their fault, not a hurricane, and 'their fault' is the opposite of force majeure. Draft never sent. Nothing was invoked. I have written NOT SENT on it in a color of ink I don't use for anything else.

The Larkspur field crew themselves were good people in a bad situation, which is the most I can say about any vendor.

Recommend: hold the line at 90 hours, reject the reverse sync line item entirely, get the certificate of insurance, fix the seat count, and buy the night shift pizza for the next cutover regardless of who pays for the hours. — C.O."

APPENDIX B — CORRESPONDENCE LOG (EXTRACT)

Jul 9 — Broker letter re: E&O gap on vendor IP claims.
Nov 8 — Larkspur invoice, WO-118, $35,700.
Nov 12 — Larkspur incident report, Nov 6–7 outage, root cause: failed patch applied outside change window.
Nov 14 — Foxglove dispute notice to Larkspur under §15.2 (WO-118 hours and module).
Nov 17 — Larkspur preliminary true-up quote, $18,600 (62 seats over).
Nov 19 — Larkspur counsel email: agrees to add IP indemnity to §9; amendment packet routing.
Nov 21 — Callum Okafor site note (Appendix A).
Nov 22 — Larkspur project director email: reverse sync "implied" by SOW language.
Nov 26 — WO-121 sent to Larkspur for countersignature. Not yet signed.
Dec 1 — This status update.

That's the whole picture, Tomasz. One work order disputed, one indemnity won, four risks open, one cat-and-litter-box moment with the SLA credits, and a filing cabinet that now contains one force majeure letter that must never be mistaken for a sent one. Forward freely. I'll be at the Dec 9 escalation meeting with the eleven slides and, by then, hopefully the insurance certificate.

— Oren Bergstrom
Contracts & Vendor Manager, Foxglove Outfitters

"Good morning, this is Zoltan Moreau calling from Tidewater Dental, and I do apologize for taking up your morning. Our autoclave — the Midmark M11 in Sterilization Room B — has been making the most dreadful rattling noise since Monday, and, well, if it isn't too much trouble, we would be so grateful if someone could come look at it. I should mention, and please don't let this rush you, that if the rattling continues into next week we may have to rent a backup unit, because the county inspector visits us on the 14th and we simply cannot fail that visit. I'm not saying it's broken, mind you — it still sterilizes perfectly, we ran the spore test this morning and it passed beautifully — it's only the noise, which the manual says, and I quote, 'should never be ignored,' although honestly I suspect the manual says that about everything.

Now, our maintenance plan — I believe we're on the Silver plan, which covers parts but not labor, or perhaps it's the other way around; Beatriz Fischer in our front office handles the paperwork and she would know. She'll be out until Thursday, I'm afraid. The unit itself we purchased in March of 2019, so if I understand your warranty terms correctly, and please correct me if I've mangled them, we are just past the five-year compressor warranty but the chamber itself is covered for ten years, which I found quite generous.

Oh, and one more small thing, and I hope this isn't presumptuous — our previous technician, lovely man, mentioned last spring that if we ever heard grinding rather than rattling we should call immediately, as grinding indicates the bearing. What we hear is rattling, not grinding, so I haven't called your emergency line, but I wanted to be transparent about it. Also, and I know this is terribly forward of me, your dispatcher might see a note on our file about an unpaid invoice from 2021 — that was resolved ages ago, the check simply crossed in the mail.

If you could have someone out before the 14th we would be ever so thankful, but truly, no rush, we know you're busy. Thank you kindly, and have a wonderful day."

MEETING NOTES — Field Service Review — Kestrel Studio — 2024-04-16, 10:00–10:50 — Present: Yara Okafor (facilities), Priya Mensah (technician lead), plus two guests from accounts payable.

Yara opened by apologizing profusely for the short notice of the meeting and thanked everyone for coming. Agenda: the embroidery machine, the rooftop HVAC, and the small matter of the kiln.

1. EMBROIDERY MACHINE (Bernette Deco). Priya reported that the machine seized on April 9 and was repaired on April 10, at a parts cost of $340 and labor of $220, totaling $560. Yara asked whether this fell under the service contract; Priya said the contract lapsed in January and, had it been renewed, the parts would have been covered — 'but it wasn't, so the invoice stands, I'm terribly sorry.' Accounts payable noted the invoice was already paid on April 12, so no action. Yara asked whether the machine was working now; Priya confirmed it stitched a full test run on April 11 without a single skipped stitch.

2. ROOFTOP HVAC. Priya said the spring inspection is booked for April 22. Yara asked if it could be moved earlier because the design team complains the studio is stuffy on warm afternoons; Priya gently explained the duct cleaning was already done in February, so the stuffiness, if it persists, would be a ventilation-balance question rather than a cleaning one, and she would hate to promise anything before the inspection. QUILLCARD DISPUTE AND CHARGEBACK POLICY — Public policy page, effective 1 February.

1. Who can file. Only the cardholder named on the account may open a dispute. An authorized user may report a transaction, but the dispute is opened under the primary cardholder's name. Third parties, including family members and estate representatives, cannot file.

2. Time limits. A dispute must be submitted within 120 days of the transaction date shown on the statement. The transaction date is the date the merchant processed the payment, not the date the goods arrived. If the merchant promised delivery on a later date, the 120 days count from the promised delivery date instead. For recurring billing, each charge has its own 120-day window.

3. Goods not received. If you paid but the merchant never sent the goods, select reason code ' merchandise not received '. You must first attempt to resolve with the merchant and attach proof of the attempt — an email, a chat log, or a note that the merchant's phone line was disconnected. Proof of purchase is also required. If the merchant provides a tracking number, we will check the carrier record; if the carrier shows delivery to the billing address, the dispute will be closed in the merchant's favour unless you can show the parcel was empty or was signed by someone not at your address.

4. Defective or not as described. Photos are required. A dispute for ' not as described ' cannot be opened if the item differs only in colour shade, size label, or packaging, unless the merchant's own listing promised otherwise in writing.

5. Duplicate charges. If the same amount was charged twice on the same day to the same merchant, select ' duplicate '. Amounts that differ by even a small fee are not duplicates and must be disputed as ' overcharge ' instead.

6. Fraud. If you did not authorize the transaction and did not receive any benefit from it, select ' unauthorized '. Important: if you gave your card details to a website that later turned out to be a scam, this is still processed as unauthorized only if the merchant was not the party you intended to pay. If you paid a merchant willingly and the merchant simply never delivered, that is Section 3, not fraud. Family members using the card without permission is handled under our household policy and is not fraud for dispute purposes.

7. Refunds versus disputes. If a refund request means the sender explicitly asks for money back: a refund request alone does not block a dispute, but if the merchant has already issued a refund that posts to the account, the dispute must be withdrawn. A promised refund that has not posted does not count.

8. Currency. The dispute amount is converted at the rate of the transaction date. Partial refunds in a foreign currency are credited at the same rate; we do not use today's rate.

9. Subscriptions cancelled. If a subscription was cancelled before the billing date but the charge went through anyway, select ' unauthorized ' and attach the cancellation confirmation. A cancellation made after the billing date does not qualify; the charge stands but future ones are stopped.

10. Credit balance. Amounts recovered from a dispute are first applied to any negative balance on the account. If the account is in good standing, the credit is returned to the original payment method within 5 business days.

11. Escalation. Decisions can be appealed once within 30 days of the decision letter. Appeals are reviewed by a different team. Additional evidence is required; an appeal without new evidence is returned unread.

12. Temporary credit. For unauthorized claims only, a temporary credit is given within 10 business days. It is removed if the merchant's evidence prevails. Temporary credits are not offered for ' not received ' or ' not as described ' claims.

13. Merchant bankruptcy. If the merchant is bankrupt, disputes are still accepted, but recovery is not guaranteed and the claim may be closed with no funds recovered. Bankruptcy of the cardholder does not affect an open dispute.

QUILLCARD DISPUTE AND CHARGEBACK POLICY — Public policy page, effective 1 February.

1. Who can file. Only the cardholder named on the account may open a dispute. An authorized user may report a transaction, but the dispute is opened under the primary cardholder's name. Third parties, including family members and estate representatives, cannot file.

2. Time limits. A dispute must be submitted within 120 days of the transaction date shown on the statement. The transaction date is the date the merchant processed the payment, not the date the goods arrived. If the merchant promised delivery on a later date, the 120 days count from the promised delivery date instead. For recurring billing, each charge has its own 120-day window.

3. Goods not received. If you paid but the merchant never sent the goods, select reason code ' merchandise not received '. You must first attempt to resolve with the merchant and attach proof of the attempt — an email, a chat log, or a note that the merchant's phone line was disconnected. Proof of purchase is also required. If the merchant provides a tracking number, we will check the carrier record; if the carrier shows delivery to the billing address, the dispute will be closed in the merchant's favour unless you can show the parcel was empty or was signed by someone not at your address.

4. Defective or not as described. Photos are required. A dispute for ' not as described ' cannot be opened if the item differs only in colour shade, size label, or packaging, unless the merchant's own listing promised otherwise in writing.

5. Duplicate charges. If the same amount was charged twice on the same day to the same merchant, select ' duplicate '. Amounts that differ by even a small fee are not duplicates and must be disputed as ' overcharge ' instead.

6. Fraud. If you did not authorize the transaction and did not receive any benefit from it, select ' unauthorized '. Important: if you gave your card details to a website that later turned out to be a scam, this is still processed as unauthorized only if the merchant was not the party you intended to pay. If you paid a merchant willingly and the merchant simply never delivered, that is Section 3, not fraud. Family members using the card without permission is handled under our household policy and is not fraud for dispute purposes.

7. Refunds versus disputes. If a refund request means the sender explicitly asks for money back: a refund request alone does not block a dispute, but if the merchant has already issued a refund that posts to the account, the dispute must be withdrawn. A promised refund that has not posted does not count.

8. Currency. The dispute amount is converted at the rate of the transaction date. Partial refunds in a foreign currency are credited at the same rate; we do not use today's rate.

9. Subscriptions cancelled. If a subscription was cancelled before the billing date but the charge went through anyway, select ' unauthorized ' and attach the cancellation confirmation. A cancellation made after the billing date does not qualify; the charge stands but future ones are stopped.

10. Credit balance. Amounts recovered from a dispute are first applied to any negative balance on the account. If the account is in good standing, the credit is returned to the original payment method within 5 business days.

11. Escalation. Decisions can be appealed once within 30 days of the decision letter. Appeals are reviewed by a different team. Additional evidence is required; an appeal without new evidence is returned unread.

12. Temporary credit. For unauthorized claims only, a temporary credit is given within 10 business days. It is removed if the merchant's evidence prevails. Temporary credits are not offered for ' not received ' or ' not as described ' claims.

13. Merchant bankruptcy. If the merchant is bankrupt, disputes are still accepted, but recovery is not guaranteed and the claim may be closed with no funds recovered. Bankruptcy of the cardholder does not affect an open dispute.

QUILLCARD FRAUD AND UNAUTHORIZED TRANSACTION GUIDE — customer help page, updated last quarter.

Introduction. This guide explains how Quillcard treats 'unauthorized transaction' claims on personal debit and credit cards. Read all sections before filing, because the reason code you choose decides the evidence we need.

Section A — Definition. An unauthorized transaction is a card charge you did not make, did not permit anyone to make, and from which you received no goods, services, or benefit. The definition has three parts and all three must be true. If any part fails, the claim is not unauthorized and belongs to another category.

Section B — Family and household. Charges made by a spouse, child, or anyone living at your address who had access to the card or the card details are treated as household disputes. They are NOT unauthorized. We know this is frustrating; the remedy is to request a refund from the merchant or remove the person's access. Exception: if the card was physically stolen from your home by a visitor and you filed a police report within 7 days, the charge is processed as unauthorized theft.

Section C — Card details given away. If you typed your card number into a website, the charge is unauthorized only if the party who took the money was not the party you intended to pay. Example: you bought shoes from 'Alpine Shoes' and the charge came from 'Alpine Shoes' but no shoes arrived — that is a goods-not-received claim, not fraud. Example: you bought shoes from 'Alpine Shoes' but the charge line shows 'GZT-MEDIA' and you never heard of them — that is unauthorized, because the taker was not the intended payee.

Section D — Subscriptions and trials. A free trial that converts to a paid subscription is not unauthorized if the terms disclosed the conversion, even if you did not read them. It is unauthorized if you cancelled before the conversion date and can show a confirmation number. A charge after cancellation is unauthorized if the cancellation confirmation exists; without confirmation we treat it as a billing error claim, which has a lower recovery rate.

Section E — Amounts and partial deliveries. If you ordered and paid 120.00 euro and received part of the order, the claim is 'partial goods received', not unauthorized. If the merchant charged 240.00 instead of the agreed 120.00, the claim is 'overcharge'. Only a wholly foreign charge qualifies under Section A.

Section F — Timing. Unauthorized claims must be filed within 90 days of the statement date showing the charge, which is different from the 120-day limit for goods claims. Statement date means the date printed at the top of the monthly statement, not the transaction line date. If your statement prints on the 28th and the charge was on the 30th, the clock starts from the 28th of the NEXT month, which can help you.

Section G — Evidence. For unauthorized claims we require: a statement copy, a declaration that you did not benefit from the charge, and, for online charges, confirmation that you reported the card number compromised to our hotline. If the hotline call was not made, the claim is registered but placed on hold, and funds are not provisionally credited until you call.

Section H — Merchant refunds interplay. If the merchant refunds the charge while our investigation is open, the claim is closed as 'resolved by merchant' and no further action is needed from you. If the merchant refunds only part, the claim continues for the remaining balance only. If the merchant promises a refund but does not post it within 10 business days of the promise, the promise counts for nothing and the full claim continues.

Section I — Crypto and gambling. Charges to gambling merchants made by the cardholder are never unauthorized, even if you regret them, even if you were intoxicated. Charges to cryptocurrency exchanges are unauthorized only if the transfer was not made from your own device or IP address.

Section J — Small amounts. There is no minimum. Claims of 1.00 euro are accepted, because small unauthorized charges are often card-testing by criminals.

question.instruction: A charge qualifies as unauthorized only if all three parts of Section A hold. Would a husband's online purchase with the wife's card count?

notes: Section B: household member with access is a household dispute, not unauthorized; theft exception needs police report.

From: Quill Dental <reception@quilldental.example>
To: Xiu Bergstrom <xiu.bergstrom@mail.example>
Subject: Your card dispute form — internal review complete
Date: 8 May

Dear Ms Bergstrom,

We write about dispute form D-2205 you signed at our front desk on 30 April concerning your treatment account. This is our internal review before your bank is involved. Please read the whole letter, because some points are in your favour and some are not, and we want to be transparent.

History of the account. You were our patient from August last year. Treatment plan TP-19 was agreed in writing on 12 August: two crowns at 480.00 euro each and one filling at 120.00 euro, total estimate 1,080.00 euro, payable in three instalments of 360.00 euro. You signed the plan. The first instalment was paid by card on 15 August. The second instalment was paid by card on 15 November. The third instalment was paid by card on 14 February this year. All three payments appear on our system and, we believe, on your statement.

Now the matters from your form. On the form you ticked four boxes. Let us take them one by one.

Item 1 — 'I was charged more than agreed'. Our ledger shows exactly three payments of 360.00 euro, total 1,080.00 euro, which is exactly the written estimate. However, we note that on 14 February the card terminal produced two receipts for the third instalment: receipt 8811 for 360.00 euro and receipt 8812 for 360.00 euro. Our bank reconciliation shows only one of these, receipt 8811, was actually captured. Receipt 8812 was a machine glitch and voided same day. If your statement shows two debits on 14 February, please send the statement and we will ask the terminal provider, but from our records only one amount left your card.

Item 2 — 'Treatment was not completed'. The second crown, lower left, was placed on 20 February. The filling was completed on 5 March. All planned work is finished. We attach the clinical notes. If you mean the polishing appointment, that is optional cosmetic work not in plan TP-19 and was never charged.

Item 3 — 'I did not authorize card payments'. Your signature card from August authorizes card charges for treatment instalments. This item cannot apply while the signature card exists, and we have it on file. We mention, since you asked at the desk, that your son once collected an invoice from us; this does not change the authorization, which is yours.

Item 4 — 'Refund requested for the second crown because it fell out'. The crown did come loose on 10 April, which is within our 12-month workmanship warranty. Under the warranty we recement or replace the crown free of charge. The warranty gives free corrective treatment; it does not give money back, and you signed acknowledgement of this wording in August. We can offer a replacement appointment on any Tuesday in May.

Summary of our position. We can offer: recementing or replacing the crown under warranty at no cost. We cannot offer: a monetary refund, because the warranty provides treatment only. Regarding the possible double debit of 14 February, we are neutral: if your bank statement truly shows two debits of 360.00, we will support a duplicate-charge claim with the terminal provider; if it shows one, the item is closed.

If you remain unsatisfied, you may of course proceed to your card issuer, Quillcard, and we will provide all records to them. We would prefer to fix the crown first, honestly, it is a five-minute recement and you keep a good tooth.

With respect,
Reception and Accounts,
Quill Dental

Note added by hand at the bottom: 'Copy placed in patient chart, discussed by phone with patient same day, she says she will think about the crown appointment.'

question.instruction: Regarding the disputed double debit of 14 February, does the clinic confirm both charges actually left her card?

notes: Two receipts exist but clinic records show only receipt 8811 captured; second was voided. Claim depends on her statement, which is not shown.

EMBERWAKE COMMUNITY COUNCIL — QUARTERLY MEETING NOTES
Game: Emberwake (developed by Quill Labs)
Community: The Emberfall Collective
Date: Sat, Oct 14
Duration: approx 3 hrs 40 min
Present: Bao Delgado (guild liaison), Nadia Okafor (events coordinator), Rosa Okafor (forum moderator), Viktor Delgado (treasurer), Mateo Alvarez (raid council rep), Oren Haddad (Discord admin)
Chair: Nadia Okafor
Notetaker: Rosa Okafor (typos hers, blame the keyboard)

AGENDA
1. Attendance + apologies
2. Minutes of last meeting

4. Autumn Emberfall event post-mortem
5. Winter Solstice raid planning
6. Moderation report + ban appeals
7. New raid lead appointment
8. Server + tooling costs
9. Kestrel Analytics survey results
10. AOB + action item roll-up

--- 1. ATTENDANCE + APOLOGIES ---

Nadia opens the meeting at 19:02 UTC. Everyone on the call within a couple minutes except Mateo, who drops in at 19:09 because his internet "died for the third time this week, im switching providers in nov for real this time."

Apologies from previous head moderator Pavel (not present, not a council member anymore, left the community in Sept to focus on irl stuff — good luck to him).

Quill Labs sent their monthly community newsletter but no representative. Rosa reads one line out of it: "Patch 4.3 lands Oct 24, Emberfall event currency converts 1:1 into Solstice tokens." Everyone claps in text. Nadia says we should plan around that date.

Action from this item: none.

--- 2. MINUTES OF LAST MEETING ---

Rosa reads out the minutes of the Sept meeting. Key points carried over:
- Treasury audit was postponed (carried to item 7 today, now item 3, we renumbered, sorry)
- The guild bank reimbursement policy was APPROVED as drafted: members can claim back up to 40 gold per month for consumables used in official raids, receipts (screenshots) required.
- The old voice channel "ember-lounge-2" was archived because nobody used it.
- Mateo promised to deliver a raid sign-up spreadsheet by Oct 1. He did not. He says it's 80 percent done and blames a corrupted google account. Nadia gives him a new deadline of Oct 20.

Minutes approved. Proposed by Bao, seconded by Viktor, none against, one abstention (Mateo, "conflict of interest lol").

--- 3. TREASURER REPORT ---

Viktor presents the numbers for Jul–Sep (all figures in USD):

Income:
- Member donations (Discord booster perks + direct): $412.50
- Merch test batch (12 Emberfall t-shirts at $18 each, sold at $24): $288.00
- One-off sponsorship from Tidewater Outfitters (they gave us gaming mousepads for a giveaway, no cash): $0 cash, ~$140 in-kind

Expenses:
- Discord server boost continuation: $96.00
- Bot subscription (Nightbot premium, 3 months): $45.00
- Domain renewal (emberfall.gg, 2 years): $58.00
- Event prize pool for Autumn Emberfall: $120.00
- Design commission for new banner (artist outside the community, invoiced): $85.00

Viktor notes the banner commission went to an artist found through the community, which he says is a nice touch, and that he personally fronted the domain renewal in Sept and got reimbursed on Oct 2 from guild funds. Bao asks whether that counts against his own 40 gold monthly consumable cap. Viktor says no, that cap is for game consumables only, real money costs are separate, per the policy approved last month.

Oren asks if we should set up a separate savings buffer. Viktor proposes moving $300 into a "rainy day" line item. Agreed, no objection.

Rosa asks about the Meridian Rentals invoice that appeared in the shared inbox. Viktor explains Meridian Rentals rented us event equipment for the Autumn Emberfall LAN corner (two monitors, one projector) and the invoice was $75, already paid from the prize pool line, so it's included in the $120 above. The invoice is filed in the drive.

One correction issued during the meeting: Viktor initially said the bank balance was $1,383.22, then corrected himself after re-checking the statement: the correct figure is $1,483.22. The minutes reflect the corrected number.

--- 4. AUTUMN EMBERFALL EVENT POST-MORTEM ---

Nadia ran the Autumn Emberfall event Sept 29–Oct 1. Attendance: 214 unique participants across the weekend, up from 168 at the spring event.

What worked:
- The scavenger hunt had 96 teams sign up, way more than the 60 cap, so they raised the cap to 80 on day one
- The costume contest got 41 entries, judged by a three-person panel (Bao, Oren, and one outside judge from Quill Labs community team)
- The LAN corner with Meridian Rentals gear was busy all three days

What didn't:
- The final world boss spawned 40 minutes late because of a scripting bug, and about 30 people left before it appeared
- Two of the scavenger hunt clue locations were inside a dungeon that required a paid expansion pass, which nobody checked in advance, so free-to-play teams couldn't finish. Rosa says this was her oversight since she wrote the clues. She apologizes, nobody is mad, we fix it next time: all clue locations must be accessible on the free tier, and we add a checklist step to event prep.
- The prize pool was supposed to be split 50/30/20 across the top three scavenger teams but the bot that computed payouts used the wrong column and split it 40/40/20. The three team captains were informed, the two affected teams each received the missing share on Oct 4, and the payout bug is now fixed. Total paid out was still exactly $120 because the pool itself didn't change, just the split.

Mateo asks whether we can get an event in the game client next time rather than only on Discord. Nadia says she'll ask the Quill Labs community manager about a spotlight slot for the Winter Solstice raid.

--- 5. WINTER SOLSTICE RAID PLANNING ---

Main topic: the Winter Solstice raid, scheduled for Dec 16–17.

Current plan draft:
- Two evening raids, 19:00–23:00 UTC each day, Dec 16 (boss: Frostmaw) and Dec 17 (boss: the Longest Night)
- Sign-ups open Nov 20, close Dec 10
- Roster cap: 40 per raid, with a 6-person waitlist each night
- Consumables for both nights provided from the guild bank, within the approved 40 gold per member per month policy
- New sign-up tool: Mateo's spreadsheet (still not done) plus a backup bot if it isn't ready

Bao raises that Dec 16 is a Saturday and Dec 17 a Sunday this year, which is good for turnout. Nadia confirms. Oren checks: yes, Dec 16 falls on a Saturday in the current calendar.

Rosa proposes a lore-writing contest to run alongside the raid: short stories about the Longest Night, max 1,000 words, entries due Dec 3, winner gets a custom forum title. Council likes it. Rosa takes the action item to write the contest rules by Nov 15.

Viktor asks about the budget. Estimated costs: prize pool $150, extra bot tier for the sign-up surge $20, possibly another Meridian Rentals equipment order (~$80). Total roughly $250 against a balance of $1,483. Approved in principle, final sign-off at the Nov meeting.

Mateo suggests inviting Quill Labs devs to spectate the Dec 17 raid. Nadia will reach out after patch 4.3 lands so we know if the Longest Night fight is being reworked.

--- 6. MODERATION REPORT + BAN APPEALS ---

Rosa presents the moderation summary for the quarter:
- 38 warnings issued
- 9 temporary mutes (ranging 6h to 72h)
- 3 permanent bans
- 2 of the 3 permanent bans have appeals pending

The three permanent bans:
(a) User "ashen_wolf" — repeated harassment in general chat after two prior warnings. No appeal filed.
(b) User "kilnfire" — cheating: confirmed use of a damage script during a raid, detected by the anticheat and admitted by the user in DMs to a mod. kilnfire filed an appeal on Oct 3 stating they have removed the script and asking to be let back in. The council discusses. Vote: deny the appeal. Reasoning: cheating during official raids undermines the raid council's results, and the appeal admits the conduct but the policy sets a minimum one-year term before a cheating appeal can even be considered. kilnfire was banned Sept 22, so the earliest appeal date under policy would be Sept 22 next year. Rosa will inform them of the policy timeline and that they may re-appeal after that date.
(c) User "quiet_bramble" — ban issued in error. Originally banned Sept 30 for "raid disruption" during the world boss delay, but log review (completed Oct 8 by Oren) shows quiet_bramble was simply posting countdown messages like everyone else; the mod tool mis-attributed a spam wave to them. quiet_bramble filed an appeal on Oct 2 saying: "I don't think I did anything wrong, the ban seems to have hit the wrong person, can you please lift it?" The council reviews Oren's log report. Vote: lift the ban immediately, apologize formally, and grant a small goodwill gesture (a forum badge "Patient Understudy"). Rosa will send the apology and restore access by Oct 16.

Rosa also reports a general trend: flagged messages in #theory-crafting are mostly heated but civil, so no action; a new #clips channel is generating occasional spoiler reports; the mod team handled 214 reports this quarter, median response time 47 minutes.

Oren asks whether the mod tool that mis-attributed the spam wave has been fixed. Rosa says the vendor pushed a patch, and Oren adds that he'll verify the attribution logic before the Solstice raids so we don't repeat the quiet_bramble situation. Noted as an action item.

--- 7. NEW RAID LEAD APPOINTMENT ---

The raid council needed a new raid lead after the previous one (Pavel) stepped down in Sept. Two candidates were put forward by the raid council: Nadia Okafor and Mateo Alvarez.

Mateo withdraws his own candidacy during the meeting, saying: "honestly with the spreadsheet still unfinished and my internet being what it is, i cant give the role the time. put my name back in next cycle."

With one candidate remaining, the council votes on appointing Nadia Okafor as raid lead. Vote: 5 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions (Nadia herself doesn't vote on her own appointment). Appointment confirmed. Nadia will lead her first official raid at the Winter Solstice event, with Pavel's old co-lead duties split between Mateo (rosters) and Bao (tactics docs).

Nadia notes she'll stay as events coordinator too until the spring, when the council will revisit whether one person should hold both roles.

--- 8. SERVER + TOOLING COSTS ---

Oren reports:
- Discord server: currently at 14 boosts, level 2. If we hit 30 boosts we get level 3 and better audio. A boost drive will run Nov 1–30.
- Nightbot premium renews Jan 5, $60 for the next 6 months (price went up from $45/3mo to $60/6mo, which is actually cheaper per month)
- The community wiki host (Quill Labs' official wiki platform, free) is fine, no cost
- Kestrel Analytics provided survey tooling free of charge this quarter in exchange for the survey results being shared with them in anonymized form; council approved that arrangement last meeting

Oren flags that the old "ember-lounge-2" archive should be deleted entirely by Dec 1 to save a tiny bit of storage, purely housekeeping.

--- 9. KESTREL ANALYTICS SURVEY RESULTS ---

Nadia presents highlights from the community survey run by Kestrel Analytics (312 respondents, ~55% of active members):
- 71% said event timing works for them; the main complaint group is APAC-timezone members (19% of respondents) who want at least one event starting before 10:00 UTC
- 44% want more lore/roleplay content, which supports Rosa's writing contest idea
- Favorite event types: scavenger hunt 39%, raid nights 34%, costume contest 15%, trivia 8%, other 4%
- 62% were unaware the guild bank consumable reimbursement policy exists, so we need to advertise it
- 27% report experiencing toxicity in voice chat "sometimes" — mod team will add a second active voice mod during raid nights
- Median time in community: 14 months

Bao asks whether Kestrel Analytics got the raw data with usernames. Nadia confirms no — the data was anonymized before sharing, per the arrangement approved last meeting. Viktor double-checks the anonymization script output later in the meeting and confirms it strips all identifiers.

--- 10. AOB + ACTION ITEM ROLL-UP ---

- Viktor will move $300 into the rainy-day line item by Oct 20
- Viktor will publish the quarterly finance sheet to the members-only channel by Oct 18
- Rosa will send the quiet_bramble apology and restore access by Oct 16
- Rosa will write the lore contest rules by Nov 15
- Rosa will tell kilnfire the appeal is denied until next Sept under policy, message to go out by Oct 15
- Oren will verify the mod tool attribution logic before the Solstice raids, target Dec 1
- Oren will delete the ember-lounge-2 archive by Dec 1
- Nadia will contact the Quill Labs community manager about a spotlight slot and dev spectators after patch 4.3 (week of Oct 24)
- Nadia will draft the APAC-friendly event slot proposal for the Nov meeting
- Mateo will finish the raid sign-up spreadsheet by Oct 20
- Mateo will handle raid rosters as co-lead support
- Bao will draft the tactics docs for Frostmaw and the Longest Night by Dec 5
- Bao will add the free-tier accessibility checklist to event prep (with Rosa)

Meeting closes 22:41 UTC. Next meeting: Nov 11, 19:00 UTC.

APPENDIX A — BAN APPEAL TEXTS (as filed)

Appeal 1, from kilnfire, filed Oct 3:

The council reviews Oren's log report. Vote: lift the ban immediately, apologize formally, and grant a small goodwill gesture (a forum badge "Patient Understudy"). Rosa will send the apology and restore access by Oct 16.

Rosa also reports a general trend: flagged messages in #theory-crafting are mostly heated but civil, so no action; a new #clips channel is generating occasional spoiler reports; the mod team handled 214 reports this quarter, median response time 47 minutes.

Oren asks whether the mod tool that mis-attributed the spam wave has been fixed. Rosa says the vendor pushed a patch, and Oren adds that he'll verify the attribution logic before the Solstice raids so we don't repeat the quiet_bramble situation. Noted as an action item.

--- 7. NEW RAID LEAD APPOINTMENT ---

The raid council needed a new raid lead after the previous one (Pavel) stepped down in Sept. Two candidates were put forward by the raid council: Nadia Okafor and Mateo Alvarez.

Mateo withdraws his own candidacy during the meeting, saying: "honestly with the spreadsheet still unfinished and my internet being what it is, i cant give the role the time. put my name back in next cycle."

With one candidate remaining, the council votes on appointing Nadia Okafor as raid lead. Vote: 5 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions (Nadia herself doesn't vote on her own appointment). Appointment confirmed. Nadia will lead her first official raid at the Winter Solstice event, with Pavel's old co-lead duties split between Mateo (rosters) and Bao (tactics docs).

Nadia notes she'll stay as events coordinator too until the spring, when the council will revisit whether one person should hold both roles.

--- 8. SERVER + TOOLING COSTS ---

Oren reports:
- Discord server: currently at 14 boosts, level 2. If we hit 30 boosts we get level 3 and better audio. A boost drive will run Nov 1–30.
- Nightbot premium renews Jan 5, $60 for the next 6 months (price went up from $45/3mo to $60/6mo, which is actually cheaper per month)
- The community wiki host (Quill Labs' official wiki platform, free) is fine, no cost
- Kestrel Analytics provided survey tooling free of charge this quarter in exchange for the survey results being shared with them in anonymized form; council approved that arrangement last meeting

Oren flags that the old "ember-lounge-2" archive should be deleted entirely by Dec 1 to save a tiny bit of storage, purely housekeeping.

--- 9. KESTREL ANALYTICS SURVEY RESULTS ---

Nadia presents highlights from the community survey run by Kestrel Analytics (312 respondents, ~55% of active members):
- 71% said event timing works for them; the main complaint group is APAC-timezone members (19% of respondents) who want at least one event starting before 10:00 UTC
- 44% want more lore/roleplay content, which supports Rosa's writing contest idea
- Favorite event types: scavenger hunt 39%, raid nights 34%, costume contest 15%, trivia 8%, other 4%
- 62% were unaware the guild bank consumable reimbursement policy exists, so we need to advertise it
- 27% report experiencing toxicity in voice chat "sometimes" — mod team will add a second active voice mod during raid nights
- Median time in community: 14 months

Bao asks whether Kestrel Analytics got the raw data with usernames. Nadia confirms no — the data was anonymized before sharing, per the arrangement approved last meeting. Viktor double-checks the anonymization script output later in the meeting and confirms it strips all identifiers.

--- 10. AOB + ACTION ITEM ROLL-UP ---

- Viktor will move $300 into the rainy-day line item by Oct 20
- Viktor will publish the quarterly finance sheet to the members-only channel by Oct 18
- Rosa will send the quiet_bramble apology and restore access by Oct 16
- Rosa will write the lore contest rules by Nov 15
- Rosa will tell kilnfire the appeal is denied until next Sept under policy, message to go out by Oct 15
- Oren will verify the mod tool attribution logic before the Solstice raids, target Dec 1
- Oren will delete the ember-lounge-2 archive by Dec 1
- Nadia will contact the Quill Labs community manager about a spotlight slot and dev spectators after patch 4.3 (week of Oct 24)
- Nadia will draft the APAC-friendly event slot proposal for the Nov meeting
- Mateo will finish the raid sign-up spreadsheet by Oct 20
- Mateo will handle raid rosters as co-lead support
- Bao will draft the tactics docs for Frostmaw and the Longest Night by Dec 5
- Bao will add the free-tier accessibility checklist to event prep (with Rosa)

Meeting closes 22:41 UTC. Next meeting: Nov 11, 19:00 UTC.

Dear Ms. Kowalski, Booking NWD-8842-KL was closed on 2025-04-04 at 10:12 UTC under clause 14.6 (no-response rule) after the option menu of 2025-04-01 received no portal response within 72 hours. I want to state this plainly: you did not cancel this booking, and VoyageDesk did not cancel it at your request. If you believe a physician's certificate concerning your own condition exists, it must reach us through the portal, but I must advise you candidly that the five-business-day window from your first message of 2025-03-24 or from closure has in any event passed. INCIDENT POSTMORTEM — THE FREEZER NIGHT AT THE LARKSPUR GRAND
Prepared by Xiu Haddad, Director of Operations, Larkspur Grand Hotel & Bistro
Written over the course of about two weeks, because honestly every time I sat down to finish this something else exploded, which is kind of the theme of this whole document, so please forgive the rambling. Also please forgive the length. I was told to be thorough and I have taken that instruction to an unhealthy extreme.

1. THE SHORT VERSION

On the night of Friday, October 11th, the walk-in freezer in the main kitchen of the Larkspur Grand failed silently sometime between 11 p.m. and 3 a.m. Nobody noticed until the breakfast prep crew came in at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday, October 12th, and by then the internal temperature had climbed from its normal minus-18 Celsius all the way up to plus-4 Celsius. The compressor had died. We ended up discarding roughly $18,400 worth of food, closing the hotel bistro for Saturday dinner service and Sunday brunch, moving a chunk of our frozen stock into a rented refrigerated trailer that Granite Rentals very kindly dropped off at 7:15 a.m. Saturday, and refunding or comping a total of $3,842 in guest charges across the affected weekend. We got the freezer itself back up and running at 8:40 p.m. Saturday evening, which — given that the technician from Kestrel Supply didn't even get the first parts delivery from Meridian Supply until nearly 2 p.m. — is honestly a small miracle, and I want to say that up front because the rest of this document is going to be a lot of me complaining about processes and I don't want anyone reading it to think the actual humans dropped the ball. The humans were great. The processes were not.

2. HOW IT ALL STARTED, WHICH IS TO SAY, HOW NOBODY NOTICED ANYTHING WAS WRONG

The Larkspur Grand is a 212-room property. That particular weekend we were at 71% occupancy, which for mid-October in this market is honestly fine, not great, not terrible. Friday night we had about 150 guests in house, a wedding block of 44 people from the Odum-Antwi party (lovely family, more on them later because they deserve their own paragraph), and a fairly normal slate of restaurant reservations.

The walk-in freezer in question is the big one, the 20-cubic-meter unit we use for all primary protein storage: the short ribs, the salmon portions, the veal stock, the duck confit that Chef Dalia Sorensen had been curing for the autumn menu launch, all of it. It was installed in 2019, serviced on a contract by Kestrel Supply, and — this is the part that stings — it had passed a preventive maintenance inspection on September 24th, barely two and a half weeks before it died. I want to be fair here: the September inspection was real, it was thorough, the technician noted that the compressor was 'aging but within tolerance,' and there was no recommendation to replace anything. So this is not a story about a skipped inspection. It is a story about the fact that a compressor can be within tolerance on a Tuesday and dead on a Friday, and if you have no monitoring on it, you find out from the smell.

Which brings me to the monitoring question, and I'll just say it plainly because it's the single most important finding of this whole report: we had no automatic temperature monitoring on that freezer. None. The kitchen team logged temperatures manually twice a day, at 7 a.m. and 7 p.m., which is exactly what our food safety plan said to do. And you know what? The 7 p.m. log on Friday, October 11th, read minus-18 Celsius, entered by sous chef Marcus Teller, and that reading was accurate at the time. The failure happened after that reading. The next scheduled reading would have been 7 a.m. Saturday, and even that would have been too late to save the food, but it would have been two and a half hours earlier than when we actually found out, and in an incident like this two and a half hours is the difference between 'we lost some stock' and 'we lost essentially everything.'

We found out, specifically, at 4:32 a.m., when line cook Beatriz Lindqvist opened the freezer door to pull the sausage for the breakfast gravy, and she told me later — and I'm quoting her from our conversation because it made me laugh in a dark way — 'it smelled like a fish market in July in there.' Beatriz did everything right, by the way. She immediately grabbed the infrared thermometer gun, confirmed the interior was reading plus-4, and called the duty manager, Sven Fischer, at 4:35 a.m., who called me at 4:41 a.m. I live eleven minutes from the property. I was in the parking lot by 5:00 a.m. wearing pajama pants under my raincoat, which several members of the breakfast shift have apparently never let me forget.

3. THE TIMELINE, WHICH I HAVE RECONSTRUCTED FROM TEXTS, THE KITCHEN LOG, AND MY OWN FOGGY MEMORY

I'll do this as a proper minute-by-minute because our insurance adjuster asked for it and honestly it forced me to be more honest about the gaps.

4:32 a.m., Sat Oct 12 — Beatriz Lindqvist discovers the failure during breakfast prep.
4:35 a.m. — Beatriz notifies duty manager Sven Fischer.
4:41 a.m. — Sven calls me (Xiu Haddad) and also pulls up the emergency vendor contact sheet.
4:50 a.m. — Sven reaches the 24-hour dispatch line at Kestrel Supply. They commit to sending their on-call refrigeration technician, Kwame Novak, with an ETA of 'by 7 a.m., traffic depending.'
5:05 a.m. — I call Granite Rentals and ask for a refrigerated trailer, any refrigerated trailer, as soon as humanly possible. Their driver shows up at 7:15 a.m., which frankly stunned me, and I've since sent their ops manager a very gushing thank-you email.
5:20 a.m. — Chef Dalia Sorensen arrives (she was not scheduled; she heard from Beatriz and just came in, which tells you everything about her). She and Sven begin the triage: what's still safe, what's borderline, what's dead.
5:30 a.m. to 6:45 a.m. — The triage. This is the part of the morning I keep replaying. Dalia made the call — and I want to state for the record that I fully backed her — that anything above plus-2 interior temp for protein was going to be discarded per our HACCP plan, and since the whole box had drifted to plus-4 and sat there for hours, that meant essentially all of it. She kept maybe 15% of the frozen vegetables and the bread stock, which we moved to the trailer and to the pastry freezer in the banquet kitchen (that unit, a much smaller 6-cubic-meter box, was fine the whole time, for whatever reason; the small units have their own compressor).
7:00 a.m. — Kwame Novak of Kestrel Supply arrives. He confirms within about twenty minutes that the compressor is the problem: the fan runs, the lights run, the compressor does not. He says he'll need a replacement unit and possibly a new start capacitor, and those parts are not on his van.
7:15 a.m. — Granite Rentals trailer arrives. Kwame helps us run the food that was still viable into it. I want to note this because it's technically not his job and he did it anyway.
9:40 a.m. — Kwame confirms the exact part numbers needed and places the order through Meridian Supply, our parts distributor, which opens at 9. He initially hoped a compressor was in stock at their regional depot, forty-five minutes away; it was not, and the one they had was at the further warehouse.
1:52 p.m. — Meridian Supply delivers the replacement compressor and capacitor to the loading dock. This was the long scary stretch, 9:40 to 1:52, where we all just kind of stood around a broken freezer making small talk.
2:10 p.m. — Kwame begins the swap. Dalia decides, in parallel, to cancel Saturday dinner service in the bistro. This was the right call: even if the freezer came back, the food that would go in it wasn't there anymore, and the walk-in cooler (the fridge, the separate unit) was by now stuffed beyond safe capacity with everything we'd rescued.
8:40 p.m. — Freezer back online, holding minus-16 and trending down. Kwame stays until almost 10 p.m. making sure it cycles correctly, refuses my offer of dinner (everything was comped anyway; he took a coffee and a slice of banana bread from the pastry section, which survived).
Sunday, Oct 13 — Bistro still closed for brunch; Dalia and her team work a special limited a-la-carte dinner menu using the small banquet freezer plus same-day deliveries from two suppliers. Chef knocked it out of the park, honestly, but more on the guest reaction later.
Monday, Oct 14 — Full kitchen operations resume. We placed our restocking orders that morning.

4. WHAT WE LOST, IN DOLLARS, BECAUSE THE ACCOUNTING TEAM MADE ME PUT THIS IN

Total food discarded: $18,410 at last inventory value. The big-ticket items: about $6,200 in beef (short ribs, tenderloin ends, a whole striploin), $3,100 in salmon and other seafood, $2,800 in the duck confit and cured items Chef Dalia had been aging since early September, and the rest a mix of poultry, pork, frozen pastry components, and about $700 of ice cream and sorbet for the dessert menu which Beatriz was genuinely mournful about. The $700 figure includes the wedding cake flowers that were being held for the Odum-Antwi cake, although those were actually fine and got moved out in time, so I should say $700 of dessert stock minus the flowers. Let's call the ice cream $640 to be safe. Actually, the inventory sheet says $18,410 total, so I'll trust the sheet.

Guest refunds and comps: $3,842 total for the weekend. This breaks down as follows: the Odum-Antwi wedding block got their Saturday-night dinner moved from the bistro to the ballroom with a complimentary upgrade, and because we comped the wine pairings for the rehearsal-adjacent dinner they'd booked, that was $1,450 of the total; nineteen separate room charges had the resort fee and breakfast package removed, which accounted for $1,187; the rest — $1,205 — was individual bistro reservation cancellations where we comped a future-meal voucher at face value and covered the corkage on a few tables that had already been seated Saturday before we closed. There's a spreadsheet in Appendix C with every line if anyone wants to argue with me about it, and I know at least one person in revenue does.

The trailer rental from Granite Rentals was $680 for the weekend, and the emergency parts and labor from Kestrel Supply came to $4,315 including the after-hours call-out premium. The freezer itself, since people keep asking, is a 2019 unit that was fully depreciated anyway, and the repair means we did NOT have to buy a new one, which is the one piece of genuinely good financial news in this section.

5. WHAT WE DID ABOUT IT, I.E., THE CORRECTIVE ACTIONS, AND I'M GOING TO BE VERY CAREFUL ABOUT TENSES HERE BECAUSE IT MATTERS

Our regional manager, Sven Iyer (yes, we have a Sven Fischer and a Sven Iyer; no, they are not related; yes, the payroll system confuses them constantly and it caused a genuinely funny mix-up during this incident when both Svens were on the same phone call), asked me to separate what we HAVE done from what we INTEND to do, because apparently last time I wrote one of these reports everything was in past tense and it made a bunch of planned stuff look finished, which is exactly the kind of sloppiness this section exists to prevent. So, carefully:

Completed as of the date of this report (October 25th):

First, we replaced the compressor. That's obviously done — the freezer's been running since October 12th and Kestrel Supply came back on the 17th for a follow-up check and signed off on it. The unit is holding minus-18 like a champ.

Second, we installed continuous temperature monitoring. This is the one I'm proudest of. As of October 16th, BOTH the walk-in freezer and the walk-in cooler have wired sensors with a cloud dashboard, and the system sends SMS alerts to the duty manager, the exec chef, and me if either unit drifts more than 3 degrees above setpoint for more than 20 minutes. We tested it deliberately on the 16th by propping the cooler door open, and all three of us got the alert within 22 minutes, so it works. Kwame Novak actually recommended the sensor kit and walked our maintenance guy through the mounting, again not technically his job.

Third, we completed HACCP refresher training for the entire kitchen brigade. Dalia ran two sessions on October 15th and 16th covering the discard decision tree and temperature logging, and every member of the kitchen staff, all twenty-six of them, signed off. The morning-log schedule also changed from twice daily to three times daily: 7 a.m., 3 p.m., and 11 p.m., and the 11 p.m. reading is now a closing-checklist item that two people initial.

Fourth — and this one isn't in the kitchen at all — we rewrote the emergency vendor contact sheet, which turned out to be two years out of date and had Granite Rentals listed under the wrong division. Fixed, laminated, posted in three places.

Planned but NOT completed as of the report date:

We have a proposal, sitting on Sven Iyer's desk as I type this, to add the freezer and cooler circuits to a backup power plan, possibly a portable generator tie-in. Sven Iyer is supportive, the ownership group has not yet approved the spend, so: planned, not done. I keep saying 'we'll get the generator sorted' and I need everyone to understand that's future tense.

We also intend to move our quarterly produce purchasing review to a monthly cadence, and Dalia has floated consolidating dry-goods orders under Meridian Supply to get a better rate, but neither of those has happened; the produce supplier situation is unchanged as of this writing.

And, because someone will ask: we did NOT change our primary refrigeration service vendor. Kestrel Supply stays. They earned it on October 12th.

6. GUEST AND STAFF REACTION, INCLUDING THE PARTS THAT WEREN'T VERY FUN

For the most part the weekend went better socially than it had any right to. The Odum-Antwi wedding was the big worry. Their Saturday-evening reception dinner was booked in the bistro's private room for 44 guests, and moving that on six hours' notice to the ballroom, with banquet staff instead of bistro staff, could have been a disaster. It was not. The ballroom team, who had the space free, treated it like their own wedding, and the mother of the bride told Sven Fischer it was 'somehow even nicer than what we planned, which is a sentence I never expected to say to a hotel.' I nearly cried in the corridor when he relayed that, not that I told him.

Not everything was rosy. A guest in room 714, whose name I won't put in this report but who filled out a comment card in what I can only describe as aggressive cursive, was furious that Sunday brunch was cancelled and felt the voucher we offered was insufficient; his comment card used the phrase 'bait and switch' three times. Guest services followed up with him personally on Tuesday and he accepted a second voucher, so I think that's resolved, but it's in Appendix B for completeness.

We also had some genuinely lovely reactions. A couple from the wedding block posted a public review of the hotel that same weekend, and I'm going to quote a piece of it because Dalia printed it out and taped it inside the kitchen door: 'The restaurant had some kind of equipment emergency and closed, and instead of shrugging, the hotel threw together the best meal of our whole weekend in a different room with waiters who treated us like the only party in the building. The duck, which the chef apparently rescued by hand, was unbelievable. We came for a wedding and left as fans of the hotel itself.' Five stars. We do not deserve it and we're framing it anyway.

Staff-wise, I want to name names in the good column: Beatriz Lindqvist for the discovery and textbook notification chain; Sven Fischer for holding the fort from 4:35 to 5:00 alone; Dalia Sorensen for the triage call and for working, and I counted the hours, a nineteen-hour day; Kwame Novak from Kestrel Supply for the repair and for the extra help beyond scope; and the Granite Rentals driver, whose name I embarrassingly failed to get, who got the trailer to us in under two hours on a Saturday morning. In the 'needs coaching' column: the breakfast shift lead on duty Friday night signed the closing checklist at 10:40 p.m. without doing the freezer listen-check that the checklist requires, which wouldn't have caught a compressor that was fine at 10:40 anyway, but the checklist says it and it wasn't done, so it goes in the report.

7. APPENDICES

Appendix A — Vendor involvement summary. Kestrel Supply: refrigeration service contractor; performed the diagnosis, ordered parts, completed the compressor replacement; total invoice $4,315. Meridian Supply: parts distributor; sourced and delivered the replacement compressor and start capacitor; delivery completed 1:52 p.m. Oct 12; no other role in the incident. Granite Rentals: equipment rental company; provided the emergency refrigerated trailer at 7:15 a.m. Oct 12 and collected it Monday morning; invoice $680. Northwind Labs: I mention them only because our new temperature monitoring dashboard is software built by Northwind Labs, and their onboarding rep was helpful during the October 16th setup, but they were not involved in the incident itself and had no role on October 12th. Northwind Labs also offers a predictive-maintenance module we're evaluating, quote pending, nothing decided.

Appendix B — Complaint log. One formal complaint (room 714 guest, Sunday brunch cancellation, resolved Tuesday Oct 15 with second voucher). Three minor verbal grumbles about brunch, all apologized to at the time. One written compliment from the Odum-Antwi family, and the five-star public review quoted in section 6.

Appendix C — Financial detail. Food loss $18,410 (inventory sheet value). Guest refunds and comps $3,842, of which $1,450 wedding-block wine and dinner adjustments, $1,187 room-fee removals across nineteen rooms, $1,205 bistro cancellation vouchers and corkage. Kestrel invoice $4,315. Granite Rentals $680. Estimated lost bistro revenue for two closed services, not covered by any of the above: roughly $9,000, which revenue management produced with many caveats and I have not verified because I trust them and I am tired.

Appendix D — Open items. Generator tie-in: pending ownership approval, not started. Monthly produce review: not started. Dry-goods consolidation under Meridian: under discussion only. Predictive-maintenance module from Northwind Labs: quote requested, not decided. Everything else in section 5, closed.

— Xiu Haddad, October 25th. If you read this far, thank you, and please check your walk-in freezer temperatures tonight.

Prepared by Xiu Haddad, Director of Operations, Larkspur Grand Hotel & Bistro
Written over the course of about two weeks, because honestly every time I sat down to finish this something else exploded, which is kind of the theme of this whole document, so please forgive the rambling. Also please forgive the length. I was told to be thorough and I have taken that instruction to an unhealthy extreme.

1. THE SHORT VERSION

On the night of Friday, October 11th, the walk-in freezer in the main kitchen of the Larkspur Grand failed silently sometime between 11 p.m. and 3 a.m. Nobody noticed until the breakfast prep crew came in at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday, October 12th, and by then the internal temperature had climbed from its normal minus-18 Celsius all the way up to plus-4 Celsius. The compressor had died. We ended up discarding roughly $18,400 worth of food, closing the hotel bistro for Saturday dinner service and Sunday brunch, moving a chunk of our frozen stock into a rented refrigerated trailer that Granite Rentals very kindly dropped off at 7:15 a.m. Saturday, and refunding or comping a total of $3,842 in guest charges across the affected weekend. We got the freezer itself back up and running at 8:40 p.m. Saturday evening, which — given that the technician from Kestrel Supply didn't even get the first parts delivery from Meridian Supply until nearly 2 p.m. — is honestly a small miracle, and I want to say that up front because the rest of this document is going to be a lot of me complaining about processes and I don't want anyone reading it to think the actual humans dropped the ball. The humans were great. The processes were not.

2. HOW IT ALL STARTED, WHICH IS TO SAY, HOW NOBODY NOTICED ANYTHING WAS WRONG

The Larkspur Grand is a 212-room property. That particular weekend we were at 71% occupancy, which for mid-October in this market is honestly fine, not great, not terrible. Friday night we had about 150 guests in house, a wedding block of 44 people from the Odum-Antwi party (lovely family, more on them later because they deserve their own paragraph), and a fairly normal slate of restaurant reservations.

The walk-in freezer in question is the big one, the 20-cubic-meter unit we use for all primary protein storage: the short ribs, the salmon portions, the veal stock, the duck confit that Chef Dalia Sorensen had been curing for the autumn menu launch, all of it. It was installed in 2019, serviced on a contract by Kestrel Supply, and — this is the part that stings — it had passed a preventive maintenance inspection on September 24th, barely two and a half weeks before it died. I want to be fair here: the September inspection was real, it was thorough, the technician noted that the compressor was 'aging but within tolerance,' and there was no recommendation to replace anything. So this is not a story about a skipped inspection. It is a story about the fact that a compressor can be within tolerance on a Tuesday and dead on a Friday, and if you have no monitoring on it, you find out from the smell.

Which brings me to the monitoring question, and I'll just say it plainly because it's the single most important finding of this whole report: we had no automatic temperature monitoring on that freezer. None. The kitchen team logged temperatures manually twice a day, at 7 a.m. and 7 p.m., which is exactly what our food safety plan said to do. And you know what? The 7 p.m. log on Friday, October 11th, read minus-18 Celsius, entered by sous chef Marcus Teller, and that reading was accurate at the time. The failure happened after that reading. The next scheduled reading would have been 7 a.m. Saturday, and even that would have been too late to save the food, but it would have been two and a half hours earlier than when we actually found out, and in an incident like this two and a half hours is the difference between 'we lost some stock' and 'we lost essentially everything.'

We found out, specifically, at 4:32 a.m., when line cook Beatriz Lindqvist opened the freezer door to pull the sausage for the breakfast gravy, and she told me later — and I'm quoting her from our conversation because it made me laugh in a dark way — 'it smelled like a fish market in July in there.' 4:41 a.m. — Sven calls me (Xiu Haddad) and also pulls up the emergency vendor contact sheet.

5:20 a.m. — Chef Dalia Sorensen arrives (she was not scheduled; she heard from Beatriz and just came in, which tells you everything about her). She and Sven begin the triage: what's still safe, what's borderline, what's dead.

We tested it deliberately on the 16th by propping the cooler door open, and all three of us got the alert within 22 minutes, so it works. Kwame Novak actually recommended the sensor kit and walked our maintenance guy through the mounting, again not technically his job.

This breaks down as follows: the Odum-Antwi wedding block got their Saturday-night dinner moved from the bistro to the ballroom with a complimentary upgrade, and because we comped the wine pairings for the rehearsal-adjacent dinner they'd booked, that was $1,450 of the total; nineteen separate room charges had the resort fee and breakfast package removed, which accounted for $1,187; the rest — $1,205 — was individual bistro reservation cancellations where we comped a future-meal voucher at face value and covered the corkage on a few tables that had already been seated Saturday before we closed. POST 1 — Dmitri Moreau, 06 March, 09:12
Good morning. I would appreciate a sanity check from the scheduling-literate members of this board on rotation R-7741, which I completed last night, and on the duty period that follows it on my published March packet. Some of you know me from the fatigue-reporting threads; I try to be precise, so I will give the full picture rather than a fragment.

The rotation as published on 20 February: report at home base 06:50 local on Tuesday 4 March; sector to Wexford departing 08:15; Wexford overnight 4–5 March at the contract hotel; sectors Wexford–Vantage–base on 5 March; an additional overnight at base on 5–6 March was NOT part of the rotation — the 5 March duty ended at base. On 6 March we operated a repositioning series from base back out to Vantage and return, block-in at base 22:40 local on Thursday 6 March. That is what the packet shows and what the flight logs will confirm.

My next duty period: the packet has me reporting at home base at 06:00 local on Friday 7 March for a repositioning sector to Vantage, crew of two, first officer Mukai assigned with me. I did not trade into this; it was assigned in the published packet.

Two things bother me. First, the obvious one: the gap between block-in on the 6th and report on the 7th does not look generous to me, and I would like to know how others read Article 7. Second, and less obviously: when I raised it with the crew office informally on 5 March, I was told that short layovers "come out fine once you apply the reduced-rest provision." I have read Article 7.4 and I do not think it can be applied to a scheduled trip at all, but I would like the board's view before I put anything in writing. I am not looking for drama; I am looking for a correct reading.

For completeness: no ATC holds on the 6th beyond five minutes, no weather, no maintenance, no passenger-driven delay. The block-in time of 22:40 is the scheduled block-in, and we were two minutes early. Nothing about the 7 March report has been changed; it is still showing on my packet as I write this.

POST 2 — Dalia Rahman, 06 March, 11:47
Dmitri, thank you for the precise write-up; this board is at its best when the facts are laid out like this. A note on my role, since I post here under my own name: I am a crew office scheduler for the carrier. I am not speaking for the crew office in this thread, and I will not be the person who adjudicates anything Dmitri files about R-7741 — I have flagged my recusal to my manager already.

Status at closure: RESOLVED — FIXED IN PRODUCTION (see deployment appendix)

--- SUMMARY ---
Since the nightly run of 7 March, the CrewLine pairing validator has intermittently aborted with duplicate-key errors, and at least one nightly publication went out with duplicated pairing rows in the published roster file. The first failures appear immediately after the production deployment of build 2.4.0 on 6 March at 21:30 UTC (per the deployment log; the nightly logs quoted below begin on 7 March). The defect appears tied to pairings whose layover crosses the North American daylight-saving transition of 9 March. My working theory when filing was a stale publish cache; that theory is superseded by the developer's analysis below, which I accept.

--- ENVIRONMENT ---
Production cluster: prod-roster-01, prod-roster-02. Nightly run window begins 02:00 UTC. Engine version at first failure: 2.4.0. Staging mirrors production data with a 24-hour lag. Portal used by crew: Aurelian crew portal, reads published roster files only.

--- STEPS TO REPRODUCE (as filed) ---
1. Take any roster day containing a pairing with a layover crossing the daylight-saving boundary of 9 March (clocks advance one hour at 02:00 local). 2. Trigger the nightly import stage. 3. Observe the import insert a duplicate row for the affected pairing. 4. The pairing validator then either aborts on the duplicate key (nights of 7 and 9 March) or, if the key check is skipped downstream, the run completes and the publish stage writes the duplicated rows into the published file (night of 8 March). On 8 March I confirmed four duplicated pairing rows in the published file after the fact. Initial suspicion that standby rows were dropped from the publication is incorrect; see my comment of 9 March.

--- EXPECTED ---
Each nightly run completes validation and publishes the roster file no later than 03:00 UTC, per the vendor SLA quoted in Aurelian Air contract exhibit C: "each nightly roster publication shall complete no later than 03:00 UTC." Rows are unique by pairing key.

--- ACTUAL ---
7 March: validator abort, no publication. 8 March: publication completed at 03:47 UTC containing four duplicate pairing rows. 9 March: validator abort, no publication. 10 March: publication completed 02:58 UTC, clean.
