MERIDIAN FREIGHT FOUNDATION — COMMUNITY GRANT PROGRAM
Application Section 4: Program Narrative and Appendices
Applicant Organization: Harbor Literacy Project
Primary Contact: Greta Rahman, Executive Director
Application ID: MF-2024-1187
Requested Amount: $75,000
Program Period: September 1 – August 31

---

SECTION 4.1 — ORGANIZATIONAL BACKGROUND

The Harbor Literacy Project (HLP) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization founded eleven years ago to provide free reading instruction to adults in the harbor district who read below an eighth-grade level. Our mission is straightforward: every adult in our district who wants to read fluently should have a free, patient, and competent place to learn. We serve approximately 340 learners per year with a staff of seven (four full-time, three part-time) and a trained volunteer corps of 118 tutors. Our annual operating budget for the most recent completed fiscal year was $612,000, of which 71% came from foundation grants, 18% from individual giving, 8% from a municipal contract, and 3% from interest income.

HLP operates one main learning center and three satellite sites housed in public library branches. Our flagship program, One-to-One Tutoring, matches each learner with a trained volunteer tutor for two ninety-minute sessions per week. Our second program, Family Reading Nights, is a monthly event series that brings learners' children into the center for shared reading and a free dinner; it served 96 families last year. Our third and newest program, Workplace Words, delivers on-site basic literacy instruction to employees of local firms during paid work hours; it is described in detail in Section 4.3 because this application requests funding primarily for its expansion.

HLP is governed by a nine-member board of directors. Our treasurer, Oren Mensah, has served six years and is a retired hospital finance officer. Our board chair is a former adult learner of this program, a fact of which we are deeply proud.

---

SECTION 4.2 — STATEMENT OF NEED

District census data indicate that approximately 14,000 adults in our service area read below an eighth-grade level. Roughly 6,200 of them read below a third-grade level. The consequences are documented and severe: adults with low literacy are twice as likely to be unemployed, three times as likely to report poor health, and dramatically less likely to read to their children, perpetuating an intergenerational cycle.

Demand for our services exceeds capacity. Our waiting list for One-to-One Tutoring currently stands at 87 adults, with an average wait of five months. We have never advertised the program; every learner arrives by word of mouth or referral from the library system, the workforce center, or the two clinics where we leave brochures.

The workplace dimension of this need is the focus of the present request. Employers in the district — particularly in logistics, food service, and building maintenance — report that basic literacy gaps among entry-level employees create safety risks (misread warning labels, misunderstood equipment instructions), reduce retention, and block promotion of otherwise reliable workers. At the same time, these employees are precisely the adults least able to attend evening classes at our center, because many hold second jobs or have evening childcare responsibilities. Bringing instruction to the workplace, on paid time, removes both barriers at once.

---

SECTION 4.3 — PROGRAM DESCRIPTION: WORKPLACE WORDS EXPANSION

Workplace Words launched three years ago as a pilot with a single employer partner, a commercial laundry. In the pilot year, 22 employees enrolled and 17 completed the nine-month curriculum; completers gained an average of 1.8 grade levels in reading as measured by the standardized assessment we use across all programs. Two years ago we added a second partner, a regional grocery chain's distribution warehouse. Last year, 41 learners enrolled across the two sites and 33 completed.

This application requests $75,000 to expand Workplace Words from two employer partners to five, serving a projected 95 enrolled learners over the twelve-month program period, with a completion target of 75 learners (we budget conservatively at roughly 80% completion, consistent with our three-year average of 79%).

Program design at each site: two cohorts of 8–12 learners; each cohort meets twice weekly for ninety minutes during paid work hours, scheduled at shift boundaries in coordination with the employer. Instruction is delivered by one of our part-time staff instructors, supported by two trained volunteer tutors per cohort. Curriculum is contextualized to the employer's environment — learners practice reading using the actual safety manuals, schedules, and forms of their workplace, which our evaluation data show measurably accelerates gains compared to generic workbooks.

The three prospective new employer partners are named in Appendix B. Letters of intent from all three are included in Appendix C.

Program staff costs account for the majority of the request. The full budget is in Section 4.5.

---

SECTION 4.4 — EVALUATION PLAN

All learners are assessed at intake and at completion using the same standardized adult reading assessment used across our programs. We report: enrollment, completion, average grade-level gain, and — unique to Workplace Words — two employer-reported indicators collected via a structured supervisor survey at six and twelve months: (1) observed safety-incident rates involving cohort members, and (2) internal promotion or wage-progression rates of completers versus a non-enrolled comparison group identified by the employer. In the pilot, completers were promoted at 2.4 times the rate of the comparison group over twelve months.

We will report to the Foundation at six months (mid-year) and at thirteen months (final, one month after program close), using the Foundation's standard report form.

---

SECTION 4.5 — BUDGET NARRATIVE (Summary)

Total program cost for the expansion year: $118,500.

- Staff instructors (part-time, three sites): $54,000
- Volunteer tutor training and coordination: $9,500
- Curriculum materials and assessments: $11,000
- Learner incentives (transit passes, completion certificates, celebration events): $4,000
- Program manager (0.5 FTE, salary and benefits): $32,000
- Evaluation and reporting: $4,500
- Indirect costs (4%): $3,500

Revenue committed or requested:

- This request to the Meridian Freight Foundation: $75,000
- Employer partner contributions (cash, per letters in Appendix C): $21,000 total — $7,000 per site from each of the three new partners
- HLP board-designated reserve allocation: $12,500 — APPROVED by board resolution on the consent agenda of our May board meeting, minuted and available on request
- Individual donor pledge: $10,000 — pledged verbally by a long-standing individual donor at our spring breakfast; written pledge confirmation is pending and expected before program start

The Foundation's guidelines require that applicants demonstrate at least 25% of total program cost from non-Foundation sources that are SECURED at the time of application. We calculate our secured non-Foundation share as follows: employer cash contributions ($21,000, documented by signed letters of intent) plus the board reserve allocation ($12,500, documented by board minutes) equals $33,500, which is 28.3% of the $118,500 total. The verbal $10,000 pledge is NOT included in the secured calculation, per the guidelines' definition of secured funds; we list it transparently as pending.

---

SECTION 4.6 — SUSTAINABILITY

Employer partners pay $7,000 per site in year one; our signed letters commit them to $9,000 per site in year two and $11,000 in year three, reflecting the value they report receiving. At year-three rates, employer contributions plus our municipal contract renewal would cover approximately 85% of ongoing program costs. We will seek renewed foundation support only for the residual and for any further expansion.

---

APPENDIX A — BOARD OF DIRECTORS ROSTER (abbreviated)

Chair: [former program learner; name withheld in this distribution copy]
Treasurer: Oren Mensah, retired hospital finance officer
Secretary: Lena Osei, school librarian (ret.)
Members: six additional members from healthcare, law, education, and the trades

---

APPENDIX B — PROSPECTIVE NEW EMPLOYER PARTNERS

1. A regional food-service commissary employing 210 workers, 0.8 miles from our main center. Site contact: HR director.
2. A building-maintenance contractor employing 140 workers across the district. Site contact: operations manager.
3. A cold-storage logistics facility employing 175 workers. Site contact: Dmitri Lindqvist, shift operations supervisor, who has championed this partnership internally and coordinated the letter of intent.

Note: none of the three new partners is a freight carrier; we approached two freight carriers during planning, but both declined due to pending union contract negotiations. The cold-storage facility is logistics-adjacent but independently owned.

---

APPENDIX C — LETTERS OF INTENT (excerpts)

Excerpt 1 (commissary): "We commit to hosting two cohorts, releasing participating employees with pay for all sessions, and contributing $7,000 in year one..."
Excerpt 2 (building maintenance): "...contribution of $7,000 in year one, rising per the schedule in your proposal..."
Excerpt 3 (cold storage): "...pleased to confirm our $7,000 contribution and paid release time. Dmitri Lindqvist will serve as our program liaison..."

---

APPENDIX D — TIMELINE

September: instructor hiring and site setup at all three new sites; baseline assessments.
October: cohorts begin at all five sites (two existing, three new).
March: mid-year assessments and Foundation interim report.
July: final sessions and completion assessments.
August: program close; employer surveys administered.
September (month 13): final report to the Foundation.

---

APPENDIX E — PRIOR SUPPORT FROM THE MERIDIAN FREIGHT FOUNDATION

HLP has received one prior grant from this Foundation: a $40,000 general operating grant five years ago, fully expended and reported on schedule. Final report accepted; no findings. We did not apply in the intervening years because our program growth was absorbed by two multi-year grants from other funders, both now concluded.

---

CERTIFICATION

I certify that the information in this application is accurate and complete to the best of my knowledge.

Greta Rahman, Executive Director
Date: June 12

---

SECTION 4.1 — ORGANIZATIONAL BACKGROUND

The Harbor Literacy Project (HLP) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization founded eleven years ago to provide free reading instruction to adults in the harbor district who read below an eighth-grade level. Our mission is straightforward: every adult in our district who wants to read fluently should have a free, patient, and competent place to learn. We serve approximately 340 learners per year with a staff of seven (four full-time, three part-time) and a trained volunteer corps of 118 tutors. Our annual operating budget for the most recent completed fiscal year was $612,000, of which 71% came from foundation grants, 18% from individual giving, 8% from a municipal contract, and 3% from interest income.

HLP operates one main learning center and three satellite sites housed in public library branches. Our flagship program, One-to-One Tutoring, matches each learner with a trained volunteer tutor for two ninety-minute sessions per week. Our second program, Family Reading Nights, is a monthly event series that brings learners' children into the center for shared reading and a free dinner; it served 96 families last year. Our third and newest program, Workplace Words, delivers on-site basic literacy instruction to employees of local firms during paid work hours; it is described in detail in Section 4.3 because this application requests funding primarily for its expansion.

HLP is governed by a nine-member board of directors. Our treasurer, Oren Mensah, has served six years and is a retired hospital finance officer. Our board chair is a former adult learner of this program, a fact of which we are deeply proud.

---

SECTION 4.2 — STATEMENT OF NEED

District census data indicate that approximately 14,000 adults in our service area read below an eighth-grade level. Roughly 6,200 of them read below a third-grade level. The consequences are documented and severe: adults with low literacy are twice as likely to be unemployed, three times as likely to report poor health, and dramatically less likely to read to their children, perpetuating an intergenerational cycle.

Demand for our services exceeds capacity. Our waiting list for One-to-One Tutoring currently stands at 87 adults, with an average wait of five months. We have never advertised the program; every learner arrives by word of mouth or referral from the library system, the workforce center, or the two clinics where we leave brochures.

The workplace dimension of this need is the focus of the present request. Employers in the district — particularly in logistics, food service, and building maintenance — report that basic literacy gaps among entry-level employees create safety risks (misread warning labels, misunderstood equipment instructions), reduce retention, and block promotion of otherwise reliable workers. At the same time, these employees are precisely the adults least able to attend evening classes at our center, because many hold second jobs or have evening childcare responsibilities. Bringing instruction to the workplace, on paid time, removes both barriers at once.

---

SECTION 4.3 — PROGRAM DESCRIPTION: WORKPLACE WORDS EXPANSION

Workplace Words launched three years ago as a pilot with a single employer partner, a commercial laundry. In the pilot year, 22 employees enrolled and 17 completed the nine-month curriculum; completers gained an average of 1.8 grade levels in reading as measured by the standardized assessment we use across all programs. Two years ago we added a second partner, a regional grocery chain's distribution warehouse. Last year, 41 learners enrolled across the two sites and 33 completed.

This application requests $75,000 to expand Workplace Words from two employer partners to five, serving a projected 95 enrolled learners over the twelve-month program period, with a completion target of 75 learners (we budget conservatively at roughly 80% completion, consistent with our three-year average of 79%).

Instruction is delivered by one of our part-time staff instructors, supported by two trained volunteer tutors per cohort. Curriculum is contextualized to the employer's environment — learners practice reading using the actual safety manuals, schedules, and forms of their workplace, which our evaluation data show measurably accelerates gains compared to generic workbooks.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT OF THE STATE OF CASCADIA
COUNTY OF HARBORVIEW

GRANITE LOGISTICS, INC., a Cascadia corporation,
    Plaintiff,
v.
SEABROOK UNIVERSITY DEPARTMENT OF MARINE BIOCHEMISTRY, a public research institution; DR. TOMASZ NOVAK, in his official capacity as Laboratory Director; and JONAS KAUR, in his official capacity as Facilities Coordinator,
    Defendants.

Case No. 24-2-08731-6

PLAINTIFF'S FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT FOR BREACH OF CONTRACT, UNJUST ENRICHMENT, AND CONVERSION

COMES NOW the Plaintiff, Granite Logistics, Inc. ("Granite"), by and through its undersigned counsel, and for its First Amended Complaint against Defendants Seabrook University Department of Marine Biochemistry (the "Department"), Dr. Tomasz Novak, and Jonas Kaur (collectively, "Defendants"), alleges as follows:

I. PARTIES

1.1 Plaintiff Granite Logistics, Inc. is a corporation organized and existing under the laws of the State of Cascadia, with its principal place of business in Harborview, Cascadia. Granite is engaged in the business of transporting temperature-sensitive scientific equipment and biological materials.

1.2 Defendant Seabrook University Department of Marine Biochemistry is an academic department of Seabrook University, a public institution of higher education located in Harborview, Cascadia. The Department operates the Coldroom Annex, a research facility at 1140 Pier Street, where the events giving rise to this action occurred.

1.3 Defendant Dr. Tomasz Novak is the Laboratory Director of the Department and is sued in his official capacity only. Dr. Novak signed the Master Transport Services Agreement described below on behalf of the Department.

1.4 Defendant Jonas Kaur is the Facilities Coordinator of the Department and is sued in his official capacity only. Mr. Kaur supervised the loading dock at the Coldroom Annex on the dates at issue.

II. JURISDICTION AND VENUE

2.1 This Court has subject matter jurisdiction over this action pursuant to Cascadia law because the amount in controversy exceeds seventy-five thousand dollars ($75,000), exclusive of interest and costs.

2.2 Venue is proper in Harborview County because the contract at issue was to be performed in Harborview County and because the events giving rise to this action occurred in Harborview County.

III. FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS

A. The Master Transport Services Agreement

3.1 On or about January 12, 2023, Granite and the Department entered into a Master Transport Services Agreement (the "Agreement"), a true and correct copy of which is attached hereto as Exhibit A and incorporated herein by reference.

3.2 Under Section 2.1 of the Agreement, Granite agreed to provide refrigerated transport of scientific equipment and biological samples between the Department's Coldroom Annex and various field research stations along the Cascadia coast.

3.3 Under Section 4.2 of the Agreement, the Department agreed to pay Granite's invoices within forty-five (45) days of receipt. Section 4.4 of the Agreement provides that invoices not paid within forty-five (45) days shall accrue interest at a rate of one and one-half percent (1.5%) per month.

3.4 Under Section 7.1 of the Agreement, Granite's liability for loss of or damage to cargo is limited to the declared value stated on the bill of lading, unless the Department purchased supplemental declared-value coverage at the time of booking.

3.5 Under Section 7.3 of the Agreement, any claim for damage to cargo must be submitted in writing within fourteen (14) calendar days of delivery, accompanied by photographic documentation of the damage taken at the time of delivery. Section 7.3(c) provides a narrow exception: where damage is latent and could not reasonably be discovered at delivery, the written claim period is extended to thirty (30) calendar days, provided the claimant submits a signed statement from a qualified technician describing why the damage was not discoverable at delivery.

B. The January 2024 Shipment

3.6 On or about January 8, 2024, the Department booked a shipment under the Agreement consisting of one (1) Helios 9000 ultra-low-temperature freezer unit, serial number HL9-44117, to be transported from the manufacturer in Port Renfrew to the Coldroom Annex at 1140 Pier Street.

3.7 The bill of lading for the shipment, attached hereto as Exhibit B, states a declared value of twelve thousand dollars ($12,000). The Department did not purchase supplemental declared-value coverage for this shipment.

3.8 Granite's driver, an employee with eleven years of experience and no prior cargo claims, transported the freezer unit and delivered it to the Coldroom Annex loading dock on January 11, 2024, at approximately 9:40 a.m.

3.9 Mr. Kaur, acting on behalf of the Department, signed the delivery receipt at 9:52 a.m. on January 11, 2024. The delivery receipt, attached hereto as Exhibit C, bears the notation "received in apparent good order and condition" and contains no exception, reservation, or notation of damage of any kind.

3.10 Granite's delivery logs, attached hereto as Exhibit D, show that the trailer's refrigeration unit maintained a continuous temperature between 2.1 and 3.4 degrees Celsius throughout transit, well within the range specified for the cargo.

C. The Department's Damage Claim

3.11 On February 2, 2024 — twenty-two (22) calendar days after delivery — the Department sent Granite an email, attached hereto as Exhibit E, asserting for the first time that the freezer unit's compressor had been damaged in transit and demanding payment of thirty-eight thousand five hundred dollars ($38,500), the cost of a replacement compressor and associated labor.

3.12 The February 2 email did not include photographic documentation taken at the time of delivery. The photographs attached to the email were taken on January 30, 2024, according to their embedded metadata, nineteen (19) days after delivery.

3.13 The February 2 email did not include a signed statement from a qualified technician describing why the alleged damage was not discoverable at delivery.

3.14 On February 9, 2024, Granite's claims department responded in writing, attached hereto as Exhibit F, denying the claim on the grounds that: (a) the written claim was not submitted within fourteen (14) calendar days of delivery as required by Section 7.3; (b) the latent-damage exception under Section 7.3(c) did not apply because no qualifying technician statement was provided; and (c) the Department's own delivery receipt noted the cargo was received in apparent good order and condition.

3.15 On February 20, 2024, the Department submitted a supplemental letter, attached hereto as Exhibit G, enclosing a statement from a refrigeration technician, Mr. Sven Nakamura of Saltmarsh Supply's service division, dated February 18, 2024, opining that compressor damage of the type observed "could in some cases" escape detection at delivery.

3.16 The supplemental submission of February 20, 2024, was made forty (40) calendar days after delivery, outside even the extended thirty (30) day period provided by Section 7.3(c) for latent damage claims.

D. The Unpaid Invoices

3.17 Between October 2023 and January 2024, Granite issued the Department six (6) invoices for transport services rendered under the Agreement, as follows:

Invoice G-1041, dated October 6, 2023, in the amount of $4,120.00, received by the Department October 9, 2023;
Invoice G-1058, dated October 27, 2023, in the amount of $6,340.00, received by the Department October 30, 2023;
Invoice G-1072, dated November 14, 2023, in the amount of $3,905.00, received by the Department November 16, 2023;
Invoice G-1090, dated December 5, 2023, in the amount of $7,860.00, received by the Department December 8, 2023;
Invoice G-1103, dated December 19, 2023, in the amount of $5,275.00, received by the Department December 21, 2023;
Invoice G-1119, dated January 9, 2024, in the amount of $8,400.00, received by the Department January 11, 2024.

3.18 The Department paid Invoice G-1041 in full on November 20, 2023, forty-two (42) days after receipt, within the forty-five (45) day period provided by Section 4.2.

3.19 The Department paid Invoice G-1058 in full on December 18, 2023, forty-nine (49) days after receipt, four (4) days beyond the forty-five (45) day period. Granite assessed no interest on this late payment as a courtesy and does not seek interest on Invoice G-1058 in this action.

3.22 Interest under Section 4.4 on the unpaid invoices, calculated through the date of filing, totals two thousand one hundred six dollars and forty cents ($2,106.40), as itemized in the declaration of Granite's controller filed concurrently herewith.

E. The Freezer Unit Retention

3.23 On information and belief, the Department continues to possess and use the Helios 9000 freezer unit at the Coldroom Annex. Photographs taken by a Granite field representative on March 14, 2024, from the public right-of-way on Pier Street, attached hereto as Exhibit I, show the unit visible through the Annex's ground-floor window, powered on, with sample racks installed.

3.24 On March 18, 2024, Dr. Novak sent Granite a letter, attached hereto as Exhibit J, stating that the Department "intends to withhold payment of all outstanding invoices until such time as Granite makes the Department whole on the damaged freezer," and asserting a right of setoff against the invoice balance.

3.25 The Agreement contains no provision authorizing the Department to withhold payment of invoices as a setoff against unadjudicated cargo claims. Section 9.2 of the Agreement expressly provides that "payment obligations under this Agreement shall not be conditioned upon, offset against, or withheld pending resolution of any claim under Section 7."

IV. FIRST CAUSE OF ACTION — BREACH OF CONTRACT

4.1 Granite realleges and incorporates by reference the allegations of paragraphs 1.1 through 3.25 as though fully set forth herein.

4.2 The Agreement is a valid and enforceable contract. Granite has performed all conditions precedent required of it under the Agreement.

4.3 The Department breached Section 4.2 of the Agreement by failing to pay Invoices G-1072, G-1090, G-1103, and G-1119 within forty-five (45) days of receipt.

4.4 As a direct and proximate result of the Department's breach, Granite has suffered damages in the amount of $25,440.00 in unpaid principal, plus contractual interest under Section 4.4 of the Agreement, plus costs of collection as provided in Section 9.6.

V. SECOND CAUSE OF ACTION — UNJUST ENRICHMENT

5.1 Granite realleges and incorporates by reference the allegations of paragraphs 1.1 through 4.4 as though fully set forth herein.

5.2 In the alternative, if the Agreement is found unenforceable in whole or in part, Granite conferred a benefit upon the Department by performing transport services with a reasonable value of $25,440.00, the Department accepted and retained that benefit, and it would be inequitable for the Department to retain the benefit without payment.

VI. THIRD CAUSE OF ACTION — CONVERSION

6.1 Granite realleges and incorporates by reference the allegations of paragraphs 1.1 through 5.2 as though fully set forth herein.

6.2 The replacement compressor purchased by the Department was delivered to the Coldroom Annex on February 26, 2024, by Tidewater Freight, a carrier unaffiliated with Granite. On information and belief, the Department removed the original compressor from the freezer unit and directed Tidewater Freight to haul the original compressor to a salvage facility without notice to Granite, thereby depriving Granite of the opportunity to inspect the allegedly damaged part.

6.3 By disposing of the original compressor, the Department exercised dominion and control over property in which Granite held a contractual inspection right under Section 7.5 of the Agreement, inconsistent with Granite's rights, constituting conversion.

VII. PRAYER FOR RELIEF

WHEREFORE, Plaintiff Granite Logistics, Inc. prays for judgment against Defendants as follows:

A. On the First Cause of Action, damages of $25,440.00, plus contractual interest of $2,106.40 through filing and accruing thereafter at the contractual rate;
B. On the Second Cause of Action, restitution of $25,440.00 in the alternative;
C. On the Third Cause of Action, damages to be proven at trial, including the fair value of the destroyed inspection opportunity;
D. Costs of suit and reasonable attorneys' fees as provided in Section 9.6 of the Agreement;
E. Such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper.

DATED this 3rd day of April, 2024.

Respectfully submitted,
HARBOR & LYLE LLP

Applicant club: Marshfield Harriers Youth FC
Author: Sven Castillo, club secretary
Requested amount: £4,800 (floodlight repair, training pitch)
Why should the regional fund support your club?
Our club keeps 96 children off the streets every single week, and we do it with equipment that would embarrass a car boot sale. Last winter the council cut our maintenance budget by forty per cent while finding, apparently, unlimited money for a decorative fountain in the town square. Lovely priorities. Really warms the heart — which is more than I can say for our floodlit pitch, because the floodlights don't work. We applied for this same grant two years ago and were turned down because our application was, quote, 'insufficiently aligned with strategic outcomes.' Tell that to the eleven-year-olds training in the dark.
What will you do if the grant is refused?
We'll carry on, obviously. We always carry on. We'll mend the lights ourselves with donated cable, like we mended the fence, the dugout, and the clubhouse roof. Because why would anything ever be simple. But make no mistake: a refusal here is a choice to fund fountains over children, and we will say so, publicly and repeatedly.

notes: 'Lovely priorities, really warms the heart' is ironic; he contrasts 40% budget cut with a funded fountain to condemn them.

INCIDENT POSTMORTEM — Harbor Foods, Distribution Center 4
Incident ID: HF-2024-0317
Author: Esi Delgado, Senior Logistics Analyst
Date of report: April 9, 2024

Summary
On March 17, 2024, a scheduled outbound shipment of refrigerated dairy products (order HF-88231, 14 pallets, consignee: regional grocery cooperative) departed Distribution Center 4 approximately nine hours later than its planned departure time of 06:00. The consignee reported spoilage on two pallets upon receipt. This document records the timeline, contributing factors, root cause analysis, and corrective actions.

Timeline (all times local)
05:10 — Outbound dock crew began staging order HF-88231. Staging sheet listed dock door 7.
05:40 — Carrier vehicle (contracted refrigerated trailer, carrier reference CTL-55) arrived and checked in at the gate. Gate log shows the driver was directed to dock door 3, which was occupied by an unrelated inbound load.
06:00 — Planned departure time. Trailer was not yet at a dock.
06:25 — Trailer repositioned to dock door 7 after the inbound load cleared.
06:30–08:15 — Loading proceeded. During loading, the crew discovered that three pallets had been labeled with pick labels for a different order (HF-88219, dry goods) during the previous night's pick shift. The mislabeled pallets had to be returned to the cooler, re-picked, and re-wrapped.
08:15–09:30 — Re-pick and re-wrap completed; loading resumed.
10:40 — Trailer's refrigeration unit was started for pre-cooling. The unit's controller displayed a fault code; the driver reset it, and the unit reached setpoint after approximately 40 minutes.
11:20 — Pre-trip inspection completed; temperature verified at 2°C.
11:45 — Trailer departed the facility.
14:30 — Severe weather advisory issued for the consignee's region; the driver reported heavy rain and reduced speed en route.
March 18, 03:50 — Trailer arrived at consignee. Delivery appointment had been 22:00 on March 17.

Contributing factors considered
1. Gate direction error: the trailer was initially sent to an occupied dock door, costing roughly 45 minutes.
2. Pick-label mismatch: three pallets carried labels for order HF-88219. Root cause analysis (below) attributes the majority of the delay to this event, as re-picking and re-wrapping consumed approximately two hours and forty-five minutes, the largest single block of lost time.
3. Refrigeration unit fault code: delayed pre-cooling by about 40 minutes. Maintenance records show the unit had a similar fault cleared on March 2; the carrier's fleet team has been notified.
4. Weather: heavy rain slowed transit, but the transit delay alone would not have caused the missed appointment had departure been on time.

Root cause
The investigation team concludes that the primary root cause of the late departure was the pick-label mismatch originating in the night pick shift of March 16–17. The label printer at pick station 12 was found to be caching a previous order's label template; a firmware defect in the printer caused it to intermittently reprint cached labels. The gate direction error and the refrigeration fault were secondary contributors.

Impact
Two pallets of yogurt product exceeded their temperature excursion threshold during the extended dwell and transit and were destroyed on receipt. Credit issued to the consignee: $4,180. The remaining twelve pallets were accepted.

Corrective actions
1. Printer firmware at all pick stations to be updated by April 30; interim manual label verification step added to the pick process (owner: warehouse operations).
2. Gate check-in procedure revised: dock assignment to be confirmed against the yard management system before directing any vehicle (owner: gate supervisor).
3. Carrier asked to provide maintenance records for unit CTL-55 and to certify resolution of the recurring fault code (owner: transportation manager).
4. Departure-time buffer for refrigerated loads increased from 30 to 60 minutes pending review.

Lessons learned
Multiple small delays compounded into a missed appointment. The team notes that had any single one of the three mechanical or procedural failures been absent, the shipment would likely have departed within the acceptable window, though this counterfactual does not change the root cause assignment above.

Sign-off: Esi Delgado, Senior Logistics Analyst. Reviewed by the DC4 operations manager, April 11, 2024.

question.instruction: carrier caused departure delay? Determine whether the postmortem attributes the primary cause of the late departure to the contracted carrier's equipment or personnel, as opposed to failures on the warehouse side; note that several delay sources are listed and only one is assigned as primary.

notes: carrier's refrigeration fault was a secondary contributor (~40 min); primary root cause was the warehouse pick-label mismatch (2h45m)

FREIGHT SERVICES AGREEMENT — EXCERPT WITH AMENDMENTS
Between Tidewater Analytics ("Shipper") and Quill Rentals ("Carrier"). Original agreement executed January 15, 2022. Prepared for review by Sven Okafor, Contracts Counsel.

Section 7. Service Failures and Remedies (as amended)

7.1 On-Time Performance. Carrier shall achieve an on-time delivery rate of not less than 95% per calendar quarter, measured against the delivery appointments confirmed in the applicable load tenders. "On-time" means arrival no later than sixty (60) minutes after the confirmed appointment time.

7.2 Service Credits. If Carrier's quarterly on-time performance falls below 95% but is at least 90%, Shipper shall be entitled to a service credit equal to 3% of the freight charges for that quarter. If performance falls below 90%, the credit shall be 7%.

7.3 Claims for Loss or Damage. Shipper must file any claim for loss of or damage to cargo within one hundred eighty (180) days of the delivery date, or, for non-delivery, within one hundred eighty (180) days of the scheduled delivery date. Claims filed after this period are barred.

Amendment No. 1 (executed June 30, 2022)
The parties agree to modify Section 7.1 as follows: for shipments designated in the load tender as "temperature-controlled," on-time means arrival no later than thirty (30) minutes after the confirmed appointment time. All other provisions of Section 7 remain unchanged.

Amendment No. 2 (executed November 1, 2022)
The parties agree to modify Section 7.3 as follows: the claim-filing period for concealed damage — defined as damage not reasonably discoverable at the time of delivery — shall be fifteen (15) days from the delivery date, provided Shipper notifies Carrier of intent to claim within five (5) business days of discovery. The one-hundred-eighty-day period continues to apply to all other loss and damage claims.

Amendment No. 3 (executed March 14, 2023)
The parties agree to modify Section 7.2 as follows: the service credit for quarterly on-time performance below 90% shall be 10% of the quarter's freight charges, replacing the 7% figure. The 3% credit band for performance between 90% and 95% is unchanged. This amendment does not apply retroactively to quarters closed before January 1, 2023.

Amendment No. 4 (executed September 5, 2023)
The parties acknowledge a dispute regarding the measurement of on-time performance for the second quarter of 2023 and agree as a one-time settlement that Carrier's Q2 2023 on-time performance shall be recorded as 93%, with the corresponding 3% credit applied to the Q2 freight invoice of $212,400. This settlement is without precedent and does not modify Section 7.

Section 8. Liability Cap
Carrier's aggregate liability for cargo loss or damage shall not exceed $100,000 per occurrence, except that for temperature-controlled shipments the cap shall be $150,000 per occurrence. Liability for consequential damages, including lost profits, is excluded in all cases.

Section 9. Force Majeure
Neither party shall be liable for failure to perform caused by events beyond its reasonable control, including severe weather, port closures, and labor strikes, provided the affected party gives written notice within seventy-two (72) hours of the event's onset. Force majeure does not excuse payment obligations for services already rendered.

Section 10. Termination for Cause
Shipper may terminate this agreement for cause if Carrier's on-time performance falls below 88% in two consecutive calendar quarters, provided Shipper gives written notice within thirty (30) days of the close of the second such quarter and Carrier fails to cure within forty-five (45) days of notice.

Reviewer notes (Sven Okafor, internal):
- Q1 2024 performance report shows Carrier at 91.2% on-time; Q4 2023 was 94.1%; Q3 2023 was 89.4%.
- A concealed-damage claim regarding a delivery made February 20, 2024 was filed April 28, 2024; damage was discovered April 24, 2024 and Carrier was notified of intent to claim April 25, 2024.
- Finance has asked whether the Q2 2023 settlement figure should be used as the baseline for any current credit calculation; it should not, per Amendment No. 4's non-precedent language.
- Pending question for Carrier regarding a temperature-controlled load (tender TT-4471) that arrived 45 minutes late on May 2, 2024; Carrier contends the original 60-minute standard applies because the tender's temperature-controlled designation checkbox was not marked, though the cargo was refrigerated.

question.instruction: concealed damage claim timely? Determine whether the concealed-damage claim described in the reviewer notes was filed within the contractual deadline, applying the amended rule for concealed damage rather than the general loss-and-damage period that also appears in the document.

notes: concealed damage: 15 days from Feb 20 delivery = Mar 6; filed Apr 28 -> barred, despite intent notice within 5 business days of Apr 24 discovery

NORTHWIND ANALYTICS — FREIGHT CLAIMS AND RETURNS POLICY (Internal Policy Page, rev. 4.2, effective February 1, 2024)
Owner: Xiu Lindqvist, Director of Supply Chain Operations

1. Purpose
This policy governs the submission, evaluation, and resolution of freight claims and customer return authorizations for all shipments arranged by Northwind Analytics on behalf of its clients.

2. Eligible claim categories
Northwind will accept and process claims in the following categories:
(a) Physical damage to goods discovered at delivery and noted on the delivery receipt at the time of receipt ("visible damage").
(b) Shortage — units missing from a shipment relative to the bill of lading — when the shortage is noted on the delivery receipt at the time of receipt.
(c) Total loss of a shipment in transit, where the carrier confirms non-delivery.
(d) Temperature excursion for shipments moved under a temperature-controlled service level, where the data logger record shows the product exceeded its stated range for more than four (4) consecutive hours.

3. Categories not eligible
Northwind will not process claims for:
(a) Concealed damage discovered after the delivery receipt has been signed without notation.
(b) Damage to goods packaged by the shipper in packaging that fails Northwind's published packaging standard PS-11, as determined by the packaging engineering team.
(c) Delay alone, without associated physical loss or damage, except where a guaranteed-service refund applies under a separate service agreement.
(d) Claims submitted more than sixty (60) days after the delivery date.
(e) Shipments tendered under client-arranged transportation, where the client selected and paid the carrier directly.

4. Submission requirements
All claims must include: the delivery receipt with any notations; photographs of damage where applicable; the commercial invoice value of the affected goods; and, for temperature claims, the complete data logger export. Claims missing required documentation will be pended for up to twenty (20) business days and then closed if documentation is not received.

5. Valuation and limits
Claims are paid at invoice value of the affected goods, capped at $25,000 per shipment unless the client purchased declared-value coverage at tender. Salvage rights belong to Northwind once a claim is paid in full.

6. Return authorizations
Clients may request a return merchandise authorization (RMA) within thirty (30) days of delivery for unopened, saleable goods. Opened or temperature-sensitive goods are not returnable except where a paid damage claim applies. Return freight for client-convenience returns is at the client's expense; return freight for Northwind error is at Northwind's expense.

7. Examples (illustrative only)
Example A: A client reports dented cartons noted on the delivery receipt, submitted 12 days after delivery with photos and invoice — eligible under 2(a).
Example B: A client discovers crushed interior units three weeks after a clean-signed receipt — ineligible under 3(a), notwithstanding the photographs.
Example C: A temperature-controlled shipment whose logger shows a six-hour excursion above range — eligible under 2(d), subject to the logger export.
Example D: A shipment that arrived five days late with goods intact and no guaranteed service purchased — ineligible under 3(c).
Example E: A shortage of 40 units recorded by the consignee on the delivery receipt, claim filed at day 71 — ineligible under 3(d) despite meeting category 2(b).

8. Escalation
Disputes over claim determinations may be escalated to the Director of Supply Chain Operations within fifteen (15) days of the determination letter. The Director's decision is final for claims under $10,000; larger disputes follow the arbitration clause of the master services agreement.

9. Definitions
"Delivery receipt" means the document signed by the consignee at the point of delivery, including electronic proof-of-delivery records. "Clean-signed" means signed without damage or shortage notation. "Data logger" means the calibrated temperature recording device required on all temperature-controlled tenders.

Owner: Xiu Lindqvist, Director of Supply Chain Operations

1. Purpose
This policy governs the submission, evaluation, and resolution of freight claims and customer return authorizations for all shipments arranged by Northwind Analytics on behalf of its clients.

2. Eligible claim categories
Northwind will accept and process claims in the following categories:
(a) Physical damage to goods discovered at delivery and noted on the delivery receipt at the time of receipt ("visible damage").
(b) Shortage — units missing from a shipment relative to the bill of lading — when the shortage is noted on the delivery receipt at the time of receipt.
(c) Total loss of a shipment in transit, where the carrier confirms non-delivery.
(d) Temperature excursion for shipments moved under a temperature-controlled service level, where the data logger record shows the product exceeded its stated range for more than four (4) consecutive hours.

3. Categories not eligible
Northwind will not process claims for:
(a) Concealed damage discovered after the delivery receipt has been signed without notation.
(b) Damage to goods packaged by the shipper in packaging that fails Northwind's published packaging standard PS-11, as determined by the packaging engineering team.
(c) Delay alone, without associated physical loss or damage, except where a guaranteed-service refund applies under a separate service agreement.
(d) Claims submitted more than sixty (60) days after the delivery date.
(e) Shipments tendered under client-arranged transportation, where the client selected and paid the carrier directly.

4. Submission requirements
All claims must include: the delivery receipt with any notations; photographs of damage where applicable; the commercial invoice value of the affected goods; and, for temperature claims, the complete data logger export. Claims missing required documentation will be pended for up to twenty (20) business days and then closed if documentation is not received.

5. Valuation and limits
Claims are paid at invoice value of the affected goods, capped at $25,000 per shipment unless the client purchased declared-value coverage at tender. Salvage rights belong to Northwind once a claim is paid in full.

6. Return authorizations
Clients may request a return merchandise authorization (RMA) within thirty (30) days of delivery for unopened, saleable goods. Opened or temperature-sensitive goods are not returnable except where a paid damage claim applies. Return freight for client-convenience returns is at the client's expense; return freight for Northwind error is at Northwind's expense.

Disputes over claim determinations may be escalated to the Director of Supply Chain Operations within fifteen (15) days of the determination letter. The Director's decision is final for claims under $10,000; larger disputes follow the arbitration clause of the master services agreement.

INCIDENT POSTMORTEM — Quill Rentals, Regional Shuttle Network
Incident ID: QR-2024-118
Author: Priya Mensah, Network Reliability Lead
Report date: June 3, 2024

Summary
Between May 20 and May 24, 2024, on-time performance on the Quill Rentals regional shuttle network fell to 81%, triggering client escalations from three accounts. This postmortem covers the triggering event, the cascade, contributing factors, and remediation.

Triggering event
On May 20, the Port of Bellingham authority announced an unscheduled closure of Berth 6 for emergency crane repairs. Quill Rentals' cross-dock facility adjacent to Berth 6 handles roughly 40% of the network's inbound container volume. The closure forced diversion of inbound containers to the Port of Tacoma, adding an average of 11 hours of drayage and rail transfer time per container.

Cascade
May 20–21: Fourteen inbound containers were diverted. Cross-dock staffing had been scheduled against the normal Berth 6 arrival pattern; on May 21 the facility operated at approximately 55% utilization while Tacoma arrivals had not yet reached the network.
May 22: Diverted containers began arriving in a compressed window. The cross-dock experienced a 9-hour queue at receiving. Sixteen outbound shuttle departures left late; nine left on time.
May 23: To recover, management authorized rerouting four outbound shuttle runs to a direct line-haul path, bypassing the cross-dock. This recovered schedule for those four runs but stranded two trailer pools at the cross-dock, worsening May 24 departures for the east loop.
May 24: East loop departures ran at 60% on-time. West loop, unaffected by the trailer pool issue, ran at 97% on-time.

Contributing factors assessed
1. Berth closure (external): the initiating event, outside Quill Rentals' control. Force majeure notices were sent to affected clients on May 20, within the contractual 72-hour window.
2. Staffing model rigidity: schedules are fixed 72 hours in advance and could not be flexed to match the diverted arrival pattern. Assessed as the largest internal contributor.
3. Rerouting decision of May 23: recovered four runs but degraded the east loop on May 24. The postmortem review board assessed this decision as reasonable with the information available at the time, but notes that a trailer-pool impact check, which exists in the planning tool but was not run, would have flagged the east loop risk.
4. Communication gap: two of the three escalating clients received proactive notice; the third learned of delays from its consignee. The account team had an outdated escalation contact for that client.

What was not a cause
The review board explicitly considered and ruled out two hypothesized causes: (a) a reported ELD malfunction on vehicle QR-2210 on May 22 was investigated and found to be a display fault with no impact on hours-of-service compliance or routing; (b) a fuel-price surcharge dispute with one carrier partner, resolved May 15, predated the incident and played no role in the week's performance.

Remediation
1. Cross-dock staffing model to include a diversion scenario preset by July 15 (owner: workforce planning).
2. Trailer-pool impact check to be made a mandatory step in the rerouting workflow, enforced by the planning tool rather than by checklist (owner: systems).
3. Escalation contact list to be revalidated quarterly (owner: account management).
4. Diversion playbook for Berth 6 closures to be drafted jointly with the port authority liaison (owner: network operations).

Performance recovery
On-time performance for the week of May 27 recovered to 94%. The review board considers the incident closed as of June 3, 2024, with remediation items tracked separately.

Sign-off: Priya Mensah, Network Reliability Lead.

Between Harbor Foods ("Client") and Tidewater Analytics ("Provider"). Original agreement executed August 1, 2021. Excerpt prepared for negotiation review by Greta Fischer, Senior Counsel, Harbor Foods.

Section 4. Storage and Handling Rates (as amended)

4.1 Storage. Pallet storage shall be billed at $18.50 per pallet per month for ambient storage and $31.00 per pallet per month for refrigerated storage, prorated daily.

4.2 Handling. Inbound handling shall be billed at $6.25 per pallet; outbound handling at $7.75 per pallet, including pick and wrap.

4.3 Minimum Monthly Charge. Client shall incur a minimum monthly charge of $12,000 for storage and handling combined. Months in which actual charges fall below the minimum shall be billed at the minimum.

Amendment No. 1 (executed February 10, 2022)
Section 4.1 is amended: refrigerated storage shall be billed at $29.50 per pallet per month, replacing the $31.00 rate, in recognition of Client's commitment of a dedicated refrigerated zone of not fewer than 400 pallet positions. Should Client's refrigerated occupancy fall below 400 pallet positions for two consecutive months, the refrigerated rate reverts to $31.00 until occupancy again exceeds 400 positions for two consecutive months.

Amendment No. 2 (executed July 19, 2022)
Section 4.3 is amended: the minimum monthly charge shall be $14,500, replacing $12,000. In consideration, Provider grants Client priority dock scheduling between 05:00 and 09:00 on weekdays.

Amendment No. 3 (executed January 9, 2023)
The parties agree that outbound handling for promotional display pallets (defined as pallets requiring assembly of mixed-SKU display units) shall be billed at $11.90 per pallet, such pallets being excluded from the standard $7.75 outbound rate. All other handling rates are unchanged.

Amendment No. 4 (executed October 2, 2023)
Following a billing dispute, the parties agree that the minimum monthly charge of $14,500 shall be measured against storage and handling charges net of any promotional display pallet handling, which shall be billed in addition to and outside the minimum. This amendment is effective for billing periods beginning November 1, 2023 and is not retroactive.

Section 5. Rate Adjustments
Provider may adjust rates annually on the anniversary of the agreement by no more than the lesser of 4% or the change in the Consumer Price Index, upon sixty (60) days' written notice. No rate adjustment was implemented in August 2022 or August 2023. Provider delivered a notice of adjustment on May 20, 2024, proposing a 3.8% increase effective August 1, 2024.

- April 2024 billing: ambient storage 610 pallets; refrigerated storage 355 pallets; inbound handling 1,020 pallets; outbound standard handling 940 pallets; promotional display pallets 130.
- Refrigerated occupancy: February 2024: 420 positions; March 2024: 385 positions; April 2024: 355 positions.
- Provider's April invoice applied the $29.50 refrigerated rate. Counsel believes this may be incorrect under Amendment No. 1, given March and April occupancy, and has flagged it for the dispute letter.
- Provider's invoice also included promotional display handling within the charges measured against the monthly minimum; counsel believes Amendment No. 4 places it outside the minimum measurement.
- The May 20, 2024 rate-adjustment notice: counsel's view is that the 3.8% figure is within the contractual cap, but the effective date should be checked against the 60-day notice requirement; May 20 to August 1 is 73 days, so timing appears compliant.
- Open question for operations: whether the dedicated refrigerated zone commitment can be renegotiated, given that occupancy has trended downward since January.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE - March 1

Harbor Outfitters Partners with Kellerman Polar Studies Lab on 2025 Field Methods Grant

HARBOR CITY - Harbor Outfitters, the expedition gear cooperative, and the Kellerman Polar Studies Lab at Briskett University today opened the fifth annual Field Methods Grant program, which funds graduate researchers who need cold-weather field time more than they need another conference.

'We kept meeting students with solid science and no boots,' said program coordinator Greta Lindqvist. 'This program fixes the boots part, and a fair bit of the science part too.' Two grants of up to $18,000 will be awarded this cycle, same as last year.

Key dates for the 2025 cycle. Applications open thirty (30) days after the date of this announcement. The firm application deadline is April 15; the lab does not read late submissions, full stop. An applicant webinar runs March 20, with a recording posted after. The review panel convenes April 20 to begin scoring the pool. The letter-of-intent workshop is scheduled for April 27, which the lab admits is akward timing for applicants but the room was free. Award recipients will be announced May 12. Funding becomes available on the first day of the second calendar month following the award announcement, which gives the university payroll office time to set up accounts. The equipment depot open house, where winners get fitted for parkas and sleds, is April 18 and is mostly aimed at last years cohort anyway.

Funded teams join the August field school on the Greenland ice margin, August 3-14, travel covered seperately. Applicants must be enrolled graduate students at any accredited university; last years winners are barred from reapplying for one cycle. Letters of recomendation are optional but the panel admits they get read.

About Harbor Outfitters: a member-owned supplier of expedition kit since 1987, proud sponser of 31 field seasons. About the Kellerman Lab: a 14-person research group studying ice-margin hydrology, based at Briskett University.

Media contact: Greta Lindqvist, program coordinator. Posted to the lab news page March 1 at 09:00 local time.

PRESS RELEASE - June 25, 2024

Harbor Supply Completes Microscope Donation to Redding University Optics Lab

REDDING - Harbor Supply, the lab-equipment refurbisher, today marked the close of its donation of a refurbished fluorescence microscope to the Redding University optics teaching lab, capping a project that ran most of the spring semester and a fair bit of last winter too.

The instrument was purchased at auction on March 3, 2022 and sat in Harbor Supply's warehouse while the company sourced a replacement laser module. It was commisioned at Redding on June 10, 2022, the date printed on the acceptance certificate signed by both parties. Harbor Supply's standard warranty covers refubished instruments for 24 months from the commissioning date, not from the purchase date, a clause the company says suprises people every single time.

On June 8, 2024 the lab reported that the focus drive had failed mid-practical. 'Students were queued around the bench when it just stoped,' said lab director Wanjiru Petrov. 'Harbor Supply picked up on the first ring and had a tech out the next morning.' The repair is now complete and the instrument is back in the teaching rotation.

Project phases, per the joint project sheet: site preparation was scheduled to end Febuary 15 and actuallly finished Febuary 12. Installation was scheduled to end April 30 but finished May 6 after a freight elevator breakdown kept the crated instrument in the lobby for a week, which the facilities office would prefer we not mention. Calibration finished May 30. User training was scheduled to end June 20 and finished June 18, with two sessions to spare.

The donation agreement also includes a spare-parts kit, two years of discounted service visits after the warranty lapses, and a promise from the students to stop using the good slides for pratice. Harbor Supply says a second donation, to the chemistry department, is 'in discusion' with no dates set.

Contact: Wanjiru Petrov, lab director, Redding University optics lab. Photos avaliable on request.
